Anatomy and Physiology: Bile is a vital digestive fluid produced by the liver.
Major components of bile include cholesterol, bilirubin, biliverdin, and bile acids.
The biliary tree functions as a conduit that drains bile from the liver into the small intestine.
Bile first accumulates in small intrahepatic biliary radicles scattered throughout the liver parenchyma.
Intrahepatic biliary radicles are part of the portal triads.
Each portal triad contains a small branch of the hepatic artery, portal vein, and an intrahepatic duct or biliary radicle.
Bile flows from the small biliary radicles into either the right hepatic duct or left hepatic duct.
The right and left hepatic ducts unite to form the common hepatic duct.
Bile then travels a short distance to the gallbladder, where it is concentrated and stored.
The gallbladder is attached to the biliary tree by the cystic duct.
The point where the cystic duct attaches marks the proximal margin of the common bile duct.
The cystic duct contains spiral valves of Heister, which prevent the duct from collapsing or distending.
When stimulated by cholecystokinin produced by the duodenum, the gallbladder contracts and empties bile into the proximal common bile duct.
Bile travels through the common bile duct to the ampulla of Vater, where it meets the main pancreatic duct before passing through the sphincter of Oddi into the duodenum.
Sonography of the Bile Ducts: Patients should have nothing to eat or drink for at least 4 hours before a biliary sonogram, although 8 hours is optimal.
The entire biliary tree should be examined during sonographic evaluation.
The common bile duct may be differentiated from the common hepatic duct when seen posterior to the pancreatic head or inferior to the gallbladder neck.
Because delineation may be difficult, the portion of the biliary tree at the porta hepatis is often described as the common duct.
A common bile duct diameter greater than 6 mm is typically considered abnormal.
When ductal dilatation is identified, the entire right upper quadrant should be assessed, including the biliary tree, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas.
Clinical history is vital because duct size alone is only part of the overall patient assessment.
At the porta hepatis, the normal adult common duct anteroposterior diameter is cited as 1 to 7 mm by some authors.
In asymptomatic patients older than 60 years or after cholecystectomy, a maximum common duct diameter of 10 mm may be considered normal.
Intrahepatic ducts are considered dilated if they measure more than 2 mm.
At the porta hepatis, the common hepatic duct measures less than 6 mm and the common bile duct less than 8 mm.
Ducts should be measured from inner wall to inner wall.
The shotgun sign or parallel tube sign describes enlargement of the common duct to the size of the adjacent portal vein at the porta hepatis.
Color Doppler helps distinguish vascular structures from bile ducts, especially with the shotgun sign or double-duct sign.
Biliary Obstruction and Jaundice: Knowledge of bile flow from liver to duodenum is essential for determining the level of biliary obstruction.
The liver is the proximal portion of the biliary tree, whereas the common bile duct near the pancreatic head is the most distal segment.
As a general rule, biliary dilatation occurs proximal to the level of obstruction.
The common bile duct, cystic duct, and part of the common hepatic duct are extrahepatic.
All remaining portions of the biliary tree are considered intrahepatic.
The most common level of obstruction is the distal common bile duct.
In most cases, the extrahepatic ducts dilate first.
With distal common bile duct obstruction, eventual dilatation may involve the common bile duct, gallbladder, common hepatic duct, and intrahepatic ducts.
The most common causes of common bile duct obstruction are choledocholithiasis, chronic pancreatitis, acute pancreatitis, and pancreatic carcinoma.
Biliary obstruction eventually produces posthepatic, or obstructive, jaundice.
Jaundice results from bilirubin accumulation within body tissues, causing yellow discoloration of the skin and sclerae.
Excess bilirubin in the body leads to elevated serum bilirubin levels.
Although obstruction commonly causes jaundice, jaundice may also occur with hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver carcinoma, pancreatic carcinoma, and hemolytic disorders.
Infant jaundice is typically caused by the newborn liver's inability to eliminate bilirubin from the bloodstream and is often treated successfully with phototherapy.
Choledocholithiasis: Choledocholithiasis is the presence of gallstones within the bile ducts.
Biliary stasis increases the likelihood of gallstone formation.
Stones usually form in the gallbladder and then pass into the biliary tree.
Rarely, stones form primarily within the ducts themselves.
Gallstones in the common bile duct are the most common cause of obstructive jaundice.
Most ductal stones are located near the ampulla of Vater.
Stones near the ampulla may be difficult to visualize sonographically because of adjacent bowel gas shadowing.
Patients with recent cholecystectomy and biliary symptoms should be carefully evaluated for retained stones in the biliary tree.
Patients may be asymptomatic, and the biliary ducts may remain normal in caliber.
If obstruction occurs, findings may include jaundice, elevated bilirubin, elevated ALP, elevated ALT, and likely right upper quadrant pain.
Ductal stones usually appear as echogenic foci within the bile duct.
About 20% of ductal stones may not shadow sonographically.
Mirizzi syndrome is an uncommon manifestation caused by a stone lodged in the cystic duct that compresses the common duct.
Mirizzi syndrome presents with jaundice, pain, and fever and may be suspected on sonography but is typically diagnosed by cholangiography or ERCP.
Cholangitis: Cholangitis is inflammation of the biliary ducts.
If bile duct walls thicken more than 5 mm, some form of cholangitis should be suspected.
Any visible bile duct wall thickening should raise suspicion for cholangitis.
The most common cause is obstructive disease, such as choledocholithiasis.
Acute bacterial cholangitis may also be called ascending cholangitis.
Other forms include AIDS cholangitis, Oriental cholangitis, and sclerosing cholangitis.
Acute bacterial cholangitis is caused by bacterial accumulation secondary to obstruction.
Bacteria may be introduced during ERCP performed for choledocholithiasis.
Patients with acute bacterial cholangitis often present with Charcot triad: fever, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice.
Leukocytosis and elevated ALP and bilirubin may also be present, with elevated ALT and GGT noted with obstruction.
Pus may be seen within the bile ducts as low-level echoes.
All types have similar sonographic features, including biliary dilatation, biliary sludge or pus, and bile duct wall thickening.
Sclerosing cholangitis is characterized by fibrotic thickening of the bile ducts and most often affects young men.
Sclerosing cholangitis is associated with inflammatory bowel disease or ulcerative colitis and increases the risk for cholangiocarcinoma.
Pneumobilia: Pneumobilia is air within the biliary tree.
It may occur after recent biliary surgery or gastric surgery.
It may also be associated with emphysematous cholecystitis, prolonged acute cholecystitis, or fistula formation.
Patients may have symptoms related to acute cholecystitis.
Sonographically, pneumobilia appears as echogenic linear structures within the ducts.
Air in the ducts most often produces ring-down artifact.
Diffuse intrahepatic air may follow the branching pattern of the ducts and portal venous tree.
Air may be seen moving during real-time observation.
Pneumobilia can be difficult to differentiate from intrahepatic stones.
Air tends to be linear and causes ring-down and dirty shadowing.
Intrahepatic stones, if large enough, produce acoustic shadowing rather than dirty shadowing.
Ascariasis: Ascariasis is an infection of the small intestine caused by Ascaris lumbricoides, a parasitic roundworm.
Transmission occurs by the fecal-oral route.
The roundworm develops in the small intestine.
It may migrate to the biliary tree through the ampulla of Vater.
Patients may also have symptoms of inflammation involving the biliary tree, gallbladder, or pancreas.
On sonography, the worm appears as an echogenic linear structure within the biliary duct.
The linear echogenic worm is described in the sagittal plane.
Real-time demonstration of worm movement confirms the diagnosis.
Cholangiocarcinoma and Klatskin Tumors: Primary cancer of the biliary tree is called cholangiocarcinoma.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is the most common risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.
Recurrent biliary infections and stone disease also increase the risk.
Cholangiocarcinoma may be intrahepatic or extrahepatic, and both locations carry a poor prognosis.
Klatskin tumors are the most common manifestation of cholangiocarcinoma.
A Klatskin tumor is located at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts.
Klatskin tumors cause dilatation of the intrahepatic ducts.
Patients may present with jaundice, pruritus, unexplained weight loss, and abdominal pain.
Laboratory findings include elevated serum bilirubin and elevated ALP.
Sonographically, dilated intrahepatic ducts that abruptly terminate at the tumor level suggest cholangiocarcinoma.
A solid mass may occasionally be seen within the liver or within the ducts.
Cholangiocarcinoma is most often an adenocarcinoma.
Other biliary malignancies include squamous cell carcinoma and cystadenocarcinoma.
Biliary Atresia: Biliary atresia is a congenital disease described as narrowing or obliteration of all or part of the biliary tree.
It is thought to be caused by a viral infection at birth, although some consider it inherited.
The disease has a poor prognosis.
Without treatment, infants eventually develop cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
Neonatal jaundice is a typical clinical finding.
Laboratory findings include elevated AST, ALT, and bilirubin.
Clinical findings may be confused with neonatal hepatitis because both conditions can elevate AST, ALT, and bilirubin.
Unlike neonatal hepatitis, which may be treated medically, biliary atresia is often fatal without surgical intervention.
Sonographically, biliary atresia appears as absent ducts.
The gallbladder may be absent or small.
The triangular cord sign is an avascular, echogenic, triangular or tubular structure anterior to the portal vein, representing fibrous replacement of the extrahepatic duct.
The pseudogallbladder sign is a cystic structure in the gallbladder fossa without a true gallbladder.
If untreated, sonographic signs of cirrhosis and portal hypertension eventually develop.
A triangular echogenic anterior wall of the right portal vein measuring more than 4 mm on longitudinal scan is specific for biliary atresia.
Choledochal Cyst: There are four types of choledochal cysts.
The most common type is cystic dilatation of the common bile duct.
Choledochal cysts are usually discovered in infancy or during the first decade of life.
Patients may present with an abdominal mass.
Clinical findings also include jaundice, pain, and fever.
Choledochal cysts can lead to cholangitis.
They may also cause portal hypertension, pancreatitis, and liver failure.
On sonography, a choledochal cyst appears as a cystic mass in the region of the porta hepatis.
The cystic mass should be separate from the gallbladder.
A fusiform cystic mass in the porta hepatis is a characteristic sonographic appearance.
Biliary dilatation may also be present.
A choledochal cyst may be seen posterior to the head of the pancreas or posterior to the gallbladder.
Caroli Disease: Caroli disease, also called Caroli syndrome, is a congenital disorder.
It is characterized by segmental dilatation of the intrahepatic ducts.
The disorder is often associated with cystic renal disease.
Caroli disease may precede development of cholangiocarcinoma.
It may also precede hepatic abscess, cholangitis, and sepsis.
Patients may present with pain, fever, and jaundice.
Signs of portal hypertension may also be present.
Sonographically, the key finding is segmental dilatation of the intrahepatic ducts.
The central dot sign may be seen with Caroli disease.
The central dot sign consists of echogenic dots in the nondependent part of the dilated duct.
These echogenic dots represent small fibrovascular bundles.
Recognition of associated cystic renal disease may support the diagnosis.

Anatomy & Physiology: The gallbladder lies posterior to the right lobe of the liver within the gallbladder fossa and is considered an intraperitoneal organ.
Its position varies with patient position, but the main lobar fissure is a useful landmark for locating the gallbladder fossa sonographically.
The gallbladder is a pear-shaped sac that stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver.
The wall has three layers: inner mucosal layer with folds and rugae, middle fibromuscular layer, and outer serosal layer.
Anatomic parts include the neck, body, and fundus.
The neck is continuous with the cystic duct, which joins the common hepatic duct to connect the gallbladder to the biliary system.
The biliary segment distal to the union of the cystic duct and hepatic duct is the common bile duct.
The fundus is the most dependent portion of the gallbladder and the most common site for gallstones to collect.
Blood supply is via the cystic artery, typically a small branch of the right hepatic artery.
As chyme leaves the stomach, enteroendocrine cells of the duodenum release cholecystokinin.
Cholecystokinin causes gallbladder contraction, moving bile through the cystic duct into the common bile duct.
Knowledge of dependent versus nondependent portions is important because stones and sludge typically settle dependently in the lumen.
Variants & Anomalies: The most common gallbladder shape variant is the Phrygian cap, in which the fundus is folded onto itself.
A bilobed gallbladder has an hourglass appearance sonographically.
A septate gallbladder contains one or more thin separations within the lumen and may be called multiseptate.
A Hartmann pouch is an outpouching of the gallbladder neck.
A junctional fold is a prominent fold at the junction of the gallbladder neck.
Developmental and positional anomalies include interposition of the gallbladder, duplication, floating gallbladder, agenesis, hypoplasia, and intrahepatic gallbladder.
Interposition of the gallbladder is a rare anomaly where the main hepatic ducts drain into the gallbladder, and the gallbladder drains into the common bile duct.
Interposition may lead to childhood jaundice, gallbladder enlargement, and intermittent abdominal pain.
Duplication means two gallbladders are present, often but not always with their own cystic ducts.
A floating gallbladder is highly mobile and prone to torsion or volvulus.
Gallbladder torsion causes right upper quadrant pain and may show the whirlpool sign, a spiral appearance of the cystic artery on color Doppler.
The gallbladder may also be located on the left side, midline, or right lower quadrant.
An intrahepatic gallbladder is completely surrounded by hepatic parenchyma and can affect visualization.
Sonography of the Gallbladder: Gallbladder sonography should be performed after at least 4 hours of fasting, although 8 hours is optimal.
A normal gallbladder appears as an anechoic, pear-shaped structure in the sagittal plane.
A true transverse image of the normal gallbladder usually appears as an anechoic circle.
Scanning at the level of the main lobar fissure and right portal vein is often helpful for locating the gallbladder.
Normal size is variable, but typical ranges are 8 to 10 cm in length and no more than 4 to 5 cm in diameter.
A transverse measurement greater than 4 cm should prompt close scrutiny of the biliary tract for obstruction.
Gallbladder volume may be calculated using V = 0.523 × L × W × H.
The gallbladder normally holds about 40 mL of bile, with slight individual variation.
Evaluate the gallbladder in supine, left lateral decubitus, prone, upright, and other needed positions to assess mobility of intraluminal objects.
Intercostal sonographic imaging is useful when bowel gas limits midline visualization.
The neck and fundus should be examined closely because stones commonly lodge in the neck and accumulate in the dependent fundus.
The gallbladder wall should measure no more than 3 mm and may be focally or diffusely thickened in disease.
Common causes of nonvisualization include cholecystectomy, WES sign, postprandial state, chronic cholecystitis, ectopic location, agenesis, hepatization, and emphysematous cholecystitis.
Helpful labs include ALP, ALT, bilirubin, GGT, LDH, and WBC, with ALT, ALP, and bilirubin especially useful for gallbladder and bile duct disease.
Cholelithiasis (Gallstones): Gallstones are biliary stones that form within the gallbladder and are called cholelithiasis.
Gallstones typically consist of a mixture of cholesterol, calcium bilirubinate, and calcium carbonate.

Risk factors and predisposing conditions include obesity, pregnancy, increased parity, gestational diabetes, estrogen therapy, oral contraceptive use, rapid weight loss, hemolytic disorder, Crohn disease, and total parenteral nutrition.
Gallstones are more common in female patients and are classically associated with the six F's: fat, female, fertile, flatulent, fair, and forty.
Gallstones may occur in children, newborns, and even the fetus.
Pediatric patients with hemolytic anemia, such as sickle cell disease, and patients with Crohn disease have increased risk.
Patients may be asymptomatic, but mobile stones can cause biliary colic and other biliary complications.
Clinical findings include right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, and pain radiating to the shoulders.
Sonographically, gallstones appear as mobile echogenic structures within the gallbladder lumen that produce acoustic shadowing.
Stones lodged in the gallbladder neck or cystic duct may not move with position changes.
A gallbladder completely filled with stones may demonstrate the wall-echo-shadow, or WES, sign.
The spiral valves of Heister within the cystic duct can mimic small stones by producing posterior shadowing; changing position and scanning plane helps.
Small adhered stones may not cast a well-defined shadow and can mimic polyps.
Twinkle artifact on color Doppler can help identify a small stone or distinguish an adhered stone from a gallbladder polyp.
Biliary Spectrum: Simple cholelithiasis refers to gallstones located in the gallbladder without causing obstruction.
Biliary colic is pain located in the right upper quadrant in the area of the gallbladder.
Biliary colic may occur after a fatty meal when gallbladder contraction pushes bile and stones toward the cystic duct.
Spasm and swelling of the bile duct cause irritation and waves of pain during biliary colic.
If the stone returns to the gallbladder lumen, the pain of biliary colic may subside.
Cholecystitis occurs when a stone causes sustained obstruction of the cystic duct, producing acute gallbladder wall inflammation.
Choledocholithiasis is the presence of one or more gallstones within the biliary tree or bile ducts.
Cholangitis is inflammation of the bile ducts and can occur when gallstones become lodged in the ampulla of Vater.
This spectrum reflects progression from nonobstructing gallstones to cystic duct obstruction, bile duct stones, and bile duct inflammation.
When gallbladder disease is identified, the liver, remaining biliary tree, and pancreas should be evaluated for obstruction and pancreatitis.
Sludge: Gallbladder sludge, or viscid bile, is most often associated with biliary stasis.
Sludge may be seen with coexisting gallstones or gallbladder carcinoma and in patients with jaundice, liver disease, hyperalimentation, or sepsis.
Extended fasting and total parenteral nutrition are additional settings associated with sludge formation.
Sonographically, sludge appears as low-level, nonshadowing, dependent echoes within the gallbladder lumen.
When sludge is present, the gallbladder should be carefully assessed for small stones and other sonographic signs of cholecystitis.
Tumefactive sludge is thick sludge that can mimic an intraluminal gallbladder mass.
Mobility of tumefactive sludge should be observed closely with patient repositioning.
If presumed sludge does not move, a solid gallbladder mass should be considered and color Doppler used to assess for vascularity.
Tumefactive sludge may form sludge balls, which are usually mobile and nonshadowing.
When the gallbladder becomes completely filled with tumefactive sludge, it may appear isoechoic to the liver.
This is called hepatization of the gallbladder and is a recognized cause of gallbladder nonvisualization.
Polyps, Cholesterolosis & Adenomyomatosi: A gallbladder polyp is a projection of tissue from the wall that protrudes into the gallbladder lumen.
Cholesterol polyps are the most common gallbladder polyps.
Cholesterol polyps are usually small, measure less than 10 mm, and result from accumulation of cholesterol and triglycerides within the gallbladder wall.
Polyps may be solitary or multiple and are most often benign and incidentally discovered.
Sonographically, polyps appear as hyperechoic, nonshadowing, nonmobile projections arising from the gallbladder wall.
Although many polyps have a stalk, it may not be visible; they often show the ball-on-the-wall sign.
Changing patient position helps confirm a polyp because it will neither move nor shadow.
A rapidly growing polyp or a large polyp is worrisome for gallbladder carcinoma.
Cholesterolosis results from disturbed cholesterol metabolism with cholesterol accumulation, typically in a focal region of the gallbladder wall.
Cholesterolosis is a subset of hyperplastic cholecystosis and may produce a diffuse polypoid strawberry gallbladder, recognized pathologically rather than distinctly on imaging.
Adenomyomatosis is another form of hyperplastic cholecystosis and is clinically silent and usually insignificant.
In adenomyomatosis, the luminal epithelium is hyperplastic and the muscular layer thickens, forming Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses.
These sinuses may contain cholesterol crystals that produce comet-tail artifact, often projecting into the lumen from the anterior wall.
Acute Cholecystitis: Acute cholecystitis is the sudden onset of gallbladder inflammation.
The most common cause is a gallstone lodged in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck.
Patients often present with right upper quadrant tenderness and epigastric or abdominal pain.
Pain may radiate to the shoulders and is commonly associated with nausea, vomiting, and fever.
Leukocytosis is often present in acute cholecystitis.
Laboratory findings may include elevated ALP and ALT, with bilirubin elevated if ductal obstruction occurs.
If the bile ducts are obstructed, posthepatic jaundice may also be present.
A positive sonographic Murphy sign is focal tenderness directly over the gallbladder with transducer pressure.
The combination of gallstones and a positive sonographic Murphy sign is a strong indicator of acute cholecystitis.
Sonographic findings include gallstones, sludge, gallbladder wall thickening, gallbladder enlargement, and pericholecystic fluid.
The thickened wall may contain pockets of edematous fluid, producing a striated appearance.
When acute cholecystitis is suspected, evaluate for progression to gangrenous cholecystitis, perforation, and other sequelae.
Complicated Cholecystitis: Gangrenous cholecystitis may evolve directly from acute cholecystitis.
In addition to acute cholecystitis findings, gangrenous cholecystitis may show focal wall necrosis, gallbladder wall bulges, sloughed membranes, and ulcerative craters.
Gallbladder perforation or rupture has high morbidity and mortality because of associated peritonitis.
Sonography may demonstrate a distinct gallbladder wall tear and an irregularly shaped gallbladder in perforation.
In gangrenous cholecystitis and perforation, the sonographic Murphy sign may be absent.
Pericholecystic fluid and sludge may accompany gangrenous change and perforation.
Empyema, also called suppurative cholecystitis, refers to pus filling the gallbladder.
Pus appears as echogenic material within the gallbladder lumen and possibly within the ducts, and biliary obstruction may also be present.
Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis is a rare chronic infection characterized by intramural accumulation of inflammatory cells.
Sonographically, xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis shows asymmetrical gallbladder wall thickening and intraluminal echogenic debris.
Echogenic pericholecystic fat may also be seen with xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis.
Emphysematous cholecystitis is a form of acute cholecystitis caused by gas-forming infection, most often discovered in diabetic patients.
Gas in the wall or lumen causes dirty shadowing, reverberation, or ring-down artifact, and gas in the nondependent wall creates the champagne sign.
Chronic cholecystitis follows intermittent cystic duct obstruction by stones, causing repeated attacks, a nontender gallbladder, wall thickening, possible WES sign, and intolerance to fatty foods.
Acalculous cholecystitis has the clinical and sonographic findings of cholecystitis without gallstones and is more common in children, recently hospitalized, and immunocompromised patients.
Hydrops, Courvoisier & Porcelain GB: The normal gallbladder should not exceed 4 to 5 cm in width or 8 to 10 cm in length.
The transverse measurement is most indicative of gallbladder enlargement, and a width greater than 4 cm warrants careful assessment for obstruction.
Gallbladder enlargement may result from blockage of the cystic duct or other portions of the biliary tree.
An enlarged gallbladder may be called a hydropic gallbladder or mucocele of the gallbladder.
Patients with a hydropic gallbladder may be asymptomatic or have epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting.
An enlarged gallbladder is often palpable on physical examination.
Courvoisier gallbladder refers to clinical detection of an enlarged, palpable gallbladder caused by a pancreatic head mass.
Patients with Courvoisier gallbladder typically also have painless jaundice.
Gallbladder hydrops in older infants and children may be associated with Kawasaki disease.
Porcelain gallbladder results from calcification of all or part of the gallbladder wall and is classically clinically silent.
Sonographically, porcelain gallbladder appears as an echogenic curvilinear structure in the gallbladder fossa with shadowing.
Porcelain gallbladder can resemble WES sign or the air seen with emphysematous cholecystitis, so clinical findings are important.
Identification of a calcified posterior gallbladder wall helps distinguish porcelain gallbladder from WES sign, where the posterior wall is usually obscured.
Gallstones and chronic inflammation are linked with porcelain gallbladder, and radiography or CT is often used to confirm the diagnosis.
Gallbladder Carcinoma: Gallbladder carcinoma is rare but is the most common cancer of the biliary tract.
It is thought to result from chronic irritation of the gallbladder wall by gallstones.
Gallbladder carcinoma is almost always associated with gallstones, and the mass itself may contain stones.
There appears to be increased risk in patients with chronic cholecystitis.
Patients may be asymptomatic at detection or may present with nausea, vomiting, unexplained weight loss, right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, or hepatomegaly.
Laboratory abnormalities may include elevated ALP, ALT, GGT, and bilirubin when obstruction is present.
Sonographically, carcinoma may appear as a distinct nonmobile hypoechoic mass within the gallbladder lumen.
It may also appear as diffuse gallbladder wall thickening or as an irregular polypoid mass.
A carcinoma may completely fill the gallbladder fossa and may invade adjacent liver tissue by the time of diagnosis.
Any mass seen within the gallbladder lumen should be measured carefully.
Gallbladder carcinoma is suspected if a polyp or mass measures greater than 1 cm.
When tumefactive sludge is a consideration, color Doppler may show vessels within the malignancy.
The most common metastatic disease involving the gallbladder is malignant melanoma.
It is difficult to differentiate metastatic disease from primary gallbladder cancer sonographically.

Sonographic Descriptive Terms: Anechoic means without echoes and appears black on the image; examples in the chapter include the gallbladder and a simple renal cyst.
Hyperechoic means having many echoes and appearing brighter than surrounding tissue; examples include cavernous hemangioma and angiomyolipoma.
Hypoechoic means having few echoes and appearing darker than surrounding tissue; examples include hepatic adenoma and thyroid adenoma.
Isoechoic means having the same echogenicity as surrounding tissue; focal nodular hyperplasia is listed as an example.
Echogenic is a comparative term describing a structure that produces echoes; examples include fatty liver and chronic renal disease.
Homogeneous describes tissue of uniform composition; normal liver and normal testicle are listed examples.
Heterogeneous describes tissue of differing composition; examples include Graves disease and diffuse liver metastasis.
Complex describes a lesion having both cystic and solid components; examples include a hemorrhagic cyst and hepatic abscess.
Pathology is often described relative to adjacent tissue, such as a hepatic mass being hyperechoic compared with normal liver.
Solid tumors may be described as hyperechoic, hypoechoic, homogeneous, heterogeneous, complex, isoechoic, cystic, or a combination.
A renal mass may be described as hypoechoic with a central area of increased echogenicity, illustrating combined descriptors.
Understanding descriptive terms and normal organ echogenicity is essential for recognizing abnormal sonographic findings.
Echogenicity of Abdominal Organs: Normal abdominal organ echogenicity should be recognized before identifying pathology.
The normal order from greatest echogenicity to least is renal sinus, pancreas, spleen, liver, renal cortex, renal pyramids, then gallbladder.
The renal sinus is the brightest normal abdominal structure listed in this sequence.
The pancreas is normally slightly less echogenic than the renal sinus and more echogenic than the spleen.
The spleen is normally more echogenic than the liver.
The liver is normally less echogenic than the spleen and more echogenic than the renal cortex.
The renal cortex should normally appear less echogenic than the liver.
Renal pyramids are darker than the renal cortex in the normal echogenicity sequence.
The gallbladder is the darkest structure in this list because it is normally anechoic.
If the right kidney appears more echogenic than the liver, both the liver and right kidney should be examined closely for the cause.
Abnormal echogenic relationships should prompt correlation with surrounding tissue and the patient’s clinical findings.
Simple Cyst Criteria (STAR): A cyst must meet specific sonographic criteria to be called a simple cyst.
STAR criteria for a simple cyst are Smooth walls, Through transmission, Anechoic contents, and Round shape.
Smooth walls or borders are required for a simple cyst designation.
Through transmission means posterior acoustic enhancement deep to the cyst.
A simple cyst should be completely anechoic sonographically.
Round shape is part of the STAR criteria for a simple cyst.
Other common simple cyst features include a clearly defined posterior wall.
Reverberation artifact may be seen with a simple cyst.
Edge shadowing is another common feature arising from a simple cyst.
With higher-frequency transducers and superior resolution, a very small amount of internal debris may occasionally be seen in a simple cyst.
Large amounts of internal debris, septations, mural nodules, or a fluid-fluid level indicate a complex cyst.
Cysts may also be described as unilocular or multiloculated.
Complex or complicated cysts may require close follow-up or further analysis with another imaging modality.
Patient Preparation: Patients undergoing an abdominal sonogram, particularly those who still have a gallbladder, should fast for 8 hours.
Some authors suggest that a 6-hour fast may be sufficient for abdominal sonography.
Emergency or nonfasting patients can still have diagnostically useful abdominal sonograms.
Fasting helps ensure that the gallbladder is fully distended.
Fasting may also reduce upper abdominal gas that could inhibit diagnostic accuracy.
For renal sonograms, fasting is not typically required.
Some facilities recommend that renal sonography patients be well hydrated, especially when the bladder must be evaluated.
A filled bladder can aid assessment for intraluminal masses, wall irregularities, or urinary stones.
Small parts sonography, including scrotal and thyroid imaging, does not require patient preparation.
Diabetic patients who must fast should be scheduled early in the morning to reduce risk of hypoglycemia.
Abdominal sonography should be performed before radiographic examinations that use barium contrast agents.
For pediatric patients needing renal sonography and a voiding cystourethrogram, the renal sonogram is typically performed first.
Clinical History & Key Labs: Before patient contact, the sonographer should review prior examinations and relevant documents.
The sonographic imaging process should be clearly explained to the patient before the examination begins.
A thorough clinical history should be obtained before each examination.
Clinical history review includes prior sonograms, CT, MRI, nuclear medicine, radiography, endoscopy, and related laboratory or diagnostic reports.
Correlating clinical findings with sonographic findings helps provide the most targeted examination possible.
Sonographers must analyze patient complaints and determine which information is clinically applicable.
Laboratory results are often electronically available for inpatients and emergency patients.
Leukocytosis means an elevated white blood cell count and generally indicates an inflammatory response from infection.
Patients with an “-itis,” such as cholecystitis or pancreatitis, or those with an abscess, will most likely have an abnormal WBC count with infection.
A decreased hematocrit can indicate bleeding.
Patients with recent trauma or active hemorrhage will most likely have a decreased hematocrit level.
Alanine aminotransferase may increase with biliary tree, pancreatic, or hepatic disease.
Amylase and lipase may increase with pancreatic disorders, gallbladder disease, or biliary/pancreatic obstruction.
BUN and creatinine may increase with renal disease, renal obstruction, renal damage, or renal infection.
Basic Patient Care: Sonographers must provide basic patient care equitably and in a timely manner for every patient.
They should be prepared to respond appropriately to emergency situations.
Basic patient assessment may include temperature, pulse, respiration, and blood pressure when needed.
Normal adult pulse is 60 to 100 beats per minute.
Normal adult blood pressure is less than 120/80 mm Hg.
Normal adult respiration is 12 to 20 breaths per minute.
Patients should be transferred safely from wheelchairs or stretchers to the examination stretcher.
During transfers, the sonographer must remain mindful of intravenous therapy, postsurgical needs, and urinary catheters.
For patients receiving intravenous therapy, the IV fluid bag should remain elevated to prevent retrograde flow.
For urinary catheter care, the urine bag should be kept below bladder level to prevent retrograde urine flow.
Retrograde urine flow can result in a urinary tract infection.
Urinary tract infection is one of the most common nosocomial, or hospital-acquired, infections.
Infection Control: Sonographers should continually use standard precautions and good hygiene to prevent spread of infection.
Standard precautions are designed to reduce microorganism transmission in the clinical setting.

Standard precautions include hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, safe injection practices, sharps safety, respiratory hygiene and coughing etiquette, sterile instruments and devices, and clean disinfected environmental surfaces.
These precautions apply to blood, nonintact skin, mucous membranes, contaminated equipment, and all body fluids except sweat.
Standard precautions are often supplemented with transmission-based precautions such as contact, droplet, or airborne precautions.
Proper hand hygiene is one of the most effective methods for preventing infection spread.
The CDC recommends an alcohol-based hand rub as the primary mode of hand hygiene in the clinical setting.
Traditional hand washing should also be used, especially when hands are visibly soiled.
Personal protective equipment may include gloves, gowns, face shields, and masks when clinically applicable.
Gloves should be worn during sonographic examinations and changed between patients.
The sonographer should be mindful of latex allergies and use synthetic alternatives when needed.
Probe covers should be used for endocavity examinations, and invasive procedures require sterile covers with sterile gel.
After each exam, the transducer, ultrasound machine, stretcher, and any used equipment should be thoroughly disinfected.
Invasive & Sterile Procedures: Patient preparation for invasive procedures varies by facility, but informed consent and laboratory results are universally obtained.
Laboratory evaluation includes prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, international normalizing ratio, fibrinogen, and platelets.
These laboratory tests help evaluate the patient for coagulopathies before the procedure.
Sterile field preparation is performed prior to the procedure.
Sterile asepsis, also called surgical asepsis, must be maintained during invasive procedures.
Surgical asepsis is always practiced in the surgical suite.
Common sonography-guided invasive procedures include thoracentesis, paracentesis, organ biopsy, mass biopsy, and abscess drainage.
Biopsies may be performed freehand or under ultrasound guidance using a needle guide attached to the transducer.
Fine needle aspiration uses a thin needle and syringe to obtain material for analysis.
Core biopsy uses a larger diameter needle to obtain a substantial tissue sample.
A thyroid biopsy is an example of fine needle aspiration.
A liver biopsy is an example of a core biopsy.
If the sterility of an item is questionable, it should be considered nonsterile.
Instrumentation: Sonographic images are typically recorded and stored in a picture-archiving and communication system, or PACS.
PACS allows easy storage, comparison of sonographic findings, and correlation with other imaging modalities.
General abdominal imaging requires a transducer that balances penetration with high-quality resolution.
Higher frequency provides better resolution but poorer penetration.
Lower frequency provides better penetration but less resolution.
Transducers used in abdominal and small parts imaging may include linear array, matrix array, curved or convex array, phased array, and vector or sector array.
Higher-frequency linear array transducers, about 7.5 to 18 MHz or higher when appropriate, are used for superficial structures.
Superficial applications listed include thyroid, scrotum, breast, musculoskeletal imaging, appendix, and pylorus.
A standoff pad or mound of gel may improve imaging of very superficial structures such as splinters, superficial masses, or foreign bodies.
Lower-frequency curved array transducers, about 2.0 to 5.0 MHz, are used for general abdominal imaging.
General abdominal applications listed include deeper or larger structures such as the liver, abdominal aorta, and pancreas.
When applicable, sonographers should use power Doppler, color Doppler, pulsed Doppler, harmonics imaging, compound imaging, extended-field of view, elastography, and 3D sonography.
Sonographic protocols must remain malleable and case specific.
Imaging Artifacts: Gray-scale B-mode imaging provides real-time two-dimensional anatomy and motion during abdominal sonography.
Artifacts are commonly encountered during real-time imaging and must be recognized accurately.
Harmonic imaging can reduce reverberation and side lobe artifacts.
Compound imaging may reduce speckle and clutter.
Simply changing transducer position or angle of insonation can eliminate some artifacts.
Anisotropy occurs when the beam strikes a structure nonperpendicularly, causing loss of true echogenicity; tendons are a classic example.
Comet-tail artifact is caused by several small highly reflective interfaces and is seen with adenomyomatosis of the gallbladder.
Dirty shadowing is caused by air or bowel gas and is often seen posterior to bowel or gas within an abscess.
Shadowing from stones or bone is due to attenuation and appears as clean shadowing, such as behind gallstones or renal stones.
Edge shadowing, also called refractive shadowing, is seen deep to margins of round structures with a significantly different speed of sound than surrounding tissue.
Mirror image artifact is produced by a strong specular reflector and places a duplicate structure deeper than its true location, often posterior to the liver and diaphragm.
Posterior acoustic enhancement occurs when sound is barely attenuated through fluid and is seen behind gallbladder, renal cysts, pleural effusions, and ascites.
Refraction results from bending of the beam at interfaces with dissimilar sound speeds when the approach is not perpendicular.
Reverberation creates false echoes from a large acoustic interface, ring-down emanates from gas bubbles, and side lobe or slice thickness artifacts can mimic debris within fluid.
Doppler Artifacts: Doppler artifacts may occur during pulsed, color, or power Doppler evaluation.
Absent Doppler signal may result from low gain, low frequency, high wall filter, or excessively high velocity scale.
To correct absent Doppler signal, decrease PRF, increase spectral gain, decrease the wall filter, or open the sample gate.
Aliasing occurs when the Doppler sampling rate, or pulse-repetition frequency, is too low to display the Doppler frequency shift accurately.
Aliasing can be corrected by increasing PRF, adjusting the baseline, switching to a lower transmitted frequency, or increasing the angle of insonation to decrease Doppler shift.
Pulsed Doppler aliasing and color Doppler aliasing are both caused by inadequate sampling for the detected velocity.
Doppler noise is caused by inappropriately high Doppler settings.
Doppler noise can be reduced by lowering color gain or adjusting the wall filter.
Flow directional abnormalities may occur when the sound beam strikes a vessel at 90 degrees, creating an area void of color.
Changing the angle of insonation helps correct flow directional abnormalities.
Twinkle artifact occurs behind strong, granular, irregular surfaces such as crystals, calculi, or calcifications.
Twinkle artifact is useful for identifying small kidney or biliary stones.
Mirror image can also be seen in Doppler modes as well as gray-scale imaging.
Body Systems & Peritoneum: Body systems work together to preserve homeostasis, the body’s tendency to maintain internal equilibrium by adjusting physiologic processes.
Relevant body systems for abdominal sonography include cardiovascular, digestive, endocrine, exocrine, lymphatic, musculoskeletal, nervous, reproductive, respiratory, and urinary systems.
The cardiovascular system has pulmonary and systemic circulations; blood returns to the right atrium via the superior vena cava and IVC.
An enlarged IVC on abdominal sonography may indicate right-sided heart failure.
Pericardial effusion and pleural effusion may be seen during abdominal sonography even though the heart is not specifically imaged.
Endocrine glands release hormones directly into the bloodstream, whereas exocrine glands secrete through ducts.
The pancreas and testicles have both endocrine and exocrine functions.
Lymph nodes filter lymphatic fluid, and enlarged nodes may be called lymphadenopathy.
The spleen is the largest mass of lymphatic tissue.
The urinary tract includes kidneys and ureters superiorly, with bladder and urethra as the lower tract.
The peritoneum is the double lining of the abdominal cavity and consists of parietal and visceral layers.

Intraperitoneal organs listed include gallbladder, liver except bare area, ovaries, spleen except hilum, stomach, appendix, transverse colon, first part of duodenum, jejunum, ileum, and sigmoid colon.

Retroperitoneal organs listed include abdominal lymph nodes, adrenal glands, aorta, ascending and descending colon, most of duodenum, IVC, kidneys, pancreas, prostate, ureters, urinary bladder, and uterus.

Ascites may collect in peritoneal spaces such as Morison pouch, lesser sac, paracolic gutters, cul-de-sacs, and retropubic space; benign transudate is typically simple anechoic, whereas exudate may be complex and loculated.
Abdominal Pathology Overview: A mass, neoplasm, or tumor may be benign, potentially malignant, or malignant.
Malignant tumors invade adjacent tissue and have the potential to metastasize through the bloodstream or lymphatic system.
Benign tumors typically do not invade neighboring tissue and do not metastasize.
Some benign tumors may still have the potential to progress to cancer.
Tumors may cause mass effect, meaning displacement or alteration of adjacent normal anatomy, which can create symptoms such as pain.
Cancer staging reflects progression and may involve tumor size, invasion, lymph node involvement, metastasis, and histologic assessment.
Common benign abdominal tumors listed include adenoma, angiomyolipoma, focal nodular hyperplasia, hemangioma, hematoma, insulinoma, lipoma, oncocytoma, pheochromocytoma, teratoma, and urinoma.

Common malignant abdominal tumors listed include adenocarcinoma, angiosarcoma, cholangiocarcinoma, cystadenocarcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma, lymphoma, seminoma, transitional cell carcinoma, and others.
Pediatric malignant abdominal tumors commonly include hepatoblastoma in the liver, nephroblastoma in the kidney, and neuroblastoma in the adrenal gland.
The word part “blast” often refers to a childhood malignancy.
A sign is objective and observable by others, such as fever, vomiting, or elevated laboratory tests.
A symptom is subjective and felt by the patient, such as nausea, headache, or abdominal pain.
Cancer may present with vague clinical findings including unexplained weight loss, fever, fatigue, pain, and skin changes.
Tumor markers relevant to abdominal imaging include alpha-fetoprotein, BTA, BRCA1/2, CA-15-3, CA-19-9, CA-125, calcitonin, carcinoembryonic antigen, beta-hCG, LDH, and PSA.
FAST Exam: Focused assessment with sonography for trauma, or FAST, is a point-of-care sonographic examination used in emergency patients.
FAST evaluates the abdomen and pelvis for free fluid after traumatic injury.
Posttraumatic free fluid may indicate internal hemorrhage.
Extended FAST, or eFAST, additionally evaluates the lungs for pneumothorax and the heart for pericardial effusion.
If appropriately trained, the examination may be performed by physicians, physician extenders, emergency medical personnel, and sonographers.
Views may include the right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant, pelvis, and pericardium.
Additional eFAST views may include the anterior thorax, right and left pericolic gutters, pleural spaces, parasternal region, and apex of the heart.
As with any abdomen or chest assessment, the exam should be performed in at least two orthogonal planes.
Representative images should be obtained for documentation.
AIUM has established guidelines for FAST examination.
The portability, safety, and effectiveness of sonography support its use in trauma assessment.

Anatomy & Physiology: The pancreas is a comma-shaped organ formed embryologically from two separate parts that eventually fuse together.
It lies in the epigastrium between the C-loop of the duodenum and the splenic hilum.
The pancreas consists of four main parts: head, neck, body, and tail.
The uncinate process is a posteromedial extension of the pancreatic head present in some individuals.
Although part of the head may be covered by peritoneum, the pancreas is a retroperitoneal organ.
The pancreas functions as both an exocrine gland and an endocrine gland.
Its exocrine role primarily aids digestion through enzyme production and ductal delivery to the duodenum.
Its endocrine role involves hormone release directly into the bloodstream from the islets of Langerhans.
The duodenum is the first segment of the small intestine and closely relates to the pancreatic head.
Detailed clinical findings are important because many pancreatic abnormalities can appear sonographically similar.
Exocrine & Endocrine Function: Acinar cells perform the exocrine function of the pancreas.
Exocrine secretions include amylase, lipase, sodium bicarbonate, trypsin, chymotrypsin, and carboxypolypeptidase.
Amylase digests carbohydrates and converts starch to sugar.
Lipase digests fats and converts fats to fatty acids and glycerol.
Trypsin, chymotrypsin, and carboxypolypeptidase break down proteins.
These enzymes drain into the main pancreatic duct, the duct of Wirsung, which travels the length of the pancreas.
The accessory duct, the duct of Santorini, is typically a branch of the main duct and empties through a separate minor sphincter.
The minor sphincter rests on the minor duodenal papilla, also called the accessory papilla.
From the main duct, enzymes collect in the ampulla of Vater, or hepatopancreatic ampulla, where they mix with bile.
The sphincter of Oddi releases bile and pancreatic enzymes into the duodenum when stimulated by cholecystokinin.
The endocrine function is performed by the islets of Langerhans, composed of alpha, beta, and delta cells.
Alpha cells produce glucagon, which promotes hepatic glucose release and raises blood sugar.
Beta cells produce insulin, and delta cells produce somatostatin, which restrains insulin and glucose level.
Vascular Anatomy: The arterial blood supply to the pancreatic head is via the gastroduodenal artery.
The body and tail receive arterial supply from the splenic artery and superior mesenteric artery.
Venous drainage occurs through the splenic vein, superior mesenteric vein, inferior mesenteric vein, and portal vein.
The pancreatic head lies right lateral to the superior mesenteric vein.
The pancreatic head is anterior to the inferior vena cava and inferior to the portal vein.
The uncinate process lies posterior to the superior mesenteric vein and may completely surround it.
The uncinate process is also anterior to the aorta.
The pancreatic neck lies anterior to the portal confluence.
The pancreatic body lies anterior to the superior mesenteric vein, splenic vein, and superior mesenteric artery.
The splenic vein marks the posterior border of the pancreatic tail.
Knowledge of adjacent vasculature is essential for locating the pancreas sonographically.
In the transverse pancreatic head, the gastroduodenal artery is anterior and the common bile duct is posterior.
Sonography of the Pancreas: The pancreas is rarely imaged without including the complete right upper quadrant examination.
A thorough sonographic evaluation generally includes the bile ducts and gallbladder for associated abnormalities.
Common obstacles to pancreatic imaging are adjacent bowel gas and patient body habitus.
To improve visualization of the pancreatic head, the patient may drink a small cup of water if protocol allows.
Water in the stomach and duodenal C-loop may enhance visualization of the pancreatic head.
Left lateral decubitus positioning may also improve pancreatic head visualization.
To better visualize the tail, scan through the left kidney and spleen with the patient in right lateral decubitus position.
Upright scanning can be exceedingly helpful for pancreatic imaging.
The adult pancreas is normally more echogenic than the liver and equal to or more echogenic than the spleen.
Some adults have a diffusely hyperechoic pancreas from pancreatic steatosis.
The pediatric pancreas may appear more hypoechoic because younger patients lack surrounding fat.
In transverse imaging, two round anechoic structures in the head are the anterior gastroduodenal artery and posterior common bile duct.
The main pancreatic duct appears as an anechoic tube with parallel walls and should not exceed 2 mm AP.
Color Doppler helps distinguish the splenic artery from the main pancreatic duct because they may run parallel in the body.
Pancreatic AP measurements are usually obtained in the transverse plane: head and body 2 to 3 cm, tail 1 to 2 cm.
Clinical history should always be considered when pancreatic enlargement is suspected.
Congenital Anomalies: The two most common congenital pancreatic anomalies are pancreatic divisum and annular pancreas.
Pancreatic divisum is the most common congenital variant of pancreatic anatomy.
Pancreatic divisum results from abnormal fusion of the pancreatic ducts during embryologic development.
In pancreatic divisum, the main pancreatic duct is shortened and drains only the pancreatic head.
The accessory duct must drain the rest of the pancreas through the minor sphincter.
This abnormal duct arrangement creates a functional obstruction and impairs proper pancreatic drainage.
Patients with pancreatic divisum may be asymptomatic but are at increased risk for both acute and chronic pancreatitis.
Annular pancreas results from maldevelopment of the two embryologic elements of the pancreas.
With annular pancreas, the most ventral part of the pancreas encases the duodenum.
Annular pancreas may lead to duodenal obstruction.
Neither pancreatic divisum nor annular pancreas is definitively diagnosed sonographically.
Definitive diagnosis typically relies on CT, MRI, and possibly radiography.
Acute Pancreatitis: Acute pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas caused by leakage of pancreatic enzymes from acinar cells into the pancreatic parenchyma.
These leaked enzymes can destroy pancreatic tissue and surrounding tissues.
The most common causes are alcohol abuse and biliary tract disease such as choledocholithiasis.
Other causes include post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and trauma.
Acute pancreatitis is commonly categorized as interstitial edematous pancreatitis or necrotizing pancreatitis.
Interstitial edematous pancreatitis is more common and involves inflammation without necrosis.
Necrotizing pancreatitis is severe and may be fatal; hemorrhagic pancreatitis is also associated with high morbidity and mortality.
Clinical findings include abdominal pain, back pain, hyperglycemia, leukocytosis, and elevated serum amylase and lipase.
Amylase rises first, and within 72 hours lipase should also rise; lipase is more specific for pancreatitis.
ALT is typically elevated in gallstone pancreatitis.
Pain is often worst when supine and may be temporarily relieved by sitting or leaning forward.
Severe cases may lead to shock, ileus, and decreased hematocrit secondary to hemorrhage.
Sonography may be normal, especially with mild acute pancreatitis.
Focal pancreatitis causes segmental enlargement, most often in the head, and appears as a hypoechoic region.
Diffuse acute pancreatitis usually causes a diffusely enlarged, hypoechoic gland with ill-defined margins.
Unencapsulated peripancreatic fluid may be present and is referred to as phlegmon.
A pancreatic pseudocyst forms when the body encapsulates leaked enzymes; the lesser sac is a common location.
Pancreatic pseudocysts appear as anechoic masses with posterior enhancement but may contain internal echoes.
Abscess formation may occur and appears as echogenic fluid containing gas bubbles.
Vascular complications include splenic vein thrombosis and pseudoaneurysm of the splenic artery.
A focal hypoechoic inflammatory mass can mimic a neoplasm, so correlation with laboratory findings and other imaging is often required.
Chronic Pancreatitis: Chronic pancreatitis is recurring destruction of pancreatic tissue that results in atrophy, fibrosis with scarring, and calcification.
Repeated bouts of pancreatic inflammation can lead to chronic pancreatitis, but not all patients with acute pancreatitis develop it.
Like acute pancreatitis, chronic alcohol abuse is a common cause.
Other causes include hyperparathyroidism, congenital anomalies such as pancreatic divisum, genetic disorders, pancreatic duct obstruction, and trauma.
Patients may be asymptomatic or have persistent epigastric pain, back pain, and jaundice.
Additional clinical findings include possible elevation of alkaline phosphatase, amylase, and lipase.
Weight loss, anorexia, vomiting, and constipation may also occur.
Sonographically, the pancreas may appear small, heterogeneous, or hyperechoic with poor margins.
Calcifications are often seen throughout the parenchyma and may also be confined to the pancreatic ducts.
Chronic pancreatitis can lead to pancreatic duct dilatation and biliary dilatation.
Stones within the pancreatic duct may contribute to biliary obstruction.
Like acute pancreatitis, chronic pancreatitis may affect only a segment of the pancreas.
Pseudocyst formation occurs in up to 40% of cases associated with chronic pancreatitis.
Possible vascular complications include portosplenic vein thrombosis.
A classic sonographic pattern is an atrophic, hyperechoic pancreas with calcifications and a prominent pancreatic duct.
Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma is the most common primary pancreatic malignancy.
It is also referred to as pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma or pancreatic ductal carcinoma.
This malignancy is most commonly discovered in men and often presents late clinically.
Risk factors include cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus, chronic pancreatitis, high-fat diet, and some genetic predispositions.
Pancreatic cancer is the fourth most common cause of cancer-related deaths in men.
The most common location is the pancreatic head, although tumors may arise elsewhere in the gland.
A pancreatic head mass often obstructs the common bile duct and may produce jaundice.
Obstruction from a pancreatic head mass may also cause a Courvoisier gallbladder, an enlarged palpable gallbladder.
Other clinical findings include elevated amylase and/or lipase, nausea, persistent back or epigastric pain, weight loss, and loss of appetite.
Elevated ALP and other liver function abnormalities may occur when biliary obstruction is present.
The most common sonographic appearance is a solid hypoechoic mass in the head of the pancreas.
Concurrent dilation of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct is called the double-duct sign.
When a pancreatic mass is found, the liver and other abdominal organs should be evaluated carefully for metastasis.
Stage I disease is confined to the pancreas, stage II involves local lymph nodes, and stage III shows distant metastasis.
The surgical treatment described is the Whipple procedure, or pancreaticoduodenectomy.
The Whipple procedure removes the pancreatic head, gallbladder, some bile ducts, and the proximal duodenum.
Cystic & Islet Cell Tumors: Pancreatic cystadenomas include serous microcystic cystadenoma and mucinous macrocystic cystadenoma.
Serous cystadenomas are small and always benign.
Because their cysts are very small, serous cystadenomas may appear solid and echogenic sonographically.
Mucinous cystadenomas are larger and have malignant potential.
Malignant mucinous tumors are called mucinous cystadenocarcinomas.
These cystic neoplasms are most often found in the pancreatic body and tail.
Patients may be asymptomatic initially and often present later than patients with pancreatic head masses.
When symptomatic, clinical findings include epigastric pain, weight loss, palpable mass, and jaundice.
Mucinous cystadenoma and cystadenocarcinoma usually appear as multilocular cystic masses.
These mucinous lesions may contain mural nodules and calcifications.
Associated dilation of the pancreatic duct may be present with mucinous tumors.
Islet cell tumors are endocrine tumors of the islets of Langerhans and are also called pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.
The two common types discussed are insulinoma and gastrinoma; insulinomas are more common.
Insulinomas are usually solitary, whereas gastrinomas are often multiple and difficult to image.
Functional gastrinomas can produce Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, causing excessive gastric acid secretion and peptic ulcers.
Functional insulinomas can cause hypoglycemia; the Whipple triad includes hypoglycemia, low fasting glucose, and relief with intravenous glucose.
Patients with insulinomas may also have palpitations, sweating, tremors, headaches, and may eventually suffer diabetic coma.
When visualized, islet cell tumors usually appear as small hypoechoic masses that may contain calcifications.
Functioning islet cell tumors often appear hypervascular with color Doppler interrogation.
Visualization of islet cell tumors is challenging because of their small size.
True pancreatic cysts may occur with von Hippel-Lindau disease, cystic fibrosis, or ADPKD.
True pancreatic cysts appear as well-defined anechoic masses with posterior enhancement.
A key pitfall is confusing a true cyst with a pancreatic pseudocyst, which is usually associated with acute or chronic pancreatitis history.
Pancreatic Transplant: Pancreatic transplantation may be performed for several reasons, including treatment of severe type 1 diabetes.
Up to 80% of patients undergo renal transplantation at the same time.
When both are transplanted, the pancreas is placed on the right side of the abdomen and the renal transplant on the left.
Two common techniques are exocrine bladder drainage and exocrine enteric drainage.
With exocrine bladder drainage, donor pancreatic vasculature is anastomosed to the recipient common iliac vessels.
In bladder drainage, the donor duodenum is anastomosed to the urinary bladder so pancreatic secretions empty through the bladder.
Exocrine bladder drainage has drawbacks including dehydration and bladder irritation.
Exocrine enteric drainage is more common and anastomoses the donor duodenum to a loop of jejunum.
In enteric drainage, the donor splenic and superior mesenteric arteries are connected to donor iliac arteries as a Y graft.
The donor common iliac portion is anastomosed to the recipient common iliac artery and external iliac artery.
Transplants may be located in the right upper quadrant or on the right side and often have a vertical orientation.
Sonographic transplant assessment includes evaluation of vascularity, pancreatic parenchyma, and fluid collections.
The transplant parenchyma should be homogeneous; it may be hypoechoic just after surgery.
A hypoechoic transplant can also indicate pancreatitis or acute rejection, so close clinical correlation is required.
With rejection, the gland may appear heterogeneous, and elevated resistive indices often indicate acute rejection.
Chronic rejection may produce a hyperechoic, atrophic pancreas containing calcifications.
Color Doppler, pulsed Doppler, and power Doppler are all useful in transplant vascular assessment.
If no flow is detected within the graft, graft thrombosis must be suspected.
Common vascular complications include arterial thrombosis, graft thrombosis, arterial stenosis, pseudoaneurysms, and splenic vein thrombosis.
Arterial stenosis causes focal areas of increased velocities, and strictures are evident with turbulent flow.
Splenic vein thrombosis may show an arterial inflow resistive index often greater than 1.0 with absent splenic inflow.
Fluid collections include abscess, ascites, hematoma, pseudocyst, and urinoma with bladder drainage technique.
Ultrasound-guided transplant biopsy may be performed when needed to differentiate rejection from other complications.

Anatomy & Physiology: The liver is the largest parenchymal organ in the body and is responsible for hemopoiesis during early embryonic life.

Vital liver functions include carbohydrate, fat, and amino acid metabolism; removal of waste products; vitamin and mineral storage; drug inactivation; bile synthesis and secretion; blood reservoir function; lymph production; and detoxification.
Most of the liver bulk is the right lobe in the right upper quadrant, while the left lobe lies in the epigastrium and may cross the midline into the left hypochondrium.
In some individuals, the liver may extend far enough left to contact the spleen.
The liver is considered intraperitoneal except for the bare area, the area of the falciform ligament, the gallbladder fossa, the porta hepatis, and an area adjacent to the IVC.
The liver is covered by Glisson capsule, a thin fibrous casing.
The liver is composed of thousands of lobules containing hepatocytes, biliary epithelial cells, and Kupffer cells.
Portal triads surround each lobule and contain small branches of the portal vein, bile duct, and hepatic artery.
Albumin may decrease with chronic liver disease and cirrhosis.
Common laboratory abnormalities include elevated ALP, ALT, AST, gamma-glutamyl transferase, LDH, bilirubin, altered PT, and elevated AFP with hepatocellular carcinoma or hepatoblastoma.
Lobes of the Liver: The liver is composed of three main hepatic lobes: right, left, and caudate.
The Couinaud classification divides the liver into eight surgical segments and describes functional liver anatomy.
The quadrate lobe lies between the gallbladder fossa and round ligament, but sonographically it is usually referred to as the medial segment of the left lobe.
The right lobe is the largest and occupies most of the right upper quadrant.
The right hepatic vein lies within the right intersegmental fissure and separates the anterior and posterior segments of the right lobe.
The middle hepatic vein lies within the main lobar fissure and separates the right lobe from the left lobe.
The gallbladder fossa is also a landmark separating the right and left lobes.
The left lobe is smaller, located in the epigastrium, and may extend into the left hypochondrium.
The left hepatic vein lies within the left intersegmental fissure and separates the medial and lateral segments of the left lobe.
The ligamentum teres and falciform ligament also separate the left medial and left lateral segments.
The caudate lobe is the smallest lobe, located in the epigastrium, and has its own separate blood supply and venous drainage.
The caudate lobe is bounded anteriorly by the ligamentum venosum and posteriorly by the IVC, which separates it from the left lobe.
Dual Blood Supply: The liver has a dual blood supply from the main portal vein and the common hepatic artery.
The main portal vein provides approximately 75% of the liver’s total blood supply.
Portal venous blood is partially oxygenated because it is derived largely from the intestines.
A primary liver function is blood filtration, including detoxification and blood storage, so nutrient- and toxin-containing blood from the intestines is routed to the liver.
Splanchnic circulation supplies the major gastrointestinal organs, including the liver, spleen, pancreas, and small and large intestines.
The primary vessels of splanchnic circulation are the celiac artery, superior mesenteric artery, and inferior mesenteric artery.
The common hepatic artery is a branch of the celiac artery, also called the celiac trunk or celiac axis.
The common hepatic artery carries highly oxygenated blood from the abdominal aorta to the liver.
Both the main portal vein and the hepatic artery transport oxygenated blood to the liver, although portal venous blood is only partially oxygenated.
Understanding this dual supply is important when evaluating perfusion abnormalities and hepatic vascular disease sonographically.
Portal vs Hepatic Veins: The main portal vein enters the liver at the porta hepatis, also called the liver hilum.
The portal vein is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein, sometimes with contribution from the inferior mesenteric vein.
The portal confluence usually lies posterior to the neck of the pancreas and anterior to the IVC.
As the main portal vein enters the liver, it divides into right and left portal veins.
The right portal vein divides into anterior and posterior branches, and the left portal vein divides into medial and lateral branches.
Portal veins are intrasegmental, have hyperechoic walls, and normally decrease in size as they approach the diaphragm.
Normal portal venous flow is hepatopetal, monophasic, and varies somewhat with respiration.
Postprandial scanning may demonstrate increased portal vein flow.
The main portal vein normally measures less than 13 mm in AP diameter; enlargement suggests portal hypertension.
Most people have three hepatic veins: right, middle, and left, which drain into the IVC.
Hepatic veins are intersegmental and interlobar, have thinner walls, and normally increase in size as they approach the diaphragm.
Normal hepatic venous flow is triphasic because of right atrial and atrial contraction influences.
Enlargement of the hepatic veins and IVC is seen with right-sided heart failure, whereas narrowing or occlusion of hepatic veins is seen with Budd–Chiari syndrome.
Porta Hepatis: The porta hepatis, or liver hilum, contains the main portal vein, common bile duct, and hepatic artery.
The common hepatic artery is a branch of the celiac artery, the first main branch of the abdominal aorta below the diaphragm.
The hepatic artery normally demonstrates a low-resistance Doppler waveform.
Typically, the hepatic artery courses anterior to the main portal vein within the porta hepatis.
On a longitudinal image, the hepatic artery is usually anterior to the main portal vein and posterior to the common bile duct.
The transverse porta hepatis image is described as the Mickey sign or Mickey Mouse sign.
In the Mickey sign, the portal vein forms the face, the hepatic artery forms the left ear, and the common bile duct forms the right ear.
In some individuals, the relationship of the hepatic artery and common bile duct may be reversed.
Knowledge of porta hepatis anatomy helps distinguish vascular from biliary structures during sonography.
This region is also important because it represents the site where the portal vein and hepatic artery enter and the bile duct exits the liver.
Ligaments & Fissures: The ligamentum venosum and falciform ligament are two readily identifiable ligaments in the normal liver sonographically.
Ligaments appear hyperechoic on sonography because of the fat within and around them.
In fetal life, the right branch of the umbilical vein, the ductus venosus, shunts blood directly into the fetal IVC.
After birth, the ductus venosus collapses and becomes the ligamentum venosum.
The ligamentum venosum appears as a hyperechoic linear structure between the caudate lobe and left lobe, anterior to the caudate lobe.
The left umbilical vein connects directly to the left portal vein in utero and becomes the ligamentum teres, or round ligament, after birth.
The ligamentum teres ascends along the falciform ligament.
Recanalization of the paraumbilical vein in the ligamentum teres can occur with portal hypertension.
The falciform ligament is often seen near the left portal vein and may appear triangular on transverse imaging between the right and left lobes.
Some texts use ligamentum teres for the falciform region, but sonographically the ligamentum teres is identified within the lower margins of the falciform ligament.
The main lobar fissure contains the middle hepatic vein and may appear as a hyperechoic line connecting the gallbladder neck to the right portal vein.
The main lobar fissure separates the right and left lobes, while diaphragmatic slips can mimic a hyperechoic mass and represent a pseudomass pitfall.
Variants & Normal Sonography: A Riedel lobe is a tongue-like inferior extension of the right hepatic lobe and is seen more often in women.
A Riedel lobe may extend as far inferiorly as the iliac crest.
To differentiate a Riedel lobe from hepatomegaly, examine the left lobe for associated enlargement.
The papillary process is an inferior extension of the caudate lobe that may mimic a mass.
If a papillary process is suspected, evaluate the caudate lobe in both transverse and sagittal planes.
Other anatomic variants include situs inversus, agenesis of a lobe, and vascular variations such as missing or extra vessels.
For right upper quadrant evaluation, patients typically fast for 8 hours, though some facilities use shorter or no fasting for focused liver follow-up.
The normal liver is homogeneous in echotexture.
Normal liver echogenicity is equal to or slightly greater than the normal right kidney, slightly less echogenic than the spleen, and slightly less echogenic than the adult pancreas.
The adult liver measures approximately 13 to 15 cm in length.
Hepatomegaly is often suspected when the liver measures greater than 15.5 cm in the midhepatic or midclavicular line.

Indirect signs of hepatomegaly include right lobe extension below the lower pole of the right kidney, rounding of the inferior right lobe tip, and left lobe extension well into the left upper quadrant.
Careful correlation with clinical history and laboratory findings is strongly recommended when hepatomegaly is suspected sonographically.
Jaundice & Bilirubin: Jaundice is yellow discoloration of the skin, mucous membranes, and sclerae caused by hyperbilirubinemia.
Bilirubin is a yellow compound produced from the breakdown of hemoglobin in red blood cells.
Serum bilirubin is an important laboratory value to assess before a right upper quadrant sonogram.
Unconjugated bilirubin, also called indirect bilirubin, is the non-water-soluble form that travels to the liver in the bloodstream.
The liver converts unconjugated bilirubin to conjugated bilirubin.
Conjugated bilirubin, also called direct bilirubin, is water soluble and is excreted into the intestines in bile and then in the stool.
Total bilirubin equals the direct plus indirect bilirubin levels.
Excess bilirubin may also be present in the urine.
Prehepatic jaundice occurs when hemolysis exceeds the liver’s processing capacity, leading to increased circulating unconjugated bilirubin; sickle cell disease is one cause.
Hepatic jaundice results from the liver’s inability to conjugate or secrete bilirubin and may occur with viral hepatitis, toxins, drugs, cirrhosis, and liver cancer.
Posthepatic or obstructive jaundice results from blocked bile flow, typically from a gallstone or pancreatic mass, and causes increased conjugated bilirubin.

An increase in conjugated bilirubin tends to be associated with gallstones or pancreatic mass, whereas unconjugated bilirubin tends to increase with hepatocellular disease such as hepatitis and cirrhosis.
Fatty Liver Disease: Fatty liver disease, or hepatic steatosis, is characterized by triglyceride deposition within hepatocytes.
It may be alcoholic or nonalcoholic, and in many cases nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is acquired and reversible.
Alcoholic fatty liver disease results from chronic alcohol abuse.

Causes of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease include starvation, obesity, chemotherapy, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, pregnancy, von Gierke disease, total parental hyperalimentation, severe hepatitis, cystic fibrosis, intestinal bypass surgery, and corticosteroids.
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is cited as the most common liver disorder in the Western world and a common cause of chronic liver disease, hepatic failure, and liver cancer.
Fatty liver is considered the hepatic manifestation of metabolic syndrome and may progress to steatohepatitis.
Steatohepatitis can be caused by alcohol or nonalcoholic conditions and may lead to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Fatty liver is often asymptomatic, but liver function tests, especially AST and ALT, may be elevated.
Diffuse fatty infiltration causes the liver to appear diffusely echogenic with increased sound attenuation and poor visualization of the diaphragm and hepatic vasculature.
Fatty liver may be graded as mild, moderate, or severe based on visualization of the hepatic vasculature and diaphragm.
Focal fatty infiltration appears as a hyperechoic area, while focal fatty sparing appears as a hypoechoic area within a diffusely fatty liver.
Focal fatty infiltration and sparing are commonly seen adjacent to the gallbladder, near the porta hepatis, and in the left medial segment, and they do not produce mass effect.
Hepatitis: Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver and may ultimately lead to cirrhosis, portal hypertension, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Acute hepatitis resolves within about 4 months, whereas chronic hepatitis persists beyond 6 months.
Hepatitis exists in many forms, including A, B, C, D, E, and G, with A and B the most common.
Hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route through contaminated food or water.
Hepatitis B spreads through contaminated body fluids, mother-to-infant transmission, or inadvertent blood contact such as intravenous drug abuse or occupational exposure.

Hepatitis C also spreads through blood and body fluids, including needlesticks, tattoos, piercings, and high-risk sexual contact, and is a leading indication for liver transplantation in the United States.
Chronic hepatitis may also be caused by Wilson disease, hemochromatosis, autoimmune disorders, or drugs.
Wilson disease causes excessive copper accumulation, whereas hemochromatosis causes excessive iron absorption; both can lead to chronic hepatitis findings.
Clinical findings may include fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, hepatosplenomegaly, dark urine, and nonobstructive hepatic jaundice.
Liver chemistries may be elevated, including PT, ALP, AST, ALT, LDH, and bilirubin; ALT is a more specific indicator of hepatic injury.
Sonographically, the liver may appear normal early, or enlarged and more hypoechoic with hepatosplenomegaly.
Periportal cuffing produces the starry sky sign, and gallbladder wall thickening may also be present.
Cirrhosis & Portal Hypertension: Cirrhosis is defined by hepatocyte death, fibrosis and necrosis of the liver, and the development of regenerating nodules.
Common sequelae of cirrhosis include portal hypertension, abdominal varicosities, portal vein thrombosis, splenomegaly, hepatocellular carcinoma, and hepatorenal syndrome.
The most common cause of cirrhosis is alcoholism, though it can also result from Wilson disease, primary biliary cirrhosis, hepatitis, cholangitis, and hemochromatosis.
Laboratory findings may remain normal until advanced disease, but abnormalities can include elevated AST, LDH, ALT, bilirubin, ALP, PT, PTT, total protein, and decreased albumin.

Clinical findings include jaundice, fatigue, weight loss, diarrhea, initial hepatomegaly, ascites, spider nevi, purpura, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, fetor hepaticus, facial telangiectasia, hepatic encephalopathy, caput medusae, muscle wasting, testicular atrophy, and hemorrhoids.
Sonographic findings include an echogenic shrunken right lobe, enlarged caudate and left lobes, nodular surface irregularity, coarse echotexture, splenomegaly, and ascites.
Alcoholic cirrhosis tends to produce micronodules less than 1 cm, whereas hepatitis-related cirrhosis tends to produce macronodules measuring 1 to 5 cm.
A high-frequency linear transducer may help demonstrate subtle surface nodularity, especially when ascites is absent.
Advanced cirrhosis may show monophasic hepatic venous flow and hepatofugal portal venous flow, both consistent with portal hypertension.
