Liver fibrosis reflects scar tissue formation during repair, and increased liver stiffness correlates with advanced complications such as variceal hemorrhage, ascites, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
Transient elastography and shear wave elastography assess liver stiffness; the stiffer the liver tissue, the more fibrosis is present.
Portal hypertension is most commonly caused by cirrhosis and may also result from portal vein thrombosis, hepatic vein thrombosis, IVC thrombosis, or tumor compression.

Portal hypertension may produce enlarged portal and superior mesenteric veins, enlarged hepatic arteries, patent paraumbilical vein, enlarged coronary vein with reversed flow, abdominal varices, ascites, and splenomegaly.
TIPS is a temporary treatment for portal hypertension that places a stent between the portal and hepatic veins to reduce portal systemic pressure.
Vascular Disorders: Portal vein compression and obstruction are most commonly caused by tumors from adjacent organs or lymphadenopathy.
Portal vein thrombosis may occur with hepatocellular carcinoma, portal hypertension, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, pregnancy, oral contraceptive use, and surgery.
Clinical findings of portal vein thrombosis include abdominal pain, low-grade fever, leukocytosis, hypovolemia, elevated liver function tests, nausea, and vomiting.
Early portal vein thrombus may be difficult to detect because it can be isoechoic to circulating blood; with time it becomes more echogenic.
Complete portal vein occlusion may lead to collateral formation around the clot, called cavernous transformation of the portal vein.
Cavernous transformation appears sonographically as multiple wormlike or serpiginous vessels in the portal vein region or porta hepatis.
Tumor invasion can also occlude the portal vein, so color Doppler should be used to assess hepatic vascularity.

Portal venous gas is classically associated with ischemic bowel disease and is typically fatal, but it may also occur with diverticulitis, appendicitis, inflammatory bowel disease, bowel obstruction, ulcers, GI cancer, or invasive procedures.
Portal venous gas appears as small bright reflectors within circulating blood in the portal vein; larger air collections may create ring-down artifact.
A pitfall is confusing portal venous gas with pneumobilia, which is air within the biliary tree.
Budd–Chiari syndrome is occlusion of the hepatic veins with possible coexisting IVC occlusion.
Budd–Chiari may occur with IVC web, coagulation abnormalities, tumor invasion from HCC, thrombosis, oral contraceptive use, pregnancy, or trauma.

Sonographic Budd–Chiari findings include nonvisualization or reduced visualization of hepatic veins, thrombus in hepatic veins, enlarged caudate lobe, absent hepatic vein flow on color Doppler, and IVC narrowing.

Hepatorenal syndrome is renal impairment or failure caused by chronic liver disease, often cirrhosis, with reduced GFR, increased creatinine, decreased urine output, and kidneys that may appear normal sonographically.
Cysts, Abscesses & Infection: True hepatic cysts are usually encountered in middle age, may be solitary and idiopathic, and are often asymptomatic.
Hepatic cysts may also occur with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease and with von Hippel–Lindau disease.
ADPKD-related hepatic cysts are often multiple and may look irregular or clustered, but simple cyst features such as anechoic content and posterior enhancement should still be present.
Complex hepatic cysts are often due to hemorrhage and may contain internal echoes, thick walls, calcification, or solid components.
Large or hemorrhagic cysts may cause right upper quadrant pain because of hemorrhage, infection, or mass effect.
Hydatid liver cysts, also called echinococcal cysts, are caused most commonly by Echinococcus granulosus from dog feces and are more common in sheep- and cattle-raising regions.
Clinical findings of hydatid disease include low-grade fever, right upper quadrant tenderness, nausea, obstructive jaundice, leukocytosis, slight ALP elevation, and possible recent travel abroad.
Hydatid cyst findings include hydatid sand, the water lily sign from detached endocyst within pericyst, mother cyst with daughter cysts, and possible dense calcification.
Amebic hepatic abscess arises from Entamoeba histolytica in the colon that invades the liver via the portal vein, often after exposure to contaminated water in endemic regions.
Amebic abscesses usually occur near the liver capsule in the right lobe and appear round, hypoechoic or anechoic, may contain debris or fluid-debris levels, and show posterior enhancement.

Pyogenic hepatic abscesses result from spread of infection such as appendicitis, diverticulitis, cholecystitis, cholangitis, or endocarditis and may appear as thick-walled complex cystic masses with debris, septations, and gas.
Gas within a pyogenic abscess may cause dirty shadowing or ring-down artifact.
Hepatic candidiasis occurs in immunocompromised patients and appears as multiple small target, halo, or bull’s-eye lesions with hyperechoic centers and hypoechoic rims; older lesions may calcify.
Schistosomiasis may cause periportal thickening, bull’s-eye lesions with anechoic center and hyperechoic rim, and chronic turtleback sign from calcified septa and fibrosis.
Benign Liver Masses: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumor and is more commonly found in women.
Hemangiomas are usually incidental and asymptomatic and most commonly located in the right lobe.
Typical hemangioma appearance is a small hyperechoic mass measuring less than 3 cm, although giant hemangiomas can occur.
Posterior enhancement may occasionally be seen with hemangiomas.
Despite being vascular, hemangiomas may show no detectable color Doppler flow because blood flow is very slow.
Hemangiomas may occasionally appear hypoechoic or complex, may be multiple, and can mimic metastatic disease.
Focal nodular hyperplasia is cited as the second most common benign liver tumor and is more commonly discovered incidentally in women.
FNH is composed of hepatocytes and fibrous tissue and may enlarge with oral contraceptive use because of estrogen exposure, though it is not caused by oral contraceptives.
FNH may be isoechoic, hyperechoic, or hypoechoic and often contains a central stellate scar that can appear hyperechoic or hypoechoic and may show hypervascularity on color Doppler.
FNH may be difficult to detect sonographically and is referred to as a stealth lesion.
Hepatocellular adenoma is a rare benign tumor associated with oral contraceptive use and may be surgically removed because of hemorrhage risk and malignant degeneration potential.
Adenomas are often hypoechoic but may also be hyperechoic, isoechoic, or mixed in echogenicity; pain often occurs with hemorrhage.
Hepatic lipoma is rare, asymptomatic, and appears as a hyperechoic mass.

Hepatic hematoma follows trauma or surgery, may be intrahepatic or subcapsular, is echogenic when acute, later complex or anechoic, and should prompt assessment for associated arteriovenous fistula with turbulent high-velocity color Doppler flow.
Liver Cancer: Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver cancer, but metastatic liver disease is more common overall.
HCC is seen most often in men and is frequently associated with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis.
Other causes linked with HCC include hemochromatosis, von Gierke disease, and Wilson disease.
The malignant mass associated with HCC is called a hepatoma.
Hepatomas can invade the portal veins or hepatic veins, so evaluation for tumor thrombus and Budd–Chiari syndrome is important.
Color Doppler may show hypervascularity within HCC, although this is not specific for malignancy.

Clinical findings of HCC include elevated AFP, possible abnormal liver function tests, cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis, unexplained weight loss, hepatomegaly, fever, palpable mass, and abdominal swelling with ascites.
HCC may appear as a solitary small hypoechoic mass, multiple heterogeneous masses, or a target lesion with a hypoechoic halo and central echogenic or isoechoic portion.
The liver is a common site of metastatic disease in the abdomen, and metastatic liver disease is the most common form of liver cancer.
Primary cancers that commonly metastasize to the liver include gallbladder, colon, stomach, pancreas, breast, and lung, with lung cited as the most common primary source.
Metastases may enter through the portal veins or lymphatic channels, and patients may have weight loss, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, ascites, or no symptoms initially.

Sonographic metastatic patterns are variable: calcified masses often arise from GI tract or pancreas, hyperechoic masses from GI tract especially colon as well as kidney, pancreas, or biliary tree, and hypoechoic masses from breast, lung, or lymphoma.
Metastatic disease may present as a single mass, several large masses, diffuse heterogeneous involvement, or target lesions, and diffuse surface nodularity may mimic cirrhosis as pseudocirrhosis.
Liver Doppler, TIPS & Transplant: Normal portal venous flow is hepatopetal, continuous, monophasic, low velocity, and typically measures 20 to 40 cm/s.
Portal venous flow may vary somewhat with respiration.
Normal hepatic venous flow is triphasic because of cardiac influences.
Flow assessment should be obtained at end respiration when possible because deep inspiration may blunt or abolish hepatic vein pulsatility.
The hepatic artery normally shows a continuous low-resistance waveform with quick upstroke and gradual diastolic deceleration.
The normal hepatic artery resistive index ranges from 0.5 to 0.8.
TIPS is placed in advanced cirrhosis and portal hypertension to reduce portal pressure and help prevent fatal gastroesophageal or other variceal hemorrhage.
The shunt is usually created between the right portal vein and the right hepatic vein and appears sonographically as a highly echogenic tube.
Post-TIPS evaluation should document shunt patency with color and spectral Doppler and establish a baseline study for future comparison.
After TIPS placement, flow within the right and left portal veins typically reverses.
Normal flow velocity within the TIPS shunt ranges from 90 to 190 cm/s.

Signs of TIPS failure include thrombus, shunt stenosis, hepatic vein stenosis, reversal of intrahepatic flow, flow void adjacent to the shunt, reversal of hepatic venous flow, a drop in shunt velocity between exams, and abnormally high or low shunt velocity.
Hepatitis C is the most common disease requiring liver transplantation, followed closely by alcoholic liver disease and cirrhosis.
A transplanted liver should resemble a normal native liver, and the portal veins, hepatic veins, hepatic artery, and IVC should be patent with normal waveforms.

The most common vascular complication after liver transplant is hepatic artery thrombosis; infarcts appear as peripheral hypoechoic wedge-shaped areas, and other complications include biliary, portal venous, arterial, and fluid-collection abnormalities at anastomotic sites.
Pediatric Liver & CEUS: Infantile hemangioendothelioma is the most common benign liver tumor of childhood.
These tumors are usually identified in the first weeks or months of life and may cause hepatomegaly or occur with hemangiomas of the skin.
Infantile hemangioendothelioma may appear sonographically as a homogeneous or complex hepatic mass and may contain calcification or cystic spaces.
Hepatoblastoma is a malignant pediatric liver tumor and is cited as the most common malignant tumor of childhood.
Hepatoblastoma is most often discovered before age 5 years, and about half of cases are identified before age 2 years.
There is a high incidence of hepatoblastoma in children with Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome, and these children are often screened with sonography.
Like adult liver carcinoma, hepatoblastoma often causes elevated AFP.
These aggressive tumors can invade surrounding vasculature and may obstruct the biliary tree.
Clinical findings of hepatoblastoma include hepatomegaly, palpable abdominal mass, jaundice, abdominal pain, weight loss, anorexia, or no symptoms.
Hepatoblastoma usually appears as a solid hyperechoic or heterogeneous mass that may contain calcifications.
Contrast-enhanced ultrasound of the liver uses intravenously injected microbubble contrast with a lipid or protein shell to aid lesion detection and characterization.
CEUS is useful when gray-scale sonography is limited by fatty or cirrhotic liver and evaluates lesions during arterial, early portal venous, and later washout phases.
The microbubbles are smaller than red blood cells, pass into capillaries, delineate masses, and are later released through the respiratory tract with little to no side effects.
CEUS can also be used in pediatric liver imaging and helps assess lesions for signs of malignancy.

Anatomy & Physiology: The spleen is the largest structure of the reticuloendothelial system and also the largest lymphatic organ of the body.
It is an intraperitoneal organ in the left upper quadrant, inferior to the diaphragm and posterolateral to the stomach.
Adjacent anatomy includes superior to the left kidney and lateral to the adrenal gland and pancreatic tail.
The gastrosplenic ligament attaches the spleen to the stomach.
Its primary function is filtration of peripheral blood.
The spleen begins to develop around the 5th week of gestation.
In the fetus, the spleen is responsible for erythropoiesis.
In children, it plays an important role in defense against infection.
In adults, it produces lymphocytes and monocytes.
In severe anemia, splenic hematopoietic function may return as extramedullary hematopoiesis.
White pulp produces and houses lymphocytes, carrying out the spleen’s lymphatic function.
Red pulp contains red blood cells and macrophages and performs the phagocytic function.
The spleen removes irregular red blood cells by culling and cleans red blood cells of unwanted material by pitting.
Vascular Anatomy: The splenic artery arises from the celiac trunk, also called the celiac artery or celiac axis.
It courses laterally toward the spleen and marks the superior border of the pancreatic body and tail.
Because of this course, the splenic artery may be mistaken sonographically for the main pancreatic duct.
The splenic artery enters the spleen at the hilum superior and anterior to the splenic vein.
Normal Doppler evaluation of the splenic artery demonstrates a low-resistance, low-pulsatility flow pattern.
The splenic vein exits the spleen and courses along the posterior border of the pancreatic tail and body.
The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein posterior to the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein.
Flow in the splenic vein is normally directed toward the liver.
In pancreatitis, the splenic vein should be evaluated for possible splenic vein thrombosis.
A malignant tumor may invade the splenic vein, producing tumor thrombus.
The splenic hilum on the medial splenic surface contains the splenic vessels.
Sonography of the Spleen: The spleen is most often best visualized with deep inspiration.
A right lateral decubitus position, with the patient lying on the right side, often improves visualization.
A normal spleen is frequently isoechoic to the liver and may be slightly more echogenic.
A key pitfall is that the spleen is not normally less echogenic than the liver in this chapter.
The adult spleen has a concave, pointed inferior margin and a convex superior border.
This contour gives the spleen a typical crescent moon shape on sonography.
The splenic hilum lies along the medial surface and is the site of the splenic vessels.
Splenic size in adults varies with age and sex.
The spleen decreases in size with advancing age.
When pathology is present, the spleen may enlarge, which is termed splenomegaly.
Congenital Anomalies: An accessory spleen may also be called a splenule, splenunculus, or supernumerary spleen.
An accessory spleen is a small, round island of splenic tissue usually near the splenic hilum or pancreatic tail.
Accessory splenic tissue appears isoechoic to the spleen on sonography.
It may mimic a splenic mass, pancreatic tail mass, left adrenal mass, or upper pole left renal mass.
When suspected, the tissue should be measured and evaluated carefully to distinguish variant from pathology.
A splenic cleft is a common anomaly in which a hyperechoic line appears to divide the spleen.
Asplenia is congenital absence of the spleen.
Polysplenia results in multiple small masses of splenic tissue.
Asplenia and polysplenia are associated with complex cardiac malformations and heterotaxia syndromes.
A wandering spleen occurs when splenic ligaments are absent or underdeveloped, allowing marked mobility.
A wandering spleen may lie well into the lower abdomen.
Because of hypermobility, a wandering spleen may undergo splenic torsion with subsequent ischemia or infarction.
Splenosis refers to ectopic splenic tissue implantation that may occur after splenic rupture.
WBC Assessment: Because lymphocytes are found in the spleen, reviewing the patient’s white blood cell count is prudent before an abdominal sonogram.
Leukocytosis is an increased number of white blood cells in the blood.
Leukocytosis commonly reflects the body’s response to infection or inflammation.
Leukocytosis may also indicate more serious disease, including acute leukemia.
Leukopenia is a reduction in the number of leukocytes in the blood.
Leukopenia may be caused by leukemia.
Leukopenia may also occur with Hodgkin lymphoma and hypersplenism.
Other causes of leukopenia listed include viral infections and diabetes mellitus.
Radiation therapy and chemotherapy can also result in leukopenia.
These laboratory abnormalities provide useful clinical context when evaluating splenic pathology.
Splenomegaly: Splenomegaly is the most common abnormality of the spleen.
Enlargement may be suspected on physical examination and then confirmed with sonography.
In adults, the spleen should never measure more than 12 to 13 cm in length.
Adult splenic thickness should not exceed 6 cm.
Suspicion for splenomegaly should arise when the spleen extends beyond the inferior pole of the left kidney.
As the spleen enlarges, it tends to become more hypoechoic.
The most common cause of splenomegaly is portal hypertension.
When portal hypertension is suspected, the splenic hilum should be evaluated closely for abdominal varices.
Other causes include trauma, leukemia, lymphoma, granulomatous disease, and pediatric sickle cell anemia crisis.
Infections associated with splenomegaly include endocarditis, AIDS, hepatitis, and Epstein–Barr infection causing infectious mononucleosis.
Clinical findings may include palpable enlargement, left upper quadrant pain or discomfort, trauma, infection, or history of cirrhosis, leukemia, or lymphoma.
Leukocytosis and or elevated red blood cell count may be present clinically.
Massive splenomegaly may lead to spontaneous splenic rupture.
Following rupture, splenosis may occur and ectopic splenic tissue can resemble a mass.
Splenic Cysts & Abscess: A true splenic cyst, also called an epithelial cyst, typically has thin walls, an anechoic center, and posterior enhancement.
Simple cysts are usually round, smooth walled, and often asymptomatic.
Pain may occur with hemorrhage into a splenic cyst.
Complex splenic cysts may be associated with trauma.
Other complex cystic considerations include displaced pancreatic pseudocyst, abscess, congenital cyst, hydatid cyst, cystic metastasis, and cystic primary cancer.
Hydatid cysts of the spleen, often due to Echinococcus granulosus, resemble hydatid liver cysts in appearance and clinical findings.
Splenic cysts may be associated with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
A pyogenic splenic abscess is uncommon and may be caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus, or Salmonella.
Clinical findings of splenic abscess include fever, leukocytosis, left upper quadrant tenderness, left flank or shoulder pain, and splenomegaly.
A history of bacteremia increases the likelihood of pyogenic splenic abscess.
Predisposing disease processes include bacterial endocarditis, diverticulitis, osteomyelitis, and pelvic infections.
A splenic abscess is usually complex, but it may be completely hypoechoic and may contain debris or gas.
Gas within an abscess may produce dirty shadowing or ring-down artifact.
Color Doppler often shows increased vascularity around an abscess but no flow within it.
Fungal abscesses, most often from Candida in immunocompromised patients, may appear as small solid masses or target or bull’s-eye lesions.
Splenic Infarct: An infarct is tissue death caused by deprivation of oxygen.
Patients with splenic infarction often present with sudden onset of left upper quadrant pain.
Causes include sickle cell disease, bacterial endocarditis, tumor embolization, vasculitis, and lymphoma.
In the acute stage, a splenic infarct appears as a hypoechoic, wedge-shaped mass within the spleen.
In the chronic stage, splenic infarcts tend to appear more echogenic than adjacent normal splenic tissue.
A classic pitfall is to recognize the characteristic wedge shape when differentiating infarct from other focal masses.
Splenic Trauma: The spleen is often injured in cases of blunt trauma.
Although not always the initial imaging choice immediately after trauma, sonography is often used once splenic trauma is established.
Patients commonly report left upper quadrant pain after splenic trauma.
A decreased hematocrit may indicate active bleeding.
A splenic hematoma may be difficult to detect because it can appear isoechoic to adjacent splenic tissue.
Hematomas may be subcapsular or intraparenchymal.
Early hemorrhage may appear complex or hypoechoic.
In the middle stage, hemorrhage may become echogenic with clot formation or appear isoechoic.
Later, the hematoma may again become hypoechoic or anechoic as it resolves.
Chronic hematomas may appear complex and may eventually develop calcified walls.
A laceration may appear as an echogenic line within the spleen immediately following trauma.
Hemorrhagic cysts resulting from trauma may later have calcified walls.
Splenic rupture may lead to splenosis, with ectopic splenic tissue mimicking neoplasm in unusual locations.
Severe splenic injury may require splenectomy; splenectomy may also be performed for cancer, severe splenomegaly, or impaired splenic function.
Benign Masses & Granulomas: Hemangioma is the most common benign tumor of the spleen.
A splenic hemangioma most often appears as a well-defined, hyperechoic mass.
Patients with splenic hemangioma are usually asymptomatic.
Pain can occur if a hemangioma hemorrhages.
Granulomas appear as small echogenic foci scattered throughout the spleen.
These echogenic foci may be single or multiple and may produce acoustic shadowing.
Granulomas are associated with histories of histoplasmosis, tuberculosis, or sarcoidosis.
Larger splenic calcifications may result from resolved hematomas, infarctions, abscesses, neoplasms, or infection.
Splenic hamartoma is a benign mass that typically appears hypoechoic, although its echotexture can vary.
Splenic hamartoma has been associated with Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome and tuberous sclerosis.
Hamartomas are typically asymptomatic, though pain can occur with rupture.
Color Doppler evaluation of a splenic hamartoma may reveal hypervascularity.
In children, splenic lymphangioma is a benign congenital malformation of the lymphatic system.
Lymphangiomas are multicystic masses containing hypoechoic or anechoic locules with hyperechoic septations and are often associated with splenomegaly.
Malignant Disease: Patients with splenic malignancy may present with left upper quadrant pain, fever, weight loss, and malaise.
Angiosarcoma is the primary malignant tumor of the spleen, but it is exceedingly rare.
Splenic angiosarcoma appears sonographically as a complex or solid mass.
Lymphoma and leukemia involve the spleen more commonly than angiosarcoma.
Lymphoma is cited as the most common malignancy of the spleen.
Diffuse involvement by lymphoma or leukemia often produces splenomegaly.
Focal malignant disease may appear as one or more hypoechoic masses throughout the spleen.
Focal masses are less commonly seen with leukemia.
Lymphoma is classified as Hodgkin lymphoma or non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Both forms are malignant disorders of lymphocytes and compromise the immune system.
The presence of Reed–Sternberg cells indicates Hodgkin lymphoma.
Hodgkin lymphoma can be treated and has a relatively high recovery rate.
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is more common but not as easily managed.
Metastatic disease to the spleen is rare and usually occurs late in the disease process.
Common primary sites for splenic metastases are breast, lung, skin melanoma, and ovary.
Sickle Cell Anemia: Sickle cell disease is a group of inherited blood disorders affecting hemoglobin and includes sickle cell anemia.
In sickle cell anemia, red blood cells are abnormally shaped like crescents.
These abnormal cells tend to attach to each other and obstruct normal vascular channels.
This vascular obstruction causes multiple clinical complications.
In the United States, sickle cell anemia is found more frequently in African-American, Middle East, Mediterranean, and Hispanic children of Caribbean descent.
During a sickle cell crisis, a child often has splenomegaly.
Occasionally, rounded focal masses of normal splenic tissue may be seen sonographically within the damaged spleen.
With recurrent crises, the spleen eventually becomes fibrotic and atrophic from multiple infarctions.
This gradual fibrosis and dysfunction is termed autosplenectomy.
Patients in crisis may have decreased hematocrit.
Bone pain may be a clinical complaint during sickle cell crisis.
These patients are at increased risk for gallstones, multiple organ damage, blindness, and stroke.

Anatomy & Physiology: The adrenal glands are paired retroperitoneal endocrine glands also called suprarenal glands.
They are controlled by the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis: hypothalamus influences the anterior pituitary, which releases ACTH to control adrenal hormone release.
Like the kidneys, the adrenal glands are enclosed within Gerota fascia.
The right adrenal gland lies posterior and right lateral to the IVC, medial to the right lobe of liver, and lateral to the crus of the diaphragm.
The left adrenal gland is medial to the upper pole of the left kidney; its superior segment is posterior to the lesser sac.
The inferior segment of the left adrenal gland lies posterior and lateral to the pancreas.
Each adrenal gland has an outer cortex and inner medulla.
The cortex contains three zones: zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, and zona reticularis.
The adrenal cortex produces glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, and androgens.
Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid that regulates blood pressure by controlling sodium and water in the body.
Cortisol controls the body’s use of fat, carbohydrates, and protein; it also affects glucose metabolism, blood pressure, immune function, and inflammatory response.
The cortex also produces androgenic hormones, estrogens, and dehydroepiandrosterone, a precursor used to convert into other hormones.
The medulla produces epinephrine and norepinephrine; epinephrine, or adrenaline, is the primary medullary hormone.
Epinephrine and norepinephrine are responsible for the fight-or-flight response and affect heart rate, blood pressure, and vascular tone.
Vascular Anatomy: The adrenal glands receive blood supply from three arterial sources.
These include suprarenal branches of the inferior phrenic arteries.
They also receive suprarenal branches directly from the aorta.
Additional supply comes from suprarenal branches of the renal arteries.
Venous drainage occurs through the suprarenal veins.
The right suprarenal vein drains directly into the IVC.
The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein.
Knowledge of venous drainage is important because some adrenal malignancies may invade the adrenal vein and IVC.
Sonography of the Adrenals: Normal adrenal glands are not routinely identified in adults because surrounding adipose tissue obscures them.
Normal adrenal glands are often easily visualized in the fetus and pediatric patient.
In fetal and pediatric patients, the adrenal glands appear as hypoechoic structures.
They are located anterior, medial, and superior to the upper pole of each kidney.
Many adrenal abnormalities are found incidentally during abdominal sonography.
An incidentally discovered adrenal-region mass may be called an incidentaloma when the patient lacks clinical findings suggesting adrenal disease.
Further evaluation of an incidentaloma may include biochemical analysis and other imaging techniques.
Some incidentally discovered adrenal masses ultimately have little or no clinical significance.
If a mass is seen in the adrenal region, the sonographer should perform a thorough analysis.
The examination should include careful measurements of the mass.
Color Doppler interrogation should also be performed.
A pitfall is confusion with masses arising from adjacent organs in the upper abdomen.
Addison Disease: Addison disease is also called primary adrenocortical insufficiency or chronic primary hypoadrenalism.
It is an endocrine disorder caused by hypofunction of the adrenal cortex with inadequate corticosteroid secretion.
Addison disease may be idiopathic or caused by autoimmune disorder, infection, or tuberculosis.
The disorder results from partial or complete destruction of the adrenal glands.
Clinical findings include increased ACTH production by the pituitary gland.
Patients commonly present with hypotension, weakness, and fatigue.
Loss of appetite and weight loss are common clinical complaints.
Bronzing of the skin, termed hyperpigmentation, is a classic finding.
Laboratory abnormalities may include elevated liver enzymes, hyperkalemia, and hyponatremia.
Personality changes or confusion may also occur.
CT is the imaging modality of choice to aid in diagnosis.
In acute stages, sonography may show enlarged, hemorrhagic adrenal glands.
In chronic disease, the glands typically become atrophic and calcified, which may be difficult to identify sonographically.
Cushing & Conn Syndromes: Cushing syndrome results from overproduction of cortisol by the adrenal cortex, termed hypercortisolism.
It can result from a tumor in the anterior pituitary gland, called Cushing disease, or from an adrenal tumor.
The adrenal tumor causing Cushing syndrome is most likely an adrenal adenoma.
Cortisol is important in glucose metabolism, blood pressure regulation, immune function, and inflammatory response.
Patients with Cushing syndrome may present with obesity and thinning arms and legs.
Other classic findings include buffalo hump, moon-shaped face, and hypertension.
Additional Cushing findings include poor wound healing, red or purple striae over the abdomen and thighs, hirsutism, hyperglycemia, and severe fatigue.
Sonographically, Cushing syndrome may be associated with an adrenal mass, most likely an adrenal adenoma.
Conn syndrome is also called primary hyperaldosteronism and results from high levels of aldosterone secretion by the adrenal cortex.
It may be caused by a functioning cortical tumor, most likely a benign aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma.
Aldosterone regulates blood pressure by controlling the amount of sodium and water in the body.
Patients with Conn syndrome typically have hypertension, excessive thirst, and excessive urination.
Laboratory findings in Conn syndrome include hypernatremia and hypokalemia.
Low potassium levels may cause muscle cramps and weakness; sonography may reveal an adrenal mass, most likely an adenoma.
Adrenal Adenoma: Adrenal adenoma is the most common benign solid mass of the adrenal gland.
It may be hyperfunctioning or non-hyperfunctioning.
Hyperfunctioning adenomas are often seen in patients with Cushing syndrome or Conn syndrome.
Some patients are asymptomatic, especially when the adenoma is non-hyperfunctioning or incidentally discovered.
Clinical findings may reflect Cushing syndrome when cortisol production is excessive.
Clinical findings may reflect Conn syndrome when aldosterone production is excessive.
Sonographically, an adrenal adenoma most often appears as a solid, hypoechoic mass in the area of the adrenal gland.
A key differential issue is distinguishing an adrenal adenoma from masses arising from adjacent organs.
Masses from the liver, spleen, or kidneys may mimic an adrenal lesion sonographically.
CT or MRI may be needed to differentiate the mass from adjacent-organ lesions.
When identified sonographically, the mass should be thoroughly assessed with measurements and Doppler interrogation.
Pheochromocytoma: Pheochromocytoma arises from the adrenal medulla.
It is typically a hyperfunctioning, benign adrenal mass, although it can be malignant.
The tumor causes excessive release of epinephrine and norepinephrine into the bloodstream.
This hormone excess leads to uncontrollable hypertension.
Other clinical complaints include headaches, tachycardia, tremors, anxiety, and excessive sweating.
Because adrenal hormones affect blood pressure regulation, clinical history is important when evaluating a solid adrenal mass.
Sonographically, a pheochromocytoma may appear as a large, hyperechoic mass in the adrenal region.
Its appearance is variable and may also be hypoechoic or diffusely heterogeneous.
Variable sonographic appearance creates overlap with other adrenal tumors, so correlation with symptoms is important.
Cysts, Rests & Malignancy: Adrenal cysts can be seen in the adrenal region and may be difficult to separate from the liver, spleen, or upper pole of the kidney.
Simple adrenal cysts may be incidental findings in asymptomatic patients.
Large cysts, infected cysts, or hemorrhage within an adrenal cyst may cause pain or other symptoms.
A simple adrenal cyst typically appears anechoic, round, and demonstrates acoustic enhancement.
Adrenal cysts with a rim of calcification are more worrisome for malignancy.
Accessory adrenal tissue is called adrenal rests.
Adrenal rests may be found in the testes, epididymis, ovaries, and inguinal canal.
They disseminate during embryologic development and can form mass-like structures within affected organs.
Adrenal rest cells respond to ACTH secretion from the pituitary gland.
Adrenal rests are often associated with congenital adrenal hyperplasia and Cushing syndrome.
Primary adrenal carcinoma, such as adenocarcinoma, is rare.
Malignant adrenal tumors may produce symptoms of Cushing syndrome because they can be functional and alter hormone production.
The adrenal glands are the fourth most common site of metastasis, often from lung, breast, gastrointestinal tract, thyroid, pancreas, kidneys, lymphoma, leukemia, or melanoma.
Adrenal cancer may appear as a solid hypoechoic mass or a large heterogeneous mass; cortical cancers tend to be large and may invade the adrenal vein and IVC.
Neuroblastoma: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid malignant tumor in children.
It arises from immature neural crest cells, or neuroblasts, along the sympathetic nervous system.
When arising in the adrenal gland, it comes from the adrenal medulla.
It typically presents before 5 years of age, with a median age at diagnosis of 19 months.
Most patients present with a palpable abdominal mass and abdominal pain.
Bone pain is a notable clinical feature.
Blue or purple spots on the skin may also be present.
Metastasis is often present at the time of discovery.
Sonographically, neuroblastoma appears as a solid, large, heterogeneous adrenal-region mass.
The average size is about 8 cm.
Calcifications and hemorrhage are commonly present within the mass.
The tumor can spread around the IVC and aorta.
When neuroblastoma is suspected, the liver and other abdominal organs should be carefully evaluated for metastatic involvement.
Adrenal Hemorrhage: The adrenal glands can spontaneously hemorrhage, particularly in stressed neonates.
Traumatic birth and perinatal anoxia are important associated factors.
Patients may present with an abdominal mass, jaundice, and anemia.
An acute drop in hematocrit and blood pressure is another key clinical finding.
Sonographically, adrenal hemorrhage often appears as a mass in the adrenal region.
The mass is typically rounded or triangle-shaped.
In the acute stage, the hemorrhage appears echogenic.
With time, the mass becomes heterogeneous, then hypoechoic, and may become cystic.
Eventually, the hemorrhage completely resolves in many cases.
Residual calcifications may remain after resolution.
These calcifications can be prominent and may produce acoustic shadowing.
Serial appearance change is an important clue and helps distinguish hemorrhage from neoplasm.

Anatomy of the GI Tract: The gastrointestinal tract, or alimentary canal, includes the mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestines, and colon.
The mouth is the most proximal portion of the gastrointestinal tract.
The pharynx lies distal to the mouth and unites the mouth to the esophagus.
The esophagus travels inferiorly within the thorax and passes through the diaphragm at the esophageal hiatus.
The distal esophagus joins the stomach at the gastroesophageal junction.
On sagittal sonography, the gastroesophageal junction appears as a bull’s-eye between the left liver lobe and the abdominal aorta.
The stomach consists of the fundus, body, and pyloric region.
The pyloric sphincter in the distal stomach controls emptying of stomach contents into the duodenum.
The proximal duodenum is C-shaped and is called the C-loop of the duodenum.
Distal to the duodenum are the jejunum and ileum of the small intestines.
The ileum meets the cecum at the ileocecal valve in the right lower quadrant.
The vermiform appendix is a blind-ended tube connected to the cecum.
The colon continues as ascending colon, hepatic flexure, transverse colon, splenic flexure, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and anus.
Most GI tract parts are intraperitoneal; the duodenum and ascending and descending colon are retroperitoneal.
Gut Signature: Sonography provides a noninvasive, nonionizing way to evaluate selected gastrointestinal abnormalities.
Common sonographic indications discussed include hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, intussusception, and acute appendicitis.
Most GI sonographic studies are performed with a high-frequency linear-array transducer.
Some examinations may require a curved-array transducer.
For possible small bowel or colon pathology, a global or panoramic view of the abdomen may be performed.
The global view assesses the abdomen from the bottom up with vertical movements from the right iliac fossa, then horizontal movements from right to left.
Normal bowel should demonstrate a characteristic gut signature on sonography.
The gastrointestinal tract has five histologic layers that appear sonographically as alternating echogenic and hypoechoic bands.
These alternating bowel wall layers create the classic target or bull’s-eye appearance.
The superficial mucosa, the innermost visible layer, is echogenic.
The deep mucosa is hypoechoic, and the submucosa interface appears echogenic.
The muscularis propria is hypoechoic, and the serosa, the outermost layer, is echogenic.
Not all five bowel wall layers are consistently identified with sonography.
Scanning Technique: Compression sonography, or graded compression, is used to differentiate normal from abnormal bowel.
Normal bowel should be compressible and should demonstrate observable peristalsis.
Compression helps move intraluminal fluid and gas away from the region of interest to improve visualization.
The involved bowel segment should be closely analyzed, especially the bowel wall.
Normal small bowel wall thickness is between 1.5 and 3 mm.
Small bowel distention is defined as 2.5 cm or greater measured outer wall to outer wall.
In the nondistended state, the colon wall should measure between 4 and 9 mm in thickness.
Colon distention has been defined as a bowel diameter exceeding 6 cm.
Bowel walls should appear thin when the bowel is distended.
Wall thickness should be measured from the central hyperechoic lumen to the outer hyperechoic margin.
A normal bowel wall produces little to no color Doppler signal.
Inflammatory changes and neoplasms in the bowel often demonstrate hyperemia on color Doppler.
Transvaginal imaging can help identify an inflamed appendix in some women and may aid evaluation of the rectum and sigmoid colon.
A water enema technique, though rarely used, can be integrated to assess the rectum and sigmoid colon for suspected pathology.
Acute Appendicitis: The appendix, or vermiform appendix, is a long, narrow, blind-ended tube commonly located in the right lower quadrant at the cecum.
Acute appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix and is cited as the most common cause of acute abdominal pain resulting in surgery.
Appendicitis may result from obstruction by an appendicolith, fecalith, lymph node, tumor, foreign body, seeds, or parasite.
Patients may first have epigastric, periumbilical, or generalized abdominal pain that later localizes to the right lower quadrant.
Rebound tenderness over McBurney point in the right lower quadrant is called McBurney sign.
Rovsing sign is pain elicited in the right lower quadrant when the left lower quadrant is palpated.
Helpful clinical findings include acute abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and possible leukocytosis.
High fever may be present when abscess formation complicates appendicitis.
Graded compression is used to sonographically investigate the abdomen for appendicitis.
The inflamed appendix appears as a noncompressible, blind-ended tube measuring more than 6 mm outer wall to outer wall.
An appendicolith appears as an echogenic shadowing structure within the appendiceal lumen.
Associated findings include periappendiceal fluid collection, fat stranding, and hyperemic flow in the appendiceal wall.
The thyroid in the belly sign describes hyperechoic edematous connective tissue surrounding the inflamed appendix.
Complications include perforation, peritonitis, abscess formation, and possibly death; a normal appendix may still be seen, especially in children and thin patients.
Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is a defect in relaxation of the pyloric sphincter that causes hypertrophy of the pyloric muscles and persistent closure.
This process produces a gastric outlet obstruction.
Although it can occur in adults, it is most commonly encountered in infants between 2 and 6 weeks old.
First-born, white male infants are more likely to be affected.
Clinical findings include nonbilious projectile vomiting, dehydration, weight loss, constipation, and an insatiable appetite.
On physical examination, the enlarged pyloric muscle may be palpable as the olive sign.
Sonography has become the modality of choice, replacing radiography as the customary test.
For examination, the infant is placed in the right lateral decubitus position.
If the stomach is empty, a small amount of glucose solution may be given to better visualize the pylorus.
Care should be taken not to overdistend the stomach, because excess fluid may prevent adequate visualization.
The pylorus lies in the epigastrium, slightly right of midline, near the gallbladder, and is normally transversely oriented.
The abnormal pylorus appears as a target or doughnut in short axis and as a cervix in long axis.
If present, the pyloric muscle wall measures 3 mm or greater, and the pyloric channel length measures 17 mm or greater.
Muscle thickness is the more specific sonographic measurement, and fluid passage from pylorus into duodenum on real-time imaging excludes HPS.
HPS Mimics: Three additional causes of nonbilious vomiting in the infant are pylorospasm, gastroesophageal reflux, and malrotation of the midgut.
These entities should be excluded in infants with clinical findings suggestive of pyloric stenosis.
Pylorospasm is a temporary spasm and thickening of the pyloric sphincter that can mimic pyloric stenosis sonographically.
Unlike hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, pylorospasm measurements tend to remain within normal limits.
On follow-up with pylorospasm, some fluid is eventually seen traveling through the pyloric channel.
Gastroesophageal reflux is another cause of nonbilious projectile vomiting in the infant.
For reflux evaluation, the gastroesophageal junction is identified posterior to the left liver lobe and anterior to the abdominal aorta in the sagittal plane.
After identifying the gastroesophageal junction, the transducer is manipulated to obtain a longitudinal image of the esophagus.
In gastroesophageal reflux, fluid mixed with gas bubbles can be seen traveling retrograde up the esophagus.
Midgut malrotation, with or without volvulus, may clinically resemble HPS but usually causes bilious rather than nonbilious vomiting.
The sonographic diagnosis of malrotation is based on the relationship of the superior mesenteric artery and superior mesenteric vein.
Normally, the SMA is to the left of the SMV; with malrotation, their positions are reversed.
Color Doppler may show a whirlpool appearance of the mesenteric vasculature, and an upper GI radiographic series typically confirms malrotation.
Intussusception: Intussusception is the telescoping of one bowel segment into another.
The intussusceptum is the proximal bowel segment that invaginates into the distal intussuscipiens.
The most common type is ileocolic intussusception at the level of the ileocecal valve in the right lower quadrant.
It is often idiopathic and occurs more often in male patients.
Intussusception is cited as the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children less than 2 years old.
It rarely occurs in patients younger than 3 months or older than 3 years.
In patients older than 2 years, a lead point may be present, such as an intestinal polyp, Meckel diverticulum, lymphoma, or intraluminal hematoma.
In adults, intussusception can be caused by a neoplasm.
Clinical findings include intermittent severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and a palpable abdominal mass.
Red currant jelly stool, a mixture of blood and mucus, is a hallmark clinical finding.
Laboratory tests may reveal anemia, dehydration, and/or leukocytosis.
With graded compression sonography, intussusception appears as a noncompressible target mass in transverse or a pseudokidney in longitudinal plane.
Alternating rings of echogenicity represent edematous bowel wall layers and may create a cinnamon-bun sign in transverse view.
The intussuscepted bowel diameter exceeds 3 cm; Doppler assesses viability, and treatment is usually therapeutic enema unless gangrene requires surgery.
Intestinal Obstruction & Bezoars: Although not typically the modality of choice, sonography may incidentally detect an intestinal or bowel obstruction during abdominal imaging.
Patients with bowel obstruction can present with abdominal distention, intermittent abdominal pain, constipation, and nausea and vomiting.
There are two types of obstruction: mechanical and nonmechanical.
Mechanical obstruction occurs when bowel is physically blocked by adhesions, volvulus, herniations, intussusception, tumors, or inflammatory bowel disease.
A nonmechanical obstruction, or paralytic ileus, occurs when the bowel lacks normal peristalsis.
Sonographically, obstruction appears as distended fluid-filled loops of bowel.
In small bowel obstruction, the bowel diameter measures 2.5 cm or greater outer wall to outer wall.
When fluid distends the small bowel, the plicae circulares become clearly visible, producing the keyboard sign.
In colonic obstruction, the colon diameter exceeds 6 cm.
An abrupt termination point of distended bowel may occasionally be identified, although bowel gas may obscure it.
Mechanical obstruction may show increased peristaltic motion with to-and-fro movement of intraluminal contents.
Bezoars are masses of ingested material that may rarely be identified sonographically as a cause of obstruction.
Trichobezoars consist of matted hair, lactobezoars consist of inadequately mixed powdered milk, and phytobezoars consist of vegetable material.
Bezoars appear as complex masses with varying degrees of acoustic enhancement and posterior shadowing, depending on their structure.
Inflammatory Bowel & Cancer: Crohn disease is an autoimmune disorder characterized by periods of gastrointestinal tract inflammation, most commonly involving the small intestine.
Its cause is unknown, and it usually affects the terminal ileum or proximal colon, although any part of the GI tract may be involved.
Patients with Crohn disease can present with episodes of diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, and rectal bleeding.
Sonographically, Crohn disease resembles a noncompressible target and shows bowel wall thickening greater than 3 mm.
Color Doppler interrogation of affected bowel in Crohn disease reveals hyperemia.
Diverticulosis is the development of small outpouchings, most often in the sigmoid colon; inflammation of these outpouchings is diverticulitis.
Patients with diverticulitis may present with constipation or diarrhea, fever, nausea and vomiting, and cramping left lower quadrant pain.
Diverticulitis appears as segmentally thickened bowel with an inflamed diverticulum and inflamed perienteric fat.
The affected diverticular segment typically shows hyperemia, and inflamed diverticula may appear as echogenic projections with shadowing or ring-down artifact.
Colitis is inflammation of the colon and includes pseudomembranous, ulcerative, ischemic, and infectious forms.
Watery and/or bloody diarrhea is common in colitis, often accompanied by pain and fever; prior antibiotic therapy may suggest pseudomembranous colitis from C. difficile.
Sonographically, colitis shows colon wall thickening with increased echogenicity, and infectious colitis especially may demonstrate hyperemia on color Doppler.
Gastric cancer is most often adenocarcinoma; patients typically present with weight loss, abdominal pain, anorexia, and vomiting.

GI malignancy often appears as a hypoechoic, irregular, bulky mass up to 10 cm, sometimes with target or pseudokidney appearance; bowel metastases commonly arise from melanoma and primary lung and breast tumors.
Anterior Abdominal Wall: The paired rectus abdominis muscles lie on either side of the anterior abdominal wall midline.
The linea alba is the band of connective tissue that divides the rectus abdominis muscles in the midline.
The rectus sheath forms a covering for the rectus abdominis muscles.
A rupture of the rectus muscle or its associated vasculature can produce a rectus sheath hematoma.
Blood accumulation within the muscle or beneath the sheath may follow abdominal trauma or occur spontaneously.
Abdominal contractions from childbirth, sneezing, coughing, defecation, urination, and intercourse have been shown to cause rectus sheath hematoma.
Clinical findings of rectus sheath hematoma include abdominal pain, a palpable abdominal mass, skin discoloration over the area, and decreased hematocrit.
Sonographically, a rectus sheath hematoma may appear anechoic, hypoechoic, complex, or hyperechoic depending on its stage of development.
The most common extrapelvic site for endometriosis is the anterior abdominal wall.
Endometriosis is ectopic functional endometrial tissue, often located within a prior cesarean section scar and termed scar endometriosis.
Patients with abdominal wall endometriosis may have a palpable mass and cyclical pain because the tissue responds to menstrual hormones.
A linear transducer should be used to evaluate suspected abdominal wall endometriosis.
Scar endometriosis may be well defined, lobulated, or infiltrative and most often appears hypoechoic or heterogeneous, sometimes with cystic change.

Abdominal wall hernias are evaluated with a high-frequency linear transducer and standoff pad; Valsalva helps show movement and size change, and complications include incarceration, strangulation, and bowel ischemia.

Abdominal Aorta Anatomy: The aorta is the largest artery in the body and originates at the left ventricle of the heart.
It is called the thoracic aorta in the chest and becomes the abdominal aorta after passing through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm.
The abdominal aorta is retroperitoneal, lies anterior to the spine, and is positioned just left of the midline.
Its main function is to supply blood to the abdominal organs, pelvis, and lower extremities.
The vessel wall has three layers: tunica intima internally, tunica media as the muscular middle layer, and tunica adventitia externally.
Arteries have a thicker tunica media than veins.
Most abdominal arteries are considered low resistance, although some demonstrate high-resistance flow at times.
A high-resistance waveform shows rapid systolic upstroke, low or absent diastolic flow, and often early diastolic flow reversal.
A low-resistance waveform shows persistent forward flow throughout diastole with a narrow spectrum and clean systolic window.
Normal abdominal aortic peak systolic velocity is about 70 to 100 cm/s.
The suprarenal aorta normally demonstrates low-resistance flow because it is proximal to major visceral branches.
The infrarenal aorta normally demonstrates high-resistance flow related to distal peripheral circulation.
Celiac Trunk: The celiac trunk, also called the celiac artery or celiac axis, is the first main visceral branch of the abdominal aorta.
It arises from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta between the crura of the diaphragm.
Its three branches are the splenic artery, common hepatic artery, and left gastric artery.
In the transverse plane, the celiac trunk with the common hepatic and splenic arteries forms a seagull or T-shaped appearance.
The common hepatic artery and splenic artery are readily seen sonographically, whereas the left gastric artery is usually not seen because of its small size.
Normal celiac artery flow should be continuous and forward; abnormal flow is associated with elevated velocities.
The celiac artery normally demonstrates low-resistance flow, with PSV approximately 98 to 105 cm/s.
The splenic artery courses toward the patient's left side and follows a tortuous route.
It is often seen along the superior margin of the pancreas and may mimic the main pancreatic duct.
Color Doppler helps distinguish the splenic artery from the pancreatic duct by confirming arterial flow.
The splenic artery enters the splenic hilum and branches into smaller arteries; normal flow is low resistance.
The common hepatic artery travels toward the right side and gives off the gastroduodenal artery at the pancreatic head.
After giving off the gastroduodenal artery, it becomes the proper hepatic artery, which enters the porta hepatis and divides into right and left hepatic arteries.
The cystic artery is an important branch of the right hepatic artery, and hepatic arterial flow should be low resistance and hepatopetal.
SMA & Other Branches: The superior mesenteric artery is the second main branch of the abdominal aorta and usually arises just distal to the celiac trunk.
In some individuals, the SMA and celiac trunk originate at the same level.
The SMA supplies portions of the small intestine, some of the colon, and the pancreas.
Sonographically, the SMA is readily identified by the echogenic fat layer that surrounds it.
It lies posterior to the splenic vein and pancreas and left lateral to the superior mesenteric vein.
The left renal vein is seen posterior to the SMA and anterior to the abdominal aorta.
In fasting patients, the SMA normally demonstrates a high-resistance waveform.
About 30 to 90 minutes after a meal, the SMA waveform becomes low resistance.
Failure to show the expected fasting-to-postprandial change may help suggest small bowel ischemia in patients with unexplained abdominal pain.
Normal SMA peak systolic velocity is about 97 to 142 cm/s.
The paired renal arteries are the third main visceral branches and arise just below the SMA.
The right renal artery arises from the right anterolateral aorta, passes posterior to the IVC, and is longer than the left.
In the sagittal plane, the right renal artery may appear as an anechoic circle posterior to the IVC.
The left renal artery arises from the left anterolateral aorta and courses posterior to the left renal vein toward the hilum.
Duplication of the renal arteries is common, and normal renal arteries typically show low-resistance flow.
The gonadal arteries arise from the anterior aortic surface just below the renal arteries and are termed testicular or ovarian arteries.
The inferior mesenteric artery arises from the anterior aorta, supplies the transverse colon, descending colon, and rectum, and may be hard to image sonographically.
The aorta bifurcates at or near the level of the umbilicus into the right and left common iliac arteries, often highlighted with color Doppler.
Sonography of the Aorta: Evaluation of the abdominal aorta may be limited by overlying bowel gas or large body habitus.
Patient fasting can improve sonographic assessment of the abdominal aorta.
Applying transducer pressure or scanning from the patient's left side may improve visualization in some patients.
The normal abdominal aorta is largest just below the diaphragm and progressively tapers as it approaches the umbilicus.
As it descends away from the diaphragm, the aorta gradually assumes a more anterior position in the abdomen.
The upper normal limit just below the diaphragm is 2.5 cm in diameter.
In the midabdomen, the aorta normally measures 2.0 cm or less.
The distal abdominal aorta should not exceed 1.8 cm in diameter.
The common iliac arteries typically measure 8 to 10 mm.
A common iliac artery is considered aneurysmal when its diameter exceeds 2.0 cm.
Spectral Doppler in the proximal aorta superior to the visceral branches is normally low resistance.
The infrarenal or mid-to-distal aorta normally demonstrates high-resistance flow.
Normal infrarenal Doppler should be triphasic, with early diastolic flow reversal and a brief final forward-flow phase.
Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm: An aneurysm is any focal or diffuse dilation of a blood vessel caused by weakening of the vessel wall.
A true aneurysm involves all three wall layers, and most abdominal aortic aneurysms are true aneurysms.
An abdominal aortic aneurysm is present when the abdominal aorta measures greater than 3 cm in diameter.
The most common aneurysm shape is fusiform, characterized by gradual enlargement of the vessel.
A saccular aneurysm shows sudden dilation, is often spherical, and may be large.
Other aneurysmal shapes include berry, bulbous, eccentric, and dumbbell.
The most common location of an AAA is infrarenal.
Assessment should determine whether the renal arteries are involved because renal perfusion may be compromised.
Distal aneurysms may also include dilation of the iliac arteries.
Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of aneurysms in the United States.
Other associations include Marfan syndrome, syphilis, familial inheritance, and infection; an infected aneurysm is called a mycotic aneurysm.
Many patients are asymptomatic, but clinical findings may include pulsatile abdominal mass, abdominal bruit, back pain, abdominal pain, and lower extremity pain.
Sonographically, the aneurysmal lumen may contain mural thrombus and varying amounts of calcification.
Calcification and thrombus may produce acoustic shadowing, which can complicate lumen assessment.
The true lumen measurement includes the entire aortic diameter including thrombus, whereas the false lumen is the residual channel remaining after thrombus narrows the lumen.
Complications of AAA include distal embolism, infection, dissection, and rupture.
EVAR, Dissection & Rupture: AAA treatment includes open surgery and endovascular aortic stent graft repair, abbreviated EVAR.
An EVAR is delivered through the common femoral artery under angiographic guidance.
On sonography, an aortic graft has hyperechoic walls that appear much brighter than normal aortic walls.
Follow-up sonography evaluates EVAR patency and looks for endoleak.
An endoleak occurs when the graft fails to isolate the aneurysm from the circulation, creating persistent flow disturbances and risk of rupture.
EVAR configurations include straight tube graft, bifurcated tube graft, and uni-iliac graft.
Normal spectral Doppler flow within the graft is triphasic.
Aortic dissection occurs when the arterial wall layers separate, predominantly disturbing the intima.
Patients with Marfan syndrome are at increased risk for dissection.
Clinical findings of dissection include intense chest pain, hypertension, abdominal pain, lower back pain, and neurologic symptoms.
Sonographically, an intimal flap may be seen as a linear echo within the aortic lumen and may sway with flowing blood.
Color Doppler can demonstrate flow within the layers of the dissection, and Doppler may show narrowed flow with increased speed.
A possible AAA may coexist with aortic dissection.
Aortic rupture has high mortality and morbidity, and aneurysms larger than 7 cm are more prone to rupture.
Clinical findings of rupture include decreased hematocrit, hypotension, pulsatile abdominal mass, abdominal bruit, back pain, abdominal pain, and lower extremity pain.
Sonographically, an abdominal aneurysm with an adjacent hematoma is diagnostic for rupture.
Pseudoaneurysm & AV Fistula: A pseudoaneurysm, or false aneurysm, is a contained rupture of a blood vessel due to disruption of one or more wall layers.
Pseudoaneurysms typically result from arterial injury after interventional procedures, surgery, or trauma and may also be associated with infection.
A common site is the groin at the femoral artery after heart catheterization.
Clinical findings include recent catheterization, surgery, or trauma and a pulsatile mass near the puncture site.
Sonographically, a pseudoaneurysm appears as a perivascular hematoma containing swirling blood.
The swirling flow creates the characteristic yin-yang sign.
A neck connecting the pseudoaneurysm sac to the parent vessel should be identified.
Color Doppler demonstrates turbulent flow within the pseudoaneurysm mass.
Pulsed Doppler at the neck characteristically shows a to-and-fro waveform.
Historical treatment was prolonged compression; ultrasound-guided thrombin injection is also used.
An arteriovenous fistula is an abnormal connection between an artery and a vein.
AV fistulas may result from simultaneous puncture of a vein and artery, trauma, or biopsy.
Color Doppler may directly show the communication between the artery and vein.
An arteriovenous malformation is also a direct artery-vein communication and may be congenital or caused by surgery, malignancy, biopsy, or trauma.
AVMs often demonstrate turbulent flow and a focal accumulation of vascular structures.
Inferior Vena Cava: The inferior vena cava is the largest vein in the body.
It is formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins, usually near the level of the umbilicus.
Like the aorta, the IVC wall has three layers: tunica intima, tunica media, and tunica adventitia.
Because it is a vein, the IVC has less smooth muscle in its tunica media than the abdominal aorta.
The IVC is retroperitoneal, courses anterior to the spine, and lies right lateral to the abdominal aorta.
It passes through the vena caval foramen of the diaphragm and terminates in the right atrium.
The IVC is divided into hepatic, prerenal, renal, and postrenal segments.
Its function is to return deoxygenated blood from the lower extremities, pelvis, and abdominal organs to the heart.
The hepatic segment lies just below the diaphragm, courses posterior to the caudate lobe, and through the bare area of the liver.
The right, middle, and left hepatic veins drain into the IVC and normally show pulsatile, triphasic flow related to the right atrium.
Below the hepatic veins, the paired renal veins join the IVC from the kidneys.
The left renal vein is longer, crossing from the left hilum anterior to the aorta and posterior to the SMA before entering the IVC.
Compression of the left renal vein between the SMA and aorta is called Nutcracker syndrome or renal vein entrapment syndrome.
A retroaortic left renal vein is a normal variant in which the vein passes posterior to the aorta.
The right renal vein is shorter because of its close proximity to the IVC.
Renal veins normally demonstrate low-velocity, continuous flow.
The right gonadal vein drains directly into the anterior aspect of the IVC, whereas the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein.
On sonography, the hepatic IVC appears as an anechoic sagittal tube forming the posterior border of the caudate lobe.
In transverse imaging, the prerenal and renal IVC are oval and seen to the right of the aorta; the postrenal segment may be difficult to visualize.
The IVC diameter should not exceed 2.5 cm and varies with respiration; it initially collapses with deep inspiration, sniffing, and Valsalva.
The IVC Doppler waveform is pulsatile near the heart and more phasic near the common iliac veins.
IVC Pathology: Budd-Chiari syndrome is occlusion of the hepatic veins, with possible coexisting occlusion of the IVC.
Budd-Chiari syndrome may occur secondary to congenital webbing, coagulation abnormalities, hepatocellular carcinoma invasion, thrombosis, oral contraceptive use, pregnancy, or trauma.
The hepatic veins may become narrowed in Budd-Chiari syndrome.
Enlargement of the hepatic veins and IVC is often seen with right-sided heart failure.
Right-sided heart failure is the most common cause of IVC obstruction leading to enlargement and is the most common cause of IVC enlargement.
IVC thrombosis commonly presents with IVC enlargement, absent flow, and intraluminal material.
Acute thrombus may be completely anechoic and therefore can be overlooked initially.
Over time, thrombus becomes more echogenic and may calcify, producing acoustic shadowing.
An IVC filter, also called a Greenfield inferior vena cava filter, is placed to trap emboli traveling upstream and help prevent pulmonary embolus.
Sonography can evaluate an IVC filter for proper placement and assess complications such as IVC perforation.
Duplex imaging can also show patency and demonstrate flow only around the filter if a large thromboembolus is trapped centrally.
Tumor invasion of the IVC is most often associated with renal cell carcinoma.
Wilms tumor and transitional cell carcinoma of the kidney may also infiltrate the IVC.
Tumors usually extend from the renal vein into the IVC and may advance into the heart.
IVC tumor extension occurs more commonly on the right because the right renal vein is shorter.
Portal Venous System: The main portal vein is formed by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein.
This junction is called the portal splenic confluence or portal confluence and lies posterior to the pancreatic neck.
The confluence consists of the splenic vein, superior mesenteric vein, and sometimes the inferior mesenteric vein.
In some individuals, the inferior mesenteric vein drains into the splenic vein instead of directly joining the confluence.
The portal confluence lies in the midabdomen and collects blood from the intestines and spleen.
The portal venous system is not directly connected to the IVC.
The main portal vein courses toward the liver and enters at the porta hepatis.
Within the liver, it divides into right and left portal veins to supply the respective lobes.
Normal portal venous flow should be hepatopetal and monophasic.
Portal venous flow may vary somewhat with respiration and after meals.
The portal vein diameter is typically less than 13 mm, although it can vary with respiration.
The splenic vein lies posterior to the pancreatic body and tail.
Normal flow in the splenic vein should be toward the midline.
Other smaller contributors to the portal venous system include the inferior mesenteric vein and coronary vein, though they are not typically seen sonographically.

Noncardiac Chest Anatomy: The noncardiac chest may be assessed sonographically when needed, and sonographers should understand basic lung and pleural anatomy.
The left lung typically contains two lobes: superior and inferior.
The right lung typically contains three lobes: superior, middle, and inferior.
Each lung is covered by a thin layer called the visceral pleura, which closely invests the lung surface.
The inner lining of the chest wall is covered by pleural tissue called the parietal pleura.
A normal small amount of fluid lies between the visceral and parietal pleurae within the pleural space.
This normal pleural fluid allows the lungs to slide freely with respiration.
Real-time assessment of pleural motion relies on recognizing normal lung sliding between the pleural layers.
The mediastinum is the central chest compartment between the pleural sacs and contains the heart, thymus, part of the trachea, esophagus, and many lymph nodes.
Knowledge of pleural anatomy is important because pleural abnormalities may be seen incidentally during abdominal sonography.
Pleural & Pericardial Effusion: During abdominal sonography, the lower chest should always be evaluated for pleural effusion.
A pleural effusion is excessive fluid accumulation around the lung within the pleural space.
Simple pleural fluid tends to collect dependently and appears anechoic sonographically.
The lung may be seen floating within pleural fluid.
Pleural effusions may be classified as transudates or exudates.
Transudative effusions result from an imbalance in oncotic and hydrostatic pressure.
Exudative effusions typically result from inflammation or reduced lymphatic drainage.
A pleural effusion associated with pneumonia is termed a parapneumonic effusion.
Pleural fluid containing pus is called empyema.
Complex pleural fluid may indicate malignancy, infection, or blood.
Thoracentesis may be performed for diagnosis or therapy, usually with the patient upright and posterior access to the fluid.
Pericardial effusion may also be detected during abdominal sonography and most often appears as anechoic fluid surrounding the heart.
Pneumothorax: A pneumothorax is free air within the chest outside the lungs and can lead to lung collapse.
One complication of thoracentesis is development of a pneumothorax.
Sonographic B-mode real-time assessment looks for normal lung sliding.
In pneumothorax, air separates the visceral and parietal pleura, preventing visualization of normal lung sliding.
M-mode may be used sonographically to demonstrate evidence of pneumothorax.
The seashore sign on M-mode is a normal finding and indicates lung sliding.
The barcode sign on M-mode indicates a pneumothorax.
The barcode sign is also referred to as the stratosphere sign.
Although pneumothorax may occasionally be seen with sonography, it is better diagnosed with a chest radiograph.
Failure to identify normal lung sliding is the key sonographic clue because pleural air blocks normal pleural apposition.
Lung Masses & Consolidation: Superficial lung masses may be detected with sonography.
Large lung cancers and pleural or surface irregularities can be further evaluated with ultrasound.
Sonography can assist biopsy of accessible superficial lung or chest masses.
In pediatric patients, sonography may evaluate pulmonary sequestration.
Congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation is another pediatric chest mass that may be assessed sonographically.
Mediastinal tumors such as lymphoma and thymoma may also be analyzed sonographically.
In children, the normal thymus lies posterior to the sternum and appears as echogenic tissue containing linear and punctate echogenicities.
Before puberty, the thymus is vital for T-cell development; after puberty it gradually atrophies and is replaced by fat in adults.
Lung consolidation is replacement of normal air-filled alveoli by fluid, inflammation, blood, or neoplastic cells.
Causes of consolidation include pneumonia, pulmonary edema, hemorrhage, and carcinoma.
Sonographically, consolidation may resemble liver or spleen tissue but usually contains several internal linear echoes from air within the bronchi.
Pleural effusion is often seen in association with lung consolidation.
Retroperitoneum Anatomy: The retroperitoneum lies posterior to the parietal peritoneum and anterior to the transversalis fascia.
Superiorly, the retroperitoneum is bounded by the diaphragm.
Inferiorly, the retroperitoneum is bounded by the pelvic brim.
Major retroperitoneal vessels include the abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava.
Smaller vascular structures in the retroperitoneum include the superior mesenteric artery, hepatic artery, splenic artery, and splenic vein.
Prominent muscles adjacent to the kidneys include the psoas muscles and the quadratus lumborum.
On transverse renal imaging, the quadratus lumborum is posterior to the kidney and more lateral on the image.
On transverse renal imaging, the psoas muscle is posterior to the kidney and closer to the spine.
The crura of the diaphragm are paired linear muscular portions of the diaphragm attached to the anterolateral surfaces of the upper lumbar vertebrae.
Sonographically, the crura appear as hypoechoic structures in the longitudinal plane extending caudally into the abdomen anterior to the spine.
The right crus can be seen as a linear hypoechoic structure anterior to the spine and posterior to the inferior vena cava.
Recognizing normal retroperitoneal muscles and crura helps avoid mistaking them for pathologic masses.
Retroperitoneal Lymphadenopathy: Retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy refers to enlargement of abdominal lymph nodes within the abdomen.
Normal abdominal lymph nodes are typically not seen sonographically.
Normal abdominal lymph nodes measure less than 1 cm.
Within the abdomen, lymph nodes are located in the mesentery, renal hilum, and along the length of the abdominal aorta.
Enlargement of abdominal lymph nodes greater than 1 cm in diameter may indicate infection.
Enlarged abdominal nodes may also indicate malignancy such as lymphoma.
The sandwich sign describes abdominal nodes surrounding and compressing the aorta and inferior vena cava.
Enlarged nodes deviate from their normal sonographic appearance and become more hypoechoic.
Some enlarged nodes may appear anechoic.
Compression or deviation of adjacent vessels by nodal tissue is an important clue to bulky retroperitoneal adenopathy.
Retroperitoneal Fibrosis & Hematoma: Retroperitoneal fibrosis is development of a fibrous mass involving the abdominal aorta, inferior vena cava, ureters, and sacrum.
The cause of retroperitoneal fibrosis is usually unknown.
Reported associations of retroperitoneal fibrosis include infections, migraine headache medication, malignant disease, and aneurysm rupture or leakage.
Clinical symptoms of retroperitoneal fibrosis include back pain, flank pain, weight loss, nausea, vomiting, and malaise.
Sonographically, retroperitoneal fibrosis appears as a large hypoechoic mass surrounding the abdominal aorta.
Retroperitoneal hematoma most commonly occurs within the psoas muscles.
Retroperitoneal hematoma is especially associated with hemophiliac patients.
Additional clinical associations for retroperitoneal hematoma include trauma and recent surgery.
Laboratory findings for retroperitoneal hematoma include a drop in hematocrit.
Pain is also a clinical finding with retroperitoneal hematoma.
Depending on the stage of blood, a retroperitoneal hematoma may appear hypoechoic, complex, or hyperechoic.
When evaluating the psoas region, variable hematoma echogenicity can mimic other masses, so clinical history and hematocrit are important clues.

Anatomy and Physiology of the Salivary G: Salivary glands are exocrine glands that produce saliva and release it into the oral cavity through ducts.
Saliva aids in digestion and is mostly composed of water.
Saliva also contains electrolytes and digestive enzymes such as amylase and lipase.
There are three paired groups of salivary glands: parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands.
The parotid glands are the largest salivary glands and therefore the most likely to be evaluated with sonography.
The parotid glands are located bilaterally anterior to the ears and extend inferiorly.
Parotid glands are bounded anteriorly by the rami of the mandibles and posteriorly by the mastoid processes of the temporal bones.
The sternocleidomastoid muscles lie posterior to the parotid glands.
The parotid gland can be divided into three anatomic lobes.
The main duct of the parotid gland is the Stensen duct.
The bilateral submandibular glands lie beneath the floor of the mouth, bordered laterally by the body of the mandible and superiorly by musculature.
The submandibular gland drains through the Wharton duct, and the sublingual glands lie under the tongue anterior to the submandibular glands.
Sonography of the Salivary Glands: Salivary glands are most often examined with a high-frequency linear transducer.
When glands are enlarged, a lower-frequency transducer may be required for adequate penetration.
A standoff device may be useful for superficial masses.
When salivary gland disease is suspected, both sides should be scanned for comparison because many disorders affect both glands.
Normal salivary glands are typically hyperechoic relative to adjacent musculature.
The ducts may be recognized as anechoic tubular structures, especially when dilated.
Color flow imaging should be used to distinguish dilated ducts from nearby vascular structures.
Salivary glands should be imaged in both sagittal and transverse planes.
The parotid gland appears elliptical in the sagittal plane.
The parotid gland appears round in the transverse plane.
The sublingual glands are round, whereas the submandibular glands are more triangular in shape.
If malignancy is suspected, the cervical lymphatic chain should also be evaluated.
Pathology of the Salivary Glands: Sjögren syndrome is an autoimmune disease affecting moisture-producing glands, causing salivary gland dysfunction and severe dryness of the eyes, nose, skin, and mouth.
Sjögren syndrome appears sonographically heterogeneous, hyperemic, visibly enlarged, and may contain diffuse hypoechoic regions.
Sialadenitis is inflammation of one or more salivary glands.
Sialadenitis may appear heterogeneous, hyperemic, visibly enlarged, and may contain diffuse hypoechoic regions.
Sialolithiasis refers to salivary duct stones and is most commonly located within the submandibular gland.
Sialolithiasis appears as a dilated duct containing one or more shadowing echogenic foci.
Sialadenosis is a benign, painless enlargement of a salivary gland, usually affecting both parotid glands.
Sialadenosis appears as an enlarged gland without hypervascularity.
Pleomorphic adenoma is benign and the most frequent salivary gland tumor, most commonly seen in the parotid gland.
Pleomorphic adenoma appears as a hypoechoic mass; biopsy is often warranted.
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common salivary gland malignancy and typically starts in the parotid gland.
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma appears as a hypoechoic or heterogeneous mass with moderate to marked internal vascularity; biopsy is often warranted.
Ranula is a mucus retention cyst in the floor of the mouth arising from an obstructed sublingual or minor salivary duct.
A ranula is well-defined and homogeneous, usually hypoechoic or anechoic; an infected cyst appears complex.
Anatomy and Physiology of the Thyroid Gl: The thyroid gland is a crucial endocrine gland that develops during the third week of gestation.
Embryologically, the thyroid begins at the base of the tongue.
It descends along the thyroglossal duct to rest anterior to the trachea.
