The thyroid is fully functional by the end of the first trimester.
The gland consists of right and left lobes connected by the isthmus.
The isthmus crosses the midline of the neck anterior to the trachea.
A superior extension of the isthmus is a normal variant called a pyramidal lobe.
Agenesis of a lobe may occur, and ectopic thyroid tissue can also occur.
The hypothalamus produces thyroid-releasing hormone, which controls release of thyroid-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary gland.
The thyroid contains multiple follicles filled with colloid.
Colloid is composed of proteins and thyroid hormones.
In response to TSH, the thyroid releases thyroxine, triiodothyronine, and calcitonin.
Thyroxine and triiodothyronine aid metabolism of fats, proteins, and carbohydrates, while calcitonin removes calcium from blood for storage in bone.
The thyroid uses iodine to produce its hormones, and thyroxine is the most abundant thyroid hormone.
Vascular Anatomy of the Thyroid Gland an: Two prominent vascular structures lateral to the thyroid are the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein.
The most medial of these vessels is the common carotid artery.
Above the thyroid gland, the common carotid artery branches into the internal and external carotid arteries.
The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid artery.
The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery.
These arteries have corresponding thyroid veins.
The thyroid veins drain into the internal jugular vein.
The jugular veins are located superior and lateral to the common carotid arteries.
On sonography, the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein are seen lateral to each thyroid lobe.
These vessels appear as anechoic tubes in longitudinal imaging and circles in transverse imaging.
Sonography of the Thyroid and Neck: A thyroid sonogram may be ordered for a palpable neck mass, abnormal laboratory findings, or follow-up of nuclear medicine or other imaging studies.
Before the examination, the sonographer should stand behind the patient and palpate the thyroid to detect palpable nodules.
A high-frequency linear transducer is used for thyroid and neck sonography.
The patient should be supine with the neck extended.
Normal thyroid tissue is homogeneous with medium- to high-level echogenicity similar to the testes.
Images are obtained in both sagittal and transverse planes of each lobe and the isthmus.
Each adult pear-shaped lobe measures about 4 to 6 cm long, 2 to 3 cm wide, and 1 to 2 cm thick.
The right thyroid lobe is typically the largest.
The isthmus normally measures 2 to 6 mm in anteroposterior dimension.
Thyroid volume is calculated as length × width × thickness × 0.529.
The strap muscles are anterior, sternocleidomastoid muscles lateral, and longus colli muscles posterior to the thyroid lobes.
The esophagus lies posterior to the thyroid, usually on the left, and can mimic a mass; swallowing demonstrates saliva passing through it.
Color Doppler should assess each lobe because Graves disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis can show increased vascularity.
Thyroid nodules should be measured in two planes and evaluated with color Doppler; elastography may help characterize relative stiffness.
Fine-needle aspiration is a low-risk, highly efficient procedure, and sonographic guidance is especially beneficial.
Goiter: A goiter is an enlarged or hyperplastic thyroid gland.
Causes of goiter include iodine deficiency, Graves disease, and thyroiditis.
Patients often have a palpable, and sometimes visibly enlarged, thyroid gland.
An enlarged thyroid may cause throat tightness, dysphagia, dyspnea, coughing, and hoarseness.
Thyroid enlargement can be assessed by calculating thyroid volume measurements.
Goiter may also be suggested by an isthmus anteroposterior measurement greater than 1.0 cm.
An enlarged thyroid with multiple nodules containing cystic and solid components may be called a multinodular goiter.
A multinodular goiter may also be referred to as an adenomatous goiter.
Graves Disease and Hyperthyroidism: Hyperthyroidism results from overproduction of thyroid hormones.
Graves disease, also called diffuse toxic goiter, is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism.
Clinical findings include exophthalmos, heat intolerance, nervousness, weight loss with increased appetite, and hair loss.
Additional findings include tachycardia, palpitations, muscle wasting, fine tremors, oligomenorrhea, and pretibial myxedema.
High-output heart failure may also occur.
Sonographically, the thyroid may be enlarged.
The gland may appear diffusely heterogeneous or diffusely hypoechoic.
Color Doppler may show marked hypervascularity throughout the thyroid gland.
This hypervascular Doppler appearance is termed thyroid inferno.
Color Doppler evaluation is important because Graves disease yields increased vascularity within the thyroid.
Hashimoto Thyroiditis and Hypothryoidism: Hypothyroidism results from underproduction of thyroid hormones.
Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease and the most common cause of hypothyroidism in the United States.
It may also be called chronic autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis.
With Hashimoto disease, the thyroid becomes inflamed and produces smaller amounts of thyroid hormones.
To compensate, the pituitary releases more TSH, which causes thyroid enlargement.
Many patients are asymptomatic in the early stages of disease.
As disease progresses, findings may include pallor, puffiness under the eyes, puffy face, dry skin, slight weight gain, and depression.
Other clinical findings include increased cold sensitivity, peripheral edema, muscle weakness, menorrhagia, slow pulse, and elevated blood cholesterol levels.
The end stage may lead to fibrosis and atrophy of the gland.
Sonographically, the thyroid appears diffusely heterogeneous and coarse.
The gland is often mildly enlarged initially.
Multiple ill-defined hypoechoic regions separated by fibrous hyperechoic tissue are often present.
Color Doppler demonstrates increased vascularity within the gland.
Hashimoto thyroiditis, like Graves disease, yields increased thyroid vascularity with color Doppler interrogation.
Benign Nodules: Benign thyroid nodules are the most common masses identified within the thyroid gland on sonography.
Up to 68% of adults have sonographically identifiable thyroid nodules.
Benign nodules may be follicular adenomas, adenomatous or hyperplastic nodules, or colloid nodules.
Follicular adenomas are often small and round.
Follicular adenomas may appear completely anechoic, isoechoic, or hyperechoic.
A surrounding halo may be present around a follicular adenoma.
Nodular hyperplasia is the most common cause of thyroid nodules.
Hyperplastic nodules, also called adenomatous nodules, are almost always multiple.
Many benign thyroid nodules contain cystic components.
Colloid cysts may contain hyperechoic foci that produce comet-tail artifact.
Benign sonographic characteristics include extensive cystic components, cysts smaller than 5 mm, hyperechoic mass, eggshell calcifications, spongiform composition, and wider-than-tall shape.
A hot nodule on nuclear medicine study is a benign characteristic.
Large benign nodules may become palpable and cause dysphagia or general neck discomfort.
Malignant Thyroid Nodules: Papillary carcinoma is the most common form of thyroid cancer.
Other thyroid malignancies include follicular carcinoma, medullary carcinoma, anaplastic carcinoma, lymphoma, and metastases to the thyroid.
Malignant thyroid nodules are difficult to diagnose with sonography alone.
Microcalcifications within a thyroid mass increase the likelihood of malignancy.
These calcifications may be called psammoma bodies.
Psammoma bodies are round calcific deposits that appear as punctate hyperechoic foci without acoustic shadowing.
A solitary hypoechoic thyroid mass is suspicious for malignancy.
Malignant sonographic features include a taller-than-wide shape and lobulated margins.
Interrupted peripheral calcification and extracapsular invasion are also concerning features.
Marked vascularity within the central part of the nodule suggests malignancy.
Enlargement of cervical lymph nodes may indicate metastatic disease.
A cold nodule on nuclear medicine imaging is a malignant characteristic, although not all cold nodules are malignant.
Elastography may be used as an adjunct; stiffer nodules generally have an increased risk for malignancy.
TI-RADS: TI-RADS was created by the American College of Radiology as a standardized system for describing thyroid nodules.
The system helps reduce unnecessary follow-up, further imaging, and biopsies.
TI-RADS places thyroid nodules into five levels, TR1 through TR5.
Classification is based on five ultrasound features: composition, echogenicity, shape, margin, and punctate echogenic foci.
The more points a nodule receives, the higher the risk for malignancy.
The most worrisome nodules tend to contain punctate echogenic foci.
They also tend to be hypoechoic.
Irregular margins that may extend beyond normal thyroid margins are worrisome.
The least worrisome nodules tend to be anechoic, wider-than-tall, and smooth-margined.
Large comet-tail artifact or no echogenic foci at all is less worrisome.
The total point sum assigns a TI-RADS score from 0 to 7 or more.
TR5 is the highest category and is considered highly suspicious.
Nuclear Medicine and Thyroid Nodules: Nuclear medicine uses thyroid scintigraphy to classify nodules as hyperfunctioning or hypofunctioning.
The examination involves injection of a radiopharmaceutical that is high in iodine.
Because the thyroid uses iodine to create hormones, the drug is absorbed by the thyroid gland.
Images are obtained with a camera that detects radioactivity within the neck.
The resulting image displays thyroid tissue and thyroid nodules.
Hyperfunctioning nodules are called hot nodules.
Hot nodules appear as dark areas on the thyroid scan.
Hypofunctioning nodules are called cold nodules.
Cold nodules appear as light or blank areas on the scan.
Most thyroid cancers are hypofunctioning and therefore appear as cold nodules.
Not all cold nodules are malignant.
Sonography and nuclear medicine can complement each other in nodule evaluation.
In almost all situations, fine-needle aspiration is needed for the most definitive diagnosis.
Anatomy and Physiology of the Parathyroi: There are typically two pairs of parathyroid glands.
Some individuals may have a fifth parathyroid gland.
Commonly, one gland is near the posterior aspect of the midportion of each thyroid lobe.
Another gland is often positioned inferior to each thyroid lobe.
Normal parathyroid glands measure approximately 5.0 mm × 3.0 mm × 1.0 mm.
Their sonographic appearance is similar to thyroid tissue.
The parathyroid glands regulate calcium for the body.
They control the release and absorption of calcium by producing parathyroid hormone.
Elevated serum calcium is called hypercalcemia.
Low serum calcium is called hypocalcemia.
Hyperparathyroidism can cause hypercalcemia, whereas hypoparathyroidism can cause hypocalcemia.
Parathyroid Adenoma: A parathyroid adenoma is the most common cause of enlargement of a parathyroid gland.
Patients typically present with elevated serum calcium levels.
Parathyroid hormone levels are also elevated, indicating hyperparathyroidism.
Hypercalcemia should prompt careful analysis of the neck for a parathyroid adenoma.
Sonographically, a parathyroid adenoma appears as a solid mass.
The mass is most likely hypoechoic relative to the adjacent thyroid gland.
The lesion is located adjacent to the thyroid.
Clinical findings specifically include elevated serum calcium and elevated PTH.
Cervical Lymph Nodes: Cervical lymphadenopathy refers to enlargement of the cervical lymph nodes.
Cervical lymph node enlargement can be established sonographically.
Normal cervical lymph nodes usually measure less than 1 cm.
They are commonly encountered during routine sonographic examination of the neck.
Normal nodes are typically oblong, hypoechoic structures with a distinguishable echogenic hilum.
Abnormal lymph nodes may result from infection or malignancy.
Abnormal nodes are enlarged, measuring greater than 1 cm.
They may become more rounded in shape.
Loss of the normal echogenic hilum is suspicious.
Calcifications within a node are abnormal.
Color Doppler may show hyperemia or other abnormal vascular patterns.
Patients may have a palpable neck mass, and enlarged nodes may be painful.
In the postsurgical neck after thyroidectomy for cancer, a thorough search for lymphadenopathy is important to assess metastatic disease.
Thyroglossal Duct Cyst: Thyroglossal duct cysts are benign congenital cysts of the neck.
They are located in the midline of the neck superior to the thyroid gland.
They are typically located below the level of the hyoid bone.
These cysts are most often asymptomatic.
They may become painful when inflamed or infected.
A simple thyroglossal duct cyst appears anechoic, well-defined, and unilocular.
Posterior acoustic enhancement is expected with a simple cyst.
Complicated or infected thyroglossal duct cysts appear more complex.
A palpable midline neck mass superior to the thyroid is a typical clinical presentation.
Branchial cleft cysts are also congenital neck cysts but are usually near the angle of the mandible.
Branchial cleft cysts typically appear as an anechoic mass with posterior enhancement and may be painful if infected.
Fibromatosis Colli: Fibromatosis colli is a rare pediatric fibrous tumor located within the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Its cause is unknown, but malposition in utero or traumatic birth is suspected to lead to fibrosis within the muscle.
The intramuscular fibrous mass shortens the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
This shortening twists the infant's chin toward the nonaffected side.
That clinical deformity is termed congenital muscular torticollis.
Patients present with a pediatric palpable neck mass.
Sonographically, the mass distorts the normal shape of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
The lesion often has a fusiform pattern.
It may appear hypoechoic, hyperechoic, or isoechoic relative to adjacent tissue.
Calcifications may be present and can shadow.
Color Doppler may show a hyperemic blood flow pattern.
Lymphangioma (Cystic Hygroma): Lymphangioma is another name for cystic hygroma.
It is a neck mass that may require sonographic evaluation.
These lesions are typically found in the posterior neck.
They are often identified in utero or during the neonatal period.
A lymphangioma consists of a buildup of lymphatic fluid.
Clinically, it may present as a pediatric palpable neck mass.
Pain may occur with inflammation or hemorrhage.
Sonographically, it is often a thin-walled mass.
The lesion is typically hypoechoic or anechoic.
Septations are commonly present within the mass.

Sonographic Appearance of Muscles, Tendo: Musculoskeletal structures are typically imaged with a linear array transducer for improved resolution.
A basic appreciation of the location of bones and superficial muscles is important during musculoskeletal imaging.
Muscles appear sonographically as hypoechoic tissue containing linear echogenic strands.
Tendons are echogenic, fibrous structures that connect muscle to bone.
Ligaments connect bone to bone and also appear echogenic sonographically.
For appropriate tendon imaging, the transducer is generally placed perpendicular to the tendon.
Altering the angle of insonation may help distinguish a tendon from adjacent fat.
Normal tendons demonstrate an echogenic fibrillated appearance.
Thin echogenic peritenon may surround a normal tendon.
Normal ligaments show a fibrillar pattern.
Ligaments may have a triangular shape with broad and tapered attachments across a joint space.
Tendonitis: Tendonitis is inflammation of a tendon and may be diffuse or focal.
It may be caused by overuse or strain.
Patients commonly present with pain in the affected region.
The painful region may be swollen.
The painful region may be warm to the touch.
Fever may be present in the troubled area.
Diffuse tendonitis appears as an enlarged, thickened, hypoechoic tendon.
Focal tendonitis appears as a localized enlarged hypoechoic area within the tendon.
Hyperemic flow may be noted within the tendon with color Doppler.
Fluid may be present around the involved tendon.
Fluid within the synovial sheath often indicates tendosynovitis.
Color Doppler hyperemia is an important supportive sonographic finding.
Tendon Rupture: A tendon rupture may also be referred to as a tear.
Tendon tears most likely result from some manner of recreational sport.
Tendon tears may be partial or complete.
Patients commonly present with significant pain in the injured region.
Edema is a typical clinical finding.
An audible snap may be heard at the time of rupture.
Partial tears appear as focal hypoechoic areas within the tendon.
Complete tears appear as an anechoic or heterogeneous area within the tendon, often indicating hematoma.
Complete ruptures may show refractive shadowing at the site of the separated tendon.
Fat, hematoma, or granulomatous material may fill the gap created by a complete tear.
Extensive surrounding edema and corresponding fluid accumulation are commonly present.
Achilles Tendon: The Achilles tendon, also called the calcaneal tendon, is the most commonly injured ankle tendon.
It is located along the posterior ankle.
It connects the calf muscle, the gastrocnemius, to the posterior surface of the heel, or calcaneus.
For sonographic evaluation, the patient lies prone with the feet hanging off the end of the bed.
Both symptomatic and asymptomatic Achilles tendons should be scanned for comparison.
The entire tendon should be evaluated in sagittal and transverse planes.
A landscape image of the entire painful tendon may be useful.
The tendon should be assessed for the sonographic signs of tendonitis and rupture.
Patients may present with posterior ankle and leg pain.
Patients with rupture may report hearing an audible snap.
The Thompson test is used clinically to evaluate for a complete tear.
During the Thompson test, squeezing the calf should cause plantarflexion if there is not a complete tear.
Achilles tendon tears follow general tendon tear patterns: partial tears are focal hypoechoic defects, and complete tears show an anechoic or heterogeneous gap, often with hematoma.
Developmental Hip Dysplasia (DDH): Developmental dysplasia of the hip is a congenital anomaly that may be described as a shallow hip socket.
In DDH, the femoral head is prevented from resting appropriately in the acetabulum.
The acetabulum is the natural socket on the pelvis for the femoral head.
A normal hip has the femoral head sitting snugly within the acetabulum.
Flattening or shallowing of the acetabulum prevents proper femoral head positioning.
The femoral head position relative to the acetabulum may be described as normal, subluxed, or dislocated.
Subluxation denotes partial dislocation of the hip.
Complete dislocation means the femoral head lies outside the acetabulum.
DDH: DDH is thought to result from abnormal fetal ligament development within the hip intensified by excessive circulating maternal estrogen.
Risk is increased by fetal malposition such as breech presentation and by oligohydramnios.
DDH is more common in female infants.
It most often affects the left side.
It has been linked with spina bifida and arthrogryposis.
A familial link is also described.
Screening is recommended between 4 and 6 weeks after birth.
Clinical findings include asymmetric skinfolds on the legs, leg length discrepancy, and limited limb abduction.
The Barlow test evaluates the hip for dislocation.
For the Barlow test, the hip is flexed and adducted, and the knee is pushed posteriorly and superiorly.
The Ortolani test evaluates reduction or relocation of a dislocated hip by abducting and lifting the thigh.
During the Ortolani test, an audible click and palpable clunk may occur as the femoral head passes over the acetabulum.
The femoral head and acetabulum should be examined sonographically in both stress and relaxed states using coronal and transverse high-frequency linear imaging.
In the coronal plane, the femoral head is a hypoechoic rounded structure with echogenic stripes, and DDH is suggested by a small alpha angle, large beta angle, or less than 50% acetabular coverage.
Infant Hip Joint Effusion: Hip joint effusion is buildup of fluid within the hip secondary to inflammation.
It typically occurs in children between 5 and 10 years of age.
It is most likely the result of transient synovitis.
Transient synovitis is also called toxic synovitis or irritable hip.
Transient synovitis is the most common cause of a painful hip and joint effusion in children.
The cause is unknown, though viral causes, trauma, and allergic reaction have been suspected.
Patients typically present with leg and knee pain.
Reluctance to walk is a common clinical finding.
Sonographically, anechoic or hypoechoic fluid elevates the anterior joint capsule.
The abnormal hip joint capsule width typically exceeds 5 mm.
Scanning the asymptomatic hip first provides a useful baseline before evaluating the symptomatic hip.
Breast Sonography: Mammography is the gold standard for breast imaging, but sonographers should understand basic breast anatomy.
Breast findings are commonly annotated by quadrant or clockface location.
Some institutions also use 123 annotation for distance from the nipple and ABC annotation for depth.
Some facilities localize pathology by fingers from the nipple or by direct measurement.
A linear transducer is typically used for breast sonography.
The patient may be placed in a slight posterior oblique position to distribute breast tissue evenly over the chest.
Superficial pathology is better visualized with a standoff device or a large amount of mounded gel.
Images may be obtained in transverse and longitudinal planes.
Because the lactiferous ducts are radially arranged, radial and antiradial planes may also be used.
The three breast tissue layers from superficial to deep are subcutaneous, mammary, and retromammary.
The subcutaneous layer is typically hypoechoic and composed mostly of fat.
The mammary layer is typically hyperechoic, contains ducts and glandular tissue, and is the functional layer of the breast.
The mammary layer appearance varies with patient age and distribution of functional elements.
The retromammary layer is typically hypoechoic and also contains fat.
Mastitis and Breast Abscess: Mastitis is breast infection and is most often associated with lactation.
Breastfeeding-related mastitis is referred to as puerperal mastitis.
Mastitis may also be encountered following trauma or surgery.
The infection is characteristically caused by Staphylococcus or Streptococcus organisms.
Patients with mastitis have pain, swelling, warmth, and redness in the area.
The primary role of sonography is to determine whether a focal abscess is present within the affected breast.
Mastitis appears as ill-defined areas of echogenicity with diffuse edema.
Hypoechoic fluid within the subcutaneous tissue may outline the fat lobules.
Affected skin may measure greater than 2 mm in thickness.
Reactive enlarged lymph nodes may be seen.
A breast abscess is a focal area of pus and may present as a palpable painful lump.
An abscess typically appears as a focal complex fluid collection containing debris, with peripheral hyperemia on color Doppler.
Postsurgical Breast: The postsurgical breast can develop complications that require sonographic evaluation.
After surgery or an invasive procedure, mastitis may occur.
A postsurgical breast abscess may also develop.
Other complications include hematoma, seroma, and lymphedema.
A breast hematoma should especially be considered after trauma or surgery.
Patients with hematoma likely have regional pain and skin discoloration.
A hematoma often appears complex sonographically.
With time, a hematoma usually disappears as it is reabsorbed by the body.
Occasionally scar tissue and calcifications may remain after hematoma resolution.
A seroma commonly results after surgery such as lumpectomy or complete mastectomy.
A seroma represents simple serous fluid filling a vacated region.
Serous fluid is sterile and contains no red blood cells.
A seroma typically appears as an anechoic fluid collection.
Galactocele: A galactocele is a milk-filled breast cyst.
Lactating patients may present with a palpable mass that may be painful.
A galactocele can develop after an abrupt termination of breastfeeding.
It may also result from obstruction of one or more lactiferous ducts.
The mass is typically palpable and located near the areola.
They can become infected as well.
Sonographically, a galactocele appears as a round mass with good borders.
A fluid-fluid level may be present within the mass.
Gynecomastia: Gynecomastia is the benign enlargement of the male breast.
It can occur at any time but is most commonly encountered just after birth, during puberty, and from 50 to 80 years of age.
It can be associated with high levels of human chorionic gonadotropin produced by some testicular tumors.
High estrogen levels are another association.
Other associations include adrenal tumors, hepatoblastoma, and Klinefelter syndrome.
Some drugs, including steroids and marijuana, are associated with gynecomastia.
Patients most often present with a tender palpable retroareolar breast mass.
The mass is typically firm to touch.
Sonographically, gynecomastia appears as a hypoechoic mass posterior to the areola.
The mass may have a triangular shape.
Sonography of Superficial Structures: Soft-tissue sonography typically requires a high-frequency linear transducer.
If the area of interest lies deeper than expected, a lower frequency transducer may be used.
Sonographers should understand the anatomy and sonographic appearance of skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, and muscle.
The skin consists of the epidermis and dermis.
The epidermis and dermis are indistinguishable sonographically.
Together, the epidermis and dermis appear as a hyperechoic linear structure.
Hyperechoic linear echoes within the subcutaneous tissue represent connective tissue septa.
Fascia appears as a hyperechoic layer of varying thickness.
Superficial Epidermoid Cyst: A superficial epidermal cyst may also be called an epidermal inclusion cyst or epidermoid cyst.
It may also be called a sebaceous cyst, although true sebaceous cysts are uncommon and the term is not always accurate.
These cysts are most likely found in the scalp, face, neck, trunk, or back.
They may also result from trauma or an obstructed hair follicle.
Patients usually have a visible palpable mass just beneath the skin that raises the skin surface.
These lesions are most likely asymptomatic.
If infected, pain and redness may develop.
Infection can also cause oozing of fluid or solid material from the cyst.
Sonographic appearance varies and may be anechoic, hypoechoic, complex, or hyperechoic.
They have been described as having a pseudotestis appearance.
A standoff device can be used to better visualize these superficial cysts.
Ganglion Cyst: A ganglion cyst is a common cyst found adjacent to a joint or tendon.
It is most often located along the dorsal aspect of the hand and wrist.
Ganglion cysts can arise from any joint and may also be found in the knee, foot, and ankle.
Within the wrist, the most common type is the dorsal ganglion cyst.
Those near the radial artery are referred to as volar ganglion cysts.
Large wrist ganglion cysts have been called Bible bumps.
Clinically, the mass may be hard to touch and painful.
Treatment may include corticosteroid injection or surgical removal.
Sonographically, a ganglion cyst typically appears as a noncompressible anechoic mass.
Posterior acoustic enhancement is usually present.
Superficial Lipoma and Hemangioma: A lipoma is a benign fatty tumor.
Superficial lipomas are typically oval in shape.
They are usually isoechoic to surrounding fat but may appear hypoechoic or hyperechoic.
They may be observed during physical examination as an obvious mass under the skin.
Some patients complain of unsightly bulging of the skin over the lipoma.
A superficial hemangioma is a benign mass composed of vascular channels.
They appear as a raised red or reddish purple skin mass.
Blood flow may be detectable with color Doppler.
Meniscal Cyst: A meniscus is thin fibrocartilaginous tissue between the surfaces of some joints, such as the knee.
Meniscal cysts are most often thought to occur from fluid collection following a meniscal tear in the knee.
A meniscal tear is typically the result of trauma or degenerative changes within the knee.
Patients often present with focal knee pain.
A palpable mass within the knee joint may be present.
Patients may also report joint popping.
Locking of the knee joint may occur.
Previous trauma is a common clinical history.
Sonographically, meniscal cysts typically appear anechoic or hypoechoic.
The cyst is typically seen in close proximity to the meniscus.
Baker Cyst: A Baker cyst is also referred to as a popliteal cyst or synovial cyst.
It is located in the popliteal fossa behind the knee.
They result from accumulation of synovial fluid due to weakening in the knee joint capsule.
They may be seen with conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or osteoarthritis.
A channel or tract may be seen connecting the cyst to the joint space.
They may also cause focal tenderness in the popliteal fossa.
Symptoms may result from hemorrhage, rupture, or impingement on adjacent structures.
Clinical findings may mimic those of deep venous thrombosis.
Sonographically, a Baker cyst appears as an anechoic mass with posterior enhancement in the popliteal fossa.
Complicated Baker cysts may contain echogenic fluid, debris, pannus, or septations.
Pilonidal Cyst: A pilonidal cyst is most often found within the natal cleft between the buttocks.
The natal cleft is also called the intergluteal cleft or gluteal cleft.
Pilonidal cysts may also be referred to as pilonidal sinus.
They may also be seen within the fingers or toes.
Pilonidal means nest of hair, and these cysts are composed of loose hairs and skin debris.
They can become infected and form an abscess requiring intervention.
Patients may present with edema, warmth, and pain in the area.
Bloody drainage from the cyst may be present.
Patients prone to pilonidal cysts include those who sit for extended periods and hairdressers.
Sonographically, pilonidal cysts appear as a complex subcutaneous mass.
A hypoechoic tract may extend from the cyst to the skin surface.
Color Doppler may confirm hyperemia related to infection.
A standoff device can improve visualization.
Cellulitis: Cellulitis is infection and subsequent inflammation of the skin and subcutaneous tissue.
It is most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes.
The affected skin is often red.
The involved area is commonly tender.
The involved area is commonly warm.
Leukocytosis may be present, especially if an abscess has developed.
Sonographically, cellulitis appears as hypoechoic edematous strands within the soft tissue.
This appearance has been described as cobblestoning or a cobblestone appearance.
When cellulitis is identified, a careful search for a focal abscess should be performed.
A hidden abscess is termed an occult abscess.
Superficial Abscess: A superficial abscess is a focal fluid collection.
Abscesses can have a wide range of sonographic features.
A superficial abscess may be seen in association with surrounding cellulitis.
Surrounding cellulitis may show hypoechoic edematous cobblestoning within the soft tissues.
Leukocytosis may be present clinically, especially with abscess development.
Color Doppler often demonstrates a peripheral rim of hyperemia.
The hyperemia is around the abscess rather than within the fluid collection.
A careful sonographic survey is important because the abscess may be occult.
Melanoma: Malignant melanoma accounts for up to 11% of skin cancers.
Primary melanoma classically appears hypoechoic sonographically.
Increased vascular flow may be noted in primary melanoma with color Doppler.
Melanoma is the most likely primary tumor to metastasize to the subcutaneous fat.
Metastatic melanoma most often appears as a solid hypoechoic mass.
Metastatic lesions are also vascular on sonography.
Sonographic Assessment of Foreign Bodies: A high-frequency linear array transducer is used to image foreign bodies.
Foreign bodies just below the skin surface may require a standoff pad for improved visualization.
Sonography can help localize and guide removal of some foreign bodies.
It is particularly helpful for wooden fragments and other radiolucent objects that may not be recognized with radiography.
Most foreign bodies appear as hyperechoic structures.
Some degree of posterior shadowing is commonly present.
Bullets, shrapnel, and other metallic objects may produce ring-down or comet-tail artifact.
Inflammation around a foreign body appears as a hypoechoic area adjacent to the structure.
Air at the site may produce bright echoes and create ambiguity about the object's orientation.
Electronic calipers can measure the distance from the skin surface to the foreign body to aid removal.

Anatomy and Physiology of the Male Pelvi: The male pelvis includes the lower ureters, urinary bladder, urethra, prostate, scrotum, testicles, penis, and accessory reproductive structures.
The paired testicles begin developing in the upper abdomen in the fetus and do not descend into the pelvis until the fourth week of gestation.
By 28 weeks of gestation, the testicles descend into the scrotum; failure to complete this descent results in cryptorchidism.
The normal adult testicles lie within the scrotum, a sac of cutaneous tissue that houses and protects the testes.
The scrotum is externally divided into two compartments by the median raphe and internally divided by the tunica dartos.
The scrotum provides temperature control for temperature-sensitive sperm, helping maintain conditions needed for normal spermatogenesis.
The cremaster muscle lies within the spermatic cord and changes testicular position for protection and temperature regulation.
The testes function as both endocrine and exocrine glands: they produce testosterone and also produce sperm for reproduction.
Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules, which converge into the rete testis located within the mediastinum testis.
Each testis is covered by a double-layered tunica vaginalis with parietal and visceral layers; hydroceles are most commonly located between these layers.
Deep to the tunica vaginalis, the dense tunica albuginea closely surrounds the testis and extends posteriorly to help form the mediastinum testis.
The epididymis is a coiled structure attached to the testicle and posterior scrotal wall; its head is superior, body posterior, and tail inferior.
The epididymis stores sperm for maturation and transports sperm into the ductus deferens, which connects the epididymis to the seminal vesicles.
The vas deferens is surgically interrupted during vasectomy; seminal vesicles add fluid to semen, ejaculatory ducts form at their junction, and the Cowper gland secretes pre-ejaculate fluid.
Vascular Anatomy of the Male Pelvis: The spermatic cord enters the scrotum through the inguinal canal and carries structures essential to testicular support and vascular supply.
Components of the spermatic cord include the testicular artery, pampiniform plexus, lymph nodes, nerves, and cremaster muscle.
The testicles receive most of their arterial blood supply from the testicular arteries.
The testicular arteries arise from the anterior abdominal aorta just below the level of the renal arteries.
Venous drainage from the testicles occurs through the pampiniform plexus within the spermatic cord.
The pampiniform plexus empties into the testicular veins.
The right testicular vein drains into the inferior vena cava.
The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein.
Knowledge of asymmetric venous drainage is important because it relates to the higher frequency of left-sided varicocele.
Sonography of the Scrotum: Scrotal sonography is typically performed with a high-frequency linear transducer because the structures are superficial and require high-resolution imaging.
The normal scrotal wall measures approximately 2 to 8 mm in thickness.
Normal testicles appear isoechoic, and a small amount of extratesticular fluid is typically present around each testicle.
The echotexture of the normal testis is similar to that of the thyroid gland.
The normal mediastinum testis appears echogenic: linear in the sagittal plane and triangular in the transverse plane.
Adult testicles normally measure 3 to 5 cm in length, 2 to 4 cm in width, and about 3 cm in thickness.
Color and pulsed Doppler evaluation should demonstrate symmetric blood flow within both testicles and epididymides.
Both venous and arterial waveforms should be assessed when vascular compromise or inflammation is suspected.
Each part of the epididymis should be evaluated for masses, enlargement, and hyperemic flow.
The epididymal head is commonly measured and compared bilaterally; the normal head measures about 10 to 12 mm.
The normal epididymis is either isoechoic or slightly more echogenic than the testis.
Post-vasectomy epididymal changes may include enlargement, heterogeneous echotexture, and possible cystic areas.
Any intratesticular or extratesticular mass should also be assessed with color Doppler imaging.
Cryptorchidism: Cryptorchidism is the condition of having an undescended testis.
It occurs in approximately 3% to 4% of full-term births.
An undescended testis may become trapped anywhere along the normal path of descent from the abdomen to the scrotum.
Although an undescended testis may be found within the abdomen, it is most often located just above the scrotum or within the inguinal canal.
An undescended testis is most often found within the inguinal canal.
The condition is associated with infertility.
Cryptorchidism also increases the risk for malignancy in the involved testis.
Seminoma is the most common cancer found in an undescended testis.
Clinically, one or both testicles are not palpable within the scrotum.
Surgical correction of an undescended testis is called orchiopexy.
Sonographically, the undescended testis is identified outside the scrotum, usually in the inguinal canal.
The cryptorchid testis typically appears hypoechoic relative to the normal testis.
Testicular Torsion: Testicular torsion, or spermatic cord torsion, occurs when twisting of the testicular axis cuts off the arterial blood supply to the testicle.
The degree of torsion varies and may be intermittent; a 360-degree torsion blocks venous drainage and arterial supply, producing ischemia.
The amount of ischemic damage is directly related to the degree of torsion.
Testicular torsion occurs most often during adolescence, especially between 12 and 18 years of age.
It is a true surgical emergency; salvage rates are 80% to 100% if treated within 6 hours of symptom onset.
After 6 hours, salvage rates drop considerably, and the testicle is usually not salvageable after 24 hours.
Predisposing factors include trauma, strenuous exercise, sexual activity, and bell-clapper deformity with absent posterior fixation of the testis and epididymis.
Bell-clapper deformity is classically bilateral and is associated with intravaginal torsion, the most common type of testicular torsion.
Extravaginal torsion occurs in the neonatal period or in utero and relates to spermatic cord torsion within the inguinal canal.
Patients usually have sudden severe testicular pain, often during sleep, with possible lower abdominal or inguinal pain, nausea, vomiting, and a swollen high-riding horizontally oriented testis.
Acute sonographic findings include enlargement of the spermatic cord, epididymis, and testis; a hypoechoic or heterogeneous testis; reactive hydrocele; and scrotal wall thickening.
A completely torsed testis has no detectable intratesticular flow, but lesser torsion may show decreased flow, so compare both testes and document venous and arterial waveforms.
Chronic torsion lasting more than 10 days causes enlarged heterogeneous epididymis, testis, and spermatic cord, with testicular necrosis and hyperemic flow around the testis.
Torsion of the Testicular Appendages: Torsion of the appendix testis is the most common cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal boys.
The testicular appendages include the appendix testis, appendix epididymis, and appendix vas.
These appendages are embryologic remnants of the Müllerian duct, Wolffian duct, and mesonephric duct, respectively.
The appendix testis lies between the head of the epididymis and the superior pole of the testis.
The appendix epididymis is located at the head of the epididymis.
The appendix vas lies between the body and tail of the epididymis.
Normal appendages are not routinely seen sonographically, but may be visible with a hydrocele or other scrotal fluid collection as small oval tissue projections.
After torsion, the appendage may become displaced and mobile; calcification of a free-floating torsed appendage can produce a scrotal pearl.
Clinically, patients have acute focal testicular pain localized to the superior pole rather than generalized testicular pain.
The classic clinical sign is the blue-dot sign, a blue discoloration just beneath the skin representing the torsed appendage.
Sonography shows normal intratesticular flow with a small avascular hypoechoic or hyperechoic mass adjacent to the superior pole of the testis.
Associated findings may include reactive hydrocele and scrotal wall thickening.
Treatment is pain medication and bed rest.
Hydrocele: A few milliliters of extratesticular fluid is a normal sonographic finding around the testis.
A simple fluid collection within the scrotum is called a hydrocele.
Hydroceles are most commonly located between the two layers of the tunica vaginalis.
Hydroceles often displace the testicles posteriorly.
Scrotal enlargement caused by fluid may transilluminate light on clinical examination.
When seen with scrotal infection, testicular torsion, trauma, or tumors, they are described as reactive hydroceles.
Patients commonly present with painless scrotal swelling, though pain may be present when an associated disorder exists.
Sonographically, a hydrocele appears as simple fluid, typically anterior to the testis.
Scrotal wall thickening commonly accompanies a hydrocele.
Chronic hydroceles may contain internal debris and septations.
Extratesticular Cysts: A spermatocele is a common cyst, most often located in the head of the epididymis.
The spermatocele is considered the most common scrotal mass.
It is composed of nonviable sperm, fat, cellular debris, and lymphocytes.
Spermatoceles may be palpable on physical examination if large enough, but they are typically not painful.
Sonographically, a spermatocele appears as a round anechoic mass with acoustic enhancement in the head of the epididymis.
A spermatocele may contain layering debris within the cyst.
An epididymal cyst has a similar sonographic appearance to a spermatocele.
Unlike spermatocele, an epididymal cyst can be located anywhere along the length of the epididymis.
Tunica albuginea cysts are located along the periphery of the testicle within the tunica albuginea.
These cystic lesions are extratesticular and usually benign in appearance.
Varicocele: A varicocele is a dilated group of veins within the scrotum caused by incompetent or abnormal valves in the pampiniform plexus.
Varicoceles are the most common cause of correctable male infertility.
Excess blood within the scrotum increases local heat, which can impair sperm formation and mobility.
Varicoceles are usually painless, although large varicoceles may cause discomfort.
Patients may present with a palpable extratesticular mass and possible infertility.
Primary varicoceles are most often left-sided and palpable on physical examination.
Their left-sided predominance is attributed to higher vascular pressure, the longer left testicular vein, and the sharp angle of entry into the left renal vein.
Right-sided varicoceles are considered secondary and may be associated with hydronephrosis, hepatomegaly, a hepatic mass, or a retroperitoneal neoplasm such as a right renal mass.
Nutcracker syndrome, left renal vein entrapment between the superior mesenteric artery and abdominal aorta, can predispose to a varicocele.
Sonographically, a varicocele appears as multiple anechoic tubular structures outside the testis, although intratesticular varicocele can occur.
With color Doppler and Valsalva, the veins fill with blood and enlarge; the patient may also stand to simulate this effect.
Dilated varicocele veins measure greater than 2 mm.
Scrotal Pearls: A scrotal pearl, or scrotolith, is an extratesticular calculus.
Scrotal pearls are often incidentally detected during sonography.
They are thought to represent remnants of a previously torsed and displaced testicular appendage.
Sonographically, they appear as extremely echogenic extratesticular structures.
They are mobile within the scrotal sac.
Their extratesticular location helps distinguish them from intratesticular calcifications such as microlithiasis.
Epididymitis and Epididymo-orchitis: Epididymitis is inflammation of the epididymis and is the most common cause of acute testicular pain in adults.
Patients may present with acute testicular pain, leukocytosis, fever, dysuria, urethral discharge, and scrotal wall edema.
Scrotal infections are ascending; they usually begin externally or in the urinary tract or prostate and spread through the vas deferens to the epididymal tail, body, head, and possibly the testis.
Inflammation of the testis is called orchitis.
Combined infection of the epididymis and testis is termed epididymo-orchitis.
A frequent cause is bacterial spread from the prostate or urinary tract, although trauma can also cause epididymitis.
In younger men, common causes are the sexually transmitted diseases chlamydia and gonorrhea.
Epididymitis may be diffuse, involving the entire epididymis, or focal, involving only one segment.
Because disease may be focal, careful evaluation of the epididymal head, body, and tail is essential.
The inflamed epididymis appears enlarged, hypoechoic or heterogeneous, and hyperemic on color or power Doppler.
Associated findings include thickened scrotal wall and reactive hydrocele.
Orchitis is almost always accompanied by epididymitis and shows increased intratesticular vascularity with a low-resistance waveform pattern; the testis may appear hypoechoic.
Chronic epididymitis may appear as an enlarged hyperechoic epididymis with calcifications.
Testicular Abscess and Pyocele: A testicular abscess usually develops as a complication of untreated epididymo-orchitis.
Patients typically present with fever, leukocytosis, and a painful swollen scrotum.
On sonography, a testicular abscess appears as a complex intratesticular mass.
Color Doppler shows no flow centrally within the abscess.
Hyperemic flow is typically present around the abscess margins.
An intratesticular abscess may coexist with a pyocele.
A pyocele is a complex hydrocele that contains pus.
Pyoceles are often seen with persistent scrotal infection or rupture of a testicular abscess.
Sonographically, a pyocele appears as a complex fluid collection within the scrotum.
A pyocele may contain septations and loculations.
Scrotal wall thickening may be present with a pyocele.
Clinical history is essential to differentiate pyocele from hematocele or complex hydrocele.
Intratesticular Cysts: Intratesticular cysts are rarely large enough to be palpable.
Multiple small intratesticular cysts are often seen along the mediastinum testis.
These small cysts are typically clinically insignificant.
They may represent tubular ectasia of the rete testis, meaning cystic dilatation of the rete testis.
Multiple small cysts along the mediastinum testis are characteristic of tubular ectasia.
Epidermoid cysts can also occur within the testicle.
An epidermoid cyst often appears as an avascular intratesticular mass with a whorled or onion-skin appearance.
Recognition of cystic lesions near the mediastinum helps avoid confusion with solid intratesticular masses.
Testicular Microcalcifications: Testicular microlithiasis appears sonographically as multiple echogenic foci within the testis without acoustic shadowing.
These tiny calcifications are associated with malignancies.
They are also associated with infertility.
Additional associations include Klinefelter syndrome and cryptorchidism.
Screening patients with intratesticular microlithiasis has been studied, and its cost-effectiveness has been questioned.
There is a proven increased risk for cancer when microlithiasis is present in one testis and an intratesticular tumor is identified in the contralateral testis.
In that setting, biopsy of the testis with microlithiasis may be warranted.
Klinefelter Syndrome: Klinefelter syndrome is a condition in which a male has an extra X chromosome.
Infertility is a typical clinical feature.
Abnormally low intelligence is listed as a characteristic feature.
The syndrome is associated with testicular microlithiasis.
Adrenal Rests: Adrenal rests are masses of ectopic adrenal tissue within the testicle.
They are associated with congenital adrenal hyperplasia or Cushing syndrome.
These lesions result from migration of adrenal tissue with gonadal tissue during fetal development.
Clinically, patients may have a history of congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
Patients typically show increased levels of adrenocorticotropic hormone.
Cushing syndrome is also associated with adrenal rests.
Sonographically, adrenal rests appear as bilateral round hypoechoic intratesticular masses.
They are most commonly located near the mediastinum testis.
Their bilateral distribution near the mediastinum can help distinguish them from other intratesticular masses.
Malignant Testicular Tumors and Tumor Ma: As a general rule, intratesticular masses are considered malignant until proven otherwise, whereas most extratesticular masses are benign.
Most malignant intratesticular tumors are of germ cell origin.
Germ cell tumors include pure seminoma, teratoma, embryonal cell carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, and burned-out germ cell tumor.
Other malignant testicular tumors include sex cord-stromal tumors, lymphoma, leukemia, and metastases.
Lymphoma and leukemia may appear as focal hypoechoic masses or may diffusely involve the testicles.
Metastatic disease to the testis most commonly originates from melanoma, lung, kidney, and prostate cancer.
Leydig cell tumors occur in younger boys and produce increased testosterone levels.
Sertoli cell tumors occur in younger boys and produce estrogens that result in gynecomastia.
Granulosa cell tumors occur in younger boys and are associated with chromosomal abnormalities.
Helpful laboratory tumor markers include human chorionic gonadotropin, alpha-fetoprotein, and sometimes lactate dehydrogenase.
hCG is elevated in about 60% of malignant intratesticular tumors because syncytiotrophoblastic cells within the tumor produce it.
AFP elevation is most often associated with embryonal cell carcinoma, teratomas, and yolk sac tumors.
LDH may be used to assess treatment effectiveness and recurrence, but its specificity is lacking.
Seminoma: Seminoma is the most common malignant neoplasm of the testicles.
It is a germ cell tumor typically found in males 30 to 50 years old.
Seminoma is often found in patients with cryptorchidism.
A seminoma may replace the entire testicle.
Patients usually present with a painless scrotal mass.
Hardening of the testis is another clinical finding.
Sonographically, seminoma is a solid hypoechoic intratesticular mass.
Other Germ Cell Tumors of the Testicles: Nonseminomatous intratesticular tumors include choriocarcinoma, embryonal cell carcinoma, yolk sac tumors, and teratomas.
A testicular tumor may contain a mixture of malignant tissues; such lesions are referred to as mixed germ cell tumors.
Choriocarcinoma is malignant, may be palpable, and is associated with elevated hCG.
Sonographically, choriocarcinoma appears as a heterogeneous mass with areas of hemorrhage, necrosis, and calcifications.
Embryonal cell carcinoma is malignant, may be palpable, and is associated with elevated AFP and hCG.
Embryonal cell carcinoma typically appears as a heterogeneous mass with cystic components.
Yolk sac tumors are malignant, may be palpable, and are associated exclusively with elevated AFP.
Sonographically, yolk sac tumors appear heterogeneous with areas of hemorrhage and calcifications.
Teratoma is described as benign with malignant potential and may be palpable.
If malignant, teratoma may be associated with elevated AFP and hCG.
Teratoma appears heterogeneous with calcifications representing cartilage, bone, and fibrosis and may contain hair and teeth.
Scrotal Trauma and Hematocele: Trauma to the scrotum can fracture the testicle and cause acute scrotal pain.
A fracture line is only rarely visualized sonographically.
Trauma may produce indistinct or unclear testicular margins.
A hematoma may be present in or around the testis after injury.
Blood within the scrotum is termed a hematocele.
Patients with significant trauma may have a low hematocrit.
Hematoceles are commonly associated with scrotal trauma.
They may also occur after recent pelvic surgery, scrotal surgery, or torsion.
Sonographically, a hematocele appears as a complex fluid collection within the scrotum.
A hematocele may contain septations and loculations.
Scrotal wall thickening may accompany a hematocele.
Clinical history is essential to distinguish hematocele from pyocele or complex hydrocele.
Inguinal Hernias: An inguinal hernia may contain intestine or omentum.
Patients often present with persistent or intermittent scrotal swelling.
Abdominal pain may accompany the swelling.
Blood in the stool may also be reported.
On sonography, an inguinal hernia usually appears as a heterogeneous scrotal mass.
Peristalsis within the mass strongly suggests herniated bowel.
The herniated bowel may contain air and fluid.
A hydrocele may be an associated finding.
The Valsalva maneuver can help demonstrate peristalsing bowel.
If the hernia becomes incarcerated and strangulated, the bowel blood supply can be lost.
Anatomy and Physiology of the Penis: The penis is a primary sex organ important for both reproduction and urination.
It is covered by skin and then by a dense fibrous layer called Buck fascia.
The penis contains three cylindrical tissue components: paired corpora cavernosa and a single corpus spongiosum.
These tissues are composed of smooth muscle, erectile tissue, and vascular structures.
The urethra is housed within the ventrally positioned corpus spongiosum.
The paired corpora cavernosa are located dorsally.
The tunica albuginea surrounds the corpora cavernosa and partially covers the corpus spongiosum.
All three corpora are covered by Buck fascia.
Arterial supply begins with the internal pudendal artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery.
The internal pudendal artery branches into the deep artery of the penis, also called the penile artery.
The deep artery of the penis supplies the corpora cavernosa.
Cavernosal arteries course bilaterally within the corpora cavernosa.
During sexual arousal, penile arteries engorge, adjacent veins are compressed, venous drainage is reduced, and erection results.
Sonography of the Penis: Penile sonography is performed with a high-frequency linear transducer.
For flow assessment, the patient is usually supine with the penis resting on the lower abdomen.
This position places the dorsal surface against the abdomen and exposes the ventral surface.
The penis should be evaluated in both transverse and sagittal planes.
In transverse imaging, the corpus spongiosum is seen ventrally and contains the urethra.
The paired corpora cavernosa are seen dorsally on transverse images.
The corpus spongiosum is elliptical and contains medium- to low-level echoes.
The corpora cavernosa have similar echogenicity to the spongiosum but are more oval in shape.
The tunica albuginea is highly echogenic and can be seen separating and covering the corpora.
The cavernosal arteries within each corpus cavernosum can be identified by bright walls and color Doppler flow.
In the sagittal plane, the spongiosum and cavernosa elongate, and the penile urethra can be followed within the corpus spongiosum.
For urethral stricture evaluation, the patient may need a full bladder and may void during the examination.
For vascular assessment, flow is first analyzed in the flaccid state and then after injection of an erection-inducing drug if needed.
A penile inflatable prosthesis reservoir may be seen incidentally in the pelvis as a well-defined anechoic round structure.
Vascular Impotence: Vascular impotence results from vascular compromise to or within the penis, causing inability to obtain or maintain an erection.
Diabetic neuropathy may cause this disorder by damaging the tiny vessels within the penis.
In normal men, pulsed Doppler shows increased arterial flow to the cavernosal arteries during erection.
This arterial increase is assessed by evaluating systolic velocities.
Normally, venous outflow becomes partially blocked during erection.
As venous outflow is restricted, diastolic flow should greatly decrease.
Venous incompetence is diagnosed when diastolic flow does not decrease appropriately.
In healthy individuals, cavernosal artery velocities measure about 10 to 15 cm per second in the flaccid state.
Peyronie Disease: Peyronie disease is caused by buildup of fibrous plaque and calcifications within the penis.
This scarring results in a painful curvature of the penis.
Poor arterial flow may be present.
Painful erections are a common complaint.
The area of scar tissue can usually be palpated clinically.
Marked penile curvature is a clinical finding.
Sonographically, Peyronie disease appears as thickening of the tunica albuginea.
Calcifications may also be present within the thickened tunica albuginea.
Penile Trauma: Penile fracture can occur with blunt sexual trauma.
Patients often report an audible popping or cracking sound during intercourse.
The sound usually occurs because one of the corpora cavernosa snaps under pressure.
Clinical diagnosis may be suggested by history and ecchymosis, which is subcutaneous bleeding.
Sonography can further evaluate soft-tissue, urethral, and vascular damage.
Hemorrhage within the penis may have variable sonographic appearances depending on whether the hematoma is new or aging.
The most likely sonographic finding is an irregular hypoechoic or hyperechoic defect at the rupture site.
Careful assessment for urethral damage is important because interruption of the urethra can cause voiding complications.
Untreated injury can permanently disrupt penile function.
Scar tissue may subsequently develop at the fracture site.
Prostate and Seminal Vesicles: The prostate is a retroperitoneal gland that produces alkaline fluid contributing about 13% to 30% of semen volume.
It is located inferior to the urinary bladder, between the symphysis pubis and the rectum.
The gland is shaped like an inverted pyramid with a superior base and inferior apex.
The prostatic urethra passes through the center of the prostate and serves as the reference point for prostatic zonal anatomy.
The peripheral zone is the largest zone, located posterolaterally and apically, and is the most common site of prostate malignancy.
The central zone is at the base of the prostate and is the second largest prostatic zone.
The transitional zone lies on both sides of the proximal urethra and is the most common site of benign prostatic hyperplasia.
The periurethral glandular zone is embedded in the muscle of the proximal urethra and is the smallest prostatic zone.
An additional region, the anterior fibromuscular stroma, lies anterior to the prostatic urethra and has little clinical significance.
The paired seminal vesicles lie superior to the prostate and posterior to the bladder base.
They secrete alkaline-based fluid and empty into the paired ejaculatory ducts.
The ejaculatory ducts are formed by union of the seminal vesicles and ductus deferens and empty into the urethra at the verumontanum.
Sonography of the Prostate Gland and Sem: A targeted prostate sonogram is often preceded by a digital rectal examination.
The prostate may be imaged transabdominally or transrectally.
Transabdominal imaging is useful for measuring overall prostate size.
Transrectal imaging provides superior resolution and is used for biopsies.
For transrectal imaging, the patient is typically placed in the left lateral decubitus position with knees flexed toward the chest.
The lithotomy position may also be used for transrectal imaging.
The prostate and seminal vesicles are examined in both coronal and sagittal planes.
Normal prostatic zones are typically homogeneous.
The zones may be differentiated using landmarks such as the prostatic urethra and ejaculatory ducts.
Benign calcifications and simple-appearing cysts may be seen within the prostate.
The seminal vesicles appear as hypoechoic structures between the bladder and the prostate.
When filled with fluid, seminal vesicles enlarge and contain low-level echoes and anechoic fluid.
The seminal vesicles may be imaged transabdominally or endorectally.
Prostate-Specific Antigen: Prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, is a protein produced by the prostate gland.
Methods used to evaluate PSA include PSA velocity, volume-corrected PSA, age-adjusted PSA, and free and attached PSA.
Elevated PSA may be seen with benign prostatic hyperplasia.
It may also be elevated with prostate cancer.
Other causes of elevation include prostatitis and prostatic infarcts.
A higher PSA level has been claimed to increase the likelihood of prostate cancer.
However, elevated PSA is not specific for prostate cancer.
A normal PSA level may still be present in a patient with prostate cancer.
Prostate Cancer: Prostate cancer, usually adenocarcinoma, is the most common cancer in men.
Patients may present with elevated PSA values and an enlarged prostate detected on digital rectal examination.
Symptoms can include hematuria, hematospermia, back pain, pelvic pain, hip or thigh pain, impotence, and decreased ejaculated fluid.
The most common location for prostate cancer is the peripheral zone.
Prostate cancer may produce areas of hypervascularity.
Most prostate cancers appear hypoechoic relative to adjacent normal prostatic tissue.
Because appearances can mimic normal anatomy, prostatitis, and BPH, experience is needed in evaluation.
Biopsy is required for definitive diagnosis.
Benign Prostatic Hypertrophy: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is the benign enlargement of the prostate gland.
BPH most commonly arises in the transitional zone.
Enlargement can obstruct urine flow through the urethra.
Symptoms include nocturia, increased urinary frequency, urinary urgency, and a constant sensation of a full bladder.
Patients may also have elevated PSA.
Sonographically, BPH causes enlargement of the inner gland.
It can produce hypoechoic areas within the gland.
Calcifications may be present within the prostate.
The gland may appear diffusely heterogeneous.
Cystic changes may also occur within the gland.
Patients with urinary complications from BPH may undergo transurethral resection of the prostate.
Prostatitis: Prostatitis is inflammation of the prostate gland.
Painful ejaculation is a common symptom.
Sonographically, the prostate appears enlarged and more hypoechoic.
Color Doppler demonstrates hyperemia within the inflamed prostate.
Seminal Vesicle cysts: Seminal vesicle cysts may appear as anechoic or complex cystic structures in the region of the seminal vesicles.
They may be congenital or acquired.
Seminal vesicle cysts may be associated with Zinner syndrome.
Zinner syndrome consists of unilateral renal agenesis, ipsilateral seminal vesicle cyst, and ejaculatory duct obstruction.
Patients with Zinner syndrome may present with perineal pain, recurrent prostatitis, painful ejaculation, and infertility.

Kidney Anatomy & Physiology: The urinary system includes the upper tract, composed of the kidneys and ureters, and the lower tract, composed of the bladder and urethra.
The functional unit of the kidney is the nephron, which begins to function by the ninth week of gestation.
Fetal urine production begins between 11 and 13 weeks and supplies most of the amniotic fluid.
Kidneys are essential for homeostasis by filtering and detoxifying blood and excreting metabolic waste.
They dynamically reabsorb amino acids, ions, glucose, and water and maintain normal blood pH, iron, and salt levels.
Kidneys regulate blood pressure by producing renin, released by specialized cells adjacent to each glomeruli.
Each kidney forms when two embryonic parenchymal masses, called renunculi, combine.
Kidneys initially develop in the pelvis and normally ascend into the fetal abdomen by 12 weeks gestation.
A pelvic kidney is the most common ectopic kidney location, although arrested ascent can occur anywhere along the migratory path.
Adult kidneys are bean-shaped retroperitoneal organs; the left kidney sits higher because of the liver.
The left kidney is also usually slightly longer than the right, but a length difference generally should not exceed 2 cm.
Protective coverings, from outer to inner, include pararenal fat, Gerota fascia, perirenal fat, and the renal capsule.
The kidney consists of renal parenchyma and renal sinus; parenchyma includes cortex and medulla.
The cortex performs filtration, the medulla performs absorption and contains the renal pyramids, and the sinus contains the minor calices, major calices, infundibula, and renal pelvis.
Renal Vasculature & Labs: The renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta just below the level of the superior mesenteric artery.
Oxygenated blood enters the renal hilum through the renal arteries and then passes into segmental branches.
Flow continues through interlobar arteries, which travel between the renal pyramids.
Interlobar arteries branch into arcuate arteries at the base of the pyramids.
Arcuate arteries branch into interlobular arteries and then afferent arterioles, which carry blood into the glomerulus for filtration.
The right renal artery is longer than the left because it courses posterior to the inferior vena cava.
Renal veins exit at the renal hilum and connect to the lateral aspects of the inferior vena cava.
The left renal vein is longer because it crosses between the superior mesenteric artery and abdominal aorta.
It is normal for the left renal vein to narrow between the superior mesenteric artery and aorta, then become more prominent beyond that point.
Urinalysis for renal function evaluates for bacteriuria, pyuria, hematuria, and proteinuria.
Abnormal urine pH may help determine urinary stone composition, and specific gravity may be low in renal failure or pyelonephritis and high with dehydration.
Blood tests used to evaluate renal function include blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, glomerular filtration rate, and lactate dehydrogenase.
Elevated BUN or creatinine indicates some form of renal disease; reduced GFR suggests renal insufficiency or chronic renal disease.
LDH may rise with renal infarction, chronic renal disease, or cell death elsewhere, so it is not specific for renal disease.
Sonography of the Kidneys: Normal adult kidneys are elliptical in the longitudinal plane and rounded in the transverse plane.
Adult kidneys typically measure about 8 to 13 cm in length, 2 to 3 cm anteroposteriorly, and 4 to 5 cm in width.
Neonatal and pediatric kidneys may appear lobulated, show prominent renal pyramids, and have subtle distinction between cortex and sinus.
The renal sinus is central and normally echogenic on sonography.
The renal cortex appears as medium- to low-level echoes surrounding the renal sinus.
Normal cortex should be more hypoechoic than, or isoechoic to, the normal liver or spleen.
Cortical thickness should measure greater than 1 cm; reduction is termed cortical thinning.
Monitoring cortical thickness is useful, especially in patients with chronic renal disease.
Increased cortical echogenicity suggests intrinsic renal disease.
Triangular medullary pyramids may be seen within the cortex and are separated by the columns of Bertin.
The renal capsule may occasionally be visualized as a highly reflective hyperechoic line surrounding the kidney.
Relative echogenicity is renal medulla less than renal cortex less than or equal to liver less than spleen less than pancreas, while the diaphragm is greater than renal sinus.
Renal Variants: The most common congenital anomaly of the urinary tract is the duplex, or duplicated, collecting system.
A duplex collecting system divides the renal sinus into two separate sinuses called the upper pole moiety and lower pole moiety.
Two ureters drain separate portions of a duplex kidney, and obstruction may affect one or both collecting systems.
A kidney with a duplex collecting system typically measures longer than a normal kidney.
A dromedary hump is a bulge on the lateral border of the kidney, often on the left kidney.
A dromedary hump has the same echogenicity as adjacent renal cortex and shows normal branching vasculature on color Doppler.
A hypertrophic column of Bertin is an enlargement of a renal column that indents the renal sinus.
Columns of Bertin are actually double layers of renal cortex and can mimic a renal mass if not recognized.
A junctional parenchymal defect results from incomplete fusion of the two embryologic renal components, the renunculi.
It appears as a hyperechoic wedge-shaped structure on the anterior kidney between the upper and middle sections.

Other described variants include fetal lobulation, extrarenal pelvis, horseshoe kidney, malrotated kidney, renal agenesis, renal hypoplasia, renal sinus lipomatosis, ectopic kidney, and supernumerary kidney.
A horseshoe kidney crosses the midline and joins at the lower poles by an isthmus that passes anterior to the aorta and inferior vena cava.
Renal Failure & Dialysis: Acute renal failure is a sudden decrease in renal function that develops over days to weeks.
The most common cause of acute renal failure is acute tubular necrosis, in which ischemic damage leads to tubular cell destruction.
Other causes of acute renal failure include renal artery stenosis, renal infection, urinary tract obstruction, polycystic kidney disease, amyloidosis, and Henoch–Schönlein purpura.
Clinical findings of acute renal failure include elevated BUN, elevated creatinine, oliguria, hypertension, leukocytosis, hematuria, edema, and hypovolemia.
Acute tubular necrosis may initially appear normal sonographically but may cause variable cortical changes and a resistive index greater than 0.7.
In acute renal failure, kidneys may appear normal or have a hyperechoic cortex, and hydronephrosis may be present if obstruction is the cause.
Chronic renal failure is a gradual decrease in renal function over months or years and can progress to end-stage renal disease.
The most common cause of chronic renal failure is diabetes mellitus.
Other causes of chronic renal failure include glomerulonephritis, chronic pyelonephritis, metabolic disorders, chronic urinary tract obstruction, tuberculosis, renal vascular disease, and infection.
Clinical findings of chronic renal failure include diabetes, malaise, elevated BUN and creatinine, fatigue, hypertension, and hyperkalemia.
Sonographically, chronic renal failure shows small echogenic kidneys, cortical thinning, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, and possible renal cysts.
Dialysis removes accumulated urea, waste products, and excess water in patients with inadequate renal function.
Hemodialysis and hemofiltration use a machine to extract, filter, and return blood, whereas peritoneal dialysis uses solution in the abdomen with diffusion and osmosis.
Patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis commonly show a minimal amount of ascites during abdominal and pelvic sonography.
Simple & Complex Renal Cysts: A simple renal cyst is the most common renal mass.
A simple cyst must be spherical, anechoic, have smooth walls, show posterior acoustic enhancement, and contain no internal echoes.
An anechoic renal mass that does not meet all simple cyst criteria should not be called a simple cyst.
Simple renal cysts are usually asymptomatic and clinically insignificant, although large cysts may cause pain by compressing adjacent renal tissue.
Once one renal cyst is identified, the kidneys should be examined closely for additional cysts.
Parapelvic cysts originate in the renal parenchyma and protrude into the renal sinus, potentially mimicking a dilated renal pelvis.
Peripelvic cysts originate in the renal sinus and may be difficult to distinguish from hydronephrosis.
Small cortical cysts lie within the cortex and may be difficult to differentiate from prominent renal pyramids, especially when solitary.
Exophytic renal cysts project outward away from the kidney.
Any renal cyst lacking all simple features is considered a complex cyst.
Complex features include septations, internal debris, mural nodules, papillary projections, irregular borders, or calcifications.
Complex cysts are concerning because renal cell carcinoma may manifest as a multicystic mass.
Hemorrhagic cysts may appear anechoic, hypoechoic, hyperechoic, or complex depending on the stage of hemolysis.
Milk of calcium cysts show a fluid-fluid level with shadowing layered calcium, and multilocular cysts contain thin septations without blood flow within them.
Polycystic & Cystic Diseases: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is a hereditary disorder also called adult polycystic kidney disease.
ADPKD often remains silent until the third or fourth decade of life, when symptoms such as hypertension and decreasing renal function appear.
Patients with ADPKD may also have urinary tract infection, renal calculi, flank pain, hematuria, and a palpable abdominal mass.
Sonographically, ADPKD produces bilateral enlarged kidneys containing numerous cortical renal cysts of varying sizes.
ADPKD is associated with cysts in other organs, including the liver, pancreas, spleen, testis, and seminal vesicles.
ADPKD has a 40% association with polycystic liver disease and is among the top causes of chronic renal failure worldwide.
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease is also called infantile polycystic kidney disease and is characterized by dilation of the renal collecting tubules.
ARPKD is often recognized in the fetus; survivors commonly die from complications of renal failure and portal hypertension caused by hepatic fibrosis.
ARPKD sonography shows bilateral enlarged echogenic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation, and high-frequency transducers help depict abnormal architecture and tiny cysts.
Multicystic dysplastic kidney disease is thought to result from an early first-trimester ureteral obstruction.
MCDK shows several smooth-walled noncommunicating cysts of varying sizes replacing all renal parenchyma in the renal fossa, with contralateral compensatory hypertrophy.
There is typically no normal functioning renal tissue in MCDK, so bilateral disease is fatal.
Acquired renal cystic disease is often the result of chronic hemodialysis and carries increased risk for renal cell carcinoma.
In acquired renal cystic disease, kidneys are initially small in end-stage renal disease with a few small cysts, then may enlarge over time with numerous small cysts throughout the parenchyma.

von Hippel–Lindau syndrome is associated with central nervous system tumors, multiple renal cysts, renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic cysts, and pheochromocytoma; cysts may show mural nodules suggesting RCC.
Tuberous sclerosis is associated with epilepsy, facial skin lesions, bilateral renal cysts, and multiple bilateral angiomyolipomas.
Renal Infection: Acute pyelonephritis is inflammation of the kidney secondary to infection and most commonly results from an ascending infection from the lower urinary tract.
It is most commonly encountered in women, while retrograde urine flow causing infection is also common in young children with structural defects.
Clinical findings of acute pyelonephritis include flank pain, bacteriuria, pyuria, leukocytosis, dysuria, and urinary frequency.
Acute pyelonephritis may have no sonographic abnormality, but possible findings include renal enlargement, focal areas of altered echotexture, and compression of the renal sinus.
Color Doppler may help identify infected parenchyma in acute pyelonephritis.
Pyonephrosis is pus within the collecting system, usually related to obstruction or infection causing urinary stasis.
Patients with pyonephrosis present with pyuria, bacteriuria, fever, flank pain, and leukocytosis; sonography shows hydronephrosis with dependent layering low-level echoes in the collecting system.
Chronic pyelonephritis results from recurrent infection or chronic obstruction and is associated with vesicoureteral reflux in children.

Sonographically, chronic pyelonephritis produces small echogenic kidneys with lobulated borders from parenchymal scarring; a scar is an echogenic area extending from the renal sinus through the parenchyma.
Renal or perinephric abscess may develop in pyelonephritis and can appear anechoic, hypoechoic, or complex.
Gas within an abscess produces dirty shadowing or reverberation artifact.
Emphysematous pyelonephritis is a life-threatening complication, more common in diabetics and immunocompromised patients, and most often due to Escherichia coli.
Its sonographic hallmark is gas within the renal parenchyma causing dirty shadowing or reverberation artifact.
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is typically due to chronic obstruction and infection; hydronephrosis, staghorn calculus, and perinephric fluid are often present.

Renal fungal disease, commonly Candida albicans, produces echogenic mobile nonshadowing fungal balls within the collecting system, especially in immunocompromised patients, diabetics, intravenous drug abusers, and infants with indwelling catheters.

Glomerulonephritis may follow a distant infection such as strep throat or an autoimmune reaction; acute disease may show enlarged echogenic kidneys with prominent pyramids, while chronic disease shows small echogenic kidneys.

Parasitic urinary infection from schistosomiasis most often causes bladder wall thickening, whereas renal hydatid cysts vary from anechoic to complex with daughter cysts, debris, or calcifications depending on maturation.
Obstruction & Hydronephrosis: Urinary tract dilation occurs proximal to the level of obstruction, so understanding the normal path of urine helps localize blockage.
If the ureter and renal collecting system are dilated while the bladder is normal, obstruction is proximal to the bladder, either in the ureter or at the ureterovesicle junction.
Hydronephrosis is dilation of the renal collecting system secondary to obstruction of normal urine flow.
Hydronephrosis includes dilation of the calices, infundibula, and renal pelvis and may also be termed pyelocaliectasis.
Related terms include caliectasis for caliceal dilation, pelviectasis or pyelectasis for renal pelvis dilation, and pelvicaliectasis for dilation of both pelvis and calices.
Mild hydronephrosis is distention of the renal pelvis.
Moderate hydronephrosis extends distention into the calices and medullary pyramids.
Marked or severe hydronephrosis extends into the cortex and causes severe parenchymal thinning.
