Intrinsic causes of hydronephrosis include urolithiasis, congenital abnormalities such as vesicoureteral reflux or posterior urethral valves, hematoma, neoplasm, ureteropelvic junction obstruction or ureteral stricture, and ureterocele.
Extrinsic causes include benign prostatic hypertrophy, neurogenic bladder, pelvic masses, pregnancy, retroperitoneal fibrosis, surgery, trauma, and urethritis.
Sonographically, hydronephrosis appears as anechoic fluid filling all or part of the collecting system.
Hydronephrosis can raise the renal artery resistive index in the arcuate or interlobar vessels to greater than 0.7.
False-positive hydronephrosis may be caused by overdistended bladder, parapelvic cysts, prominent renal vein, or extrarenal pelvis.
Color Doppler imaging and postvoid imaging help resolve uncertainty in suspected false-positive hydronephrosis.
Stones & Nephrocalcinosis: Urolithiasis refers to stones anywhere in the urinary tract; within the kidney they may be called nephrolithiasis, kidney stones, renal stones, or renal calculi.
Most urinary stones are composed of calcium oxalate and are more frequently found in males.
A staghorn calculus completely fills and takes the shape of the renal pelvis.
The most common site for a stone to lodge is the ureterovesicle junction near the bladder.
Other common impaction sites are just distal to the ureteropelvic junction and at the pelvic brim where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels.
Nonobstructing stones may be painless, but obstructing stones can cause hematuria, renal colic, oliguria, and urinary tract infection.
Men with renal colic may also have ipsilateral testicular pain.
Renal stones smaller than 5 mm may be difficult to visualize sonographically.
When visible, a stone appears as an echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing.
Color Doppler may show the twinkle sign, an increased color signal posterior to the stone.
Hydronephrosis and ureteral dilation may accompany obstructing stones, and distal ureteral stones may be better assessed with transvaginal or transperineal scanning.
Nephrocalcinosis is calcium deposition within the renal parenchyma and may be medullary or cortical.
Medullary nephrocalcinosis is commonly caused by hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia and may also occur with medullary sponge kidney.
Medullary sponge kidney is a congenital disorder with calcium in abnormally dilated collecting ducts of the medulla and appears as highly echogenic renal pyramids that may shadow.
Cortical nephrocalcinosis may be caused by hyperparathyroidism, AIDS, or some malignancies and appears as echogenic calculi within the cortex.
Benign Renal Masses: Angiomyolipoma is the most common benign renal tumor and consists of blood vessels, muscle, and fat; it is also called a renal hamartoma.
Most angiomyolipomas are unilateral, asymptomatic, and found incidentally in the general population.
Patients with tuberous sclerosis tend to have multiple bilateral angiomyolipomas.
If hemorrhage occurs within an angiomyolipoma, patients may present with pain, hematuria, and hypertension.
Classically, an angiomyolipoma appears as a solid echogenic renal mass.
Because of its high fat content, 20% to 30% of angiomyolipomas produce acoustic shadowing; this favors angiomyolipoma because RCC rarely shadows.
Oncocytoma is the second most common renal mass after angiomyolipoma and is often found in men in their 60s.
Oncocytomas are often asymptomatic but may cause pain or hematuria and can contain a stellate central scar from previous infarction.
Sonographically, oncocytomas may be isoechoic, hyperechoic, or hypoechoic and may contain a hypoechoic central scar, but they are difficult to distinguish from RCC.
Renal hemangioma is a benign vascular mass, often small and hyperechoic, usually asymptomatic unless hemorrhage causes pain and hematuria.
Renal lipoma is a benign fatty tumor usually found in women and appears as a well-circumscribed hyperechoic mass typically less than 5 mm.
Renal adenoma is a benign mass that can mimic RCC; it is often asymptomatic, may cause hematuria when larger, and usually measures less than 1 cm.
A renal adenoma appears as a vascular hyperechoic mass with internal calcifications that may produce acoustic shadowing.
Renal hematoma may follow blunt trauma, biopsy, surgery, or lithotripsy and presents with flank pain, abdominal pain, hematuria, and decreased hematocrit.
Hematomas have variable sonographic appearance depending on age and location; chronic hematomas may calcify and shadow, and renal fracture appears as a linear anechoic or hypoechoic defect.
Malignant Renal Masses: Renal cell carcinoma is a primary renal cancer arising from the renal tubular epithelium and may also be called hypernephroma or adenocarcinoma of the kidney.
Risk factors for RCC include smoking, hypertension, obesity, tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel–Lindau disease, and acquired renal cystic disease from long-term dialysis.
Symptoms often appear late and include flank pain, palpable mass, gross hematuria, weight loss, anorexia, and hypertension.
RCC may extend beyond the kidney and invade the renal vein and inferior vena cava as tumor thrombus.
Sonographic appearance of RCC is variable; it may be hypoechoic, isoechoic, hyperechoic, or even have a complex cystic appearance.
The ipsilateral renal vein and inferior vena cava should be carefully examined for tumor invasion when RCC is suspected.
Patients with RCC should also be evaluated for distant metastasis, including the contralateral kidney, liver, and other major organs.
Transitional cell carcinoma of the kidney is a malignant tumor most often located in the renal pelvis.
Like RCC, smoking increases the risk for renal transitional cell carcinoma.
TCC may produce gross hematuria and pain from obstruction and can cause focal dilation of the calices.
Small renal pelvic TCC lesions can be difficult to identify sonographically.
Larger TCC lesions usually appear as hypoechoic or isoechoic masses within the renal sinus, and varying degrees of hydronephrosis may be present.
Metastases to the kidneys most commonly arise from the lungs or breast, with prostate, pancreas, melanoma, and contralateral RCC occurring less often.
Renal metastases are usually solid masses that are hypoechoic or hyperechoic.
Lymphoma and leukemia may appear as multiple hypoechoic masses or bilateral renal enlargement with decreased overall echogenicity; lymphoma commonly affects both kidneys.
Renal Vascular Disease: Nutcracker syndrome is compression or entrapment of the left renal vein between the superior mesenteric artery and abdominal aorta.
Patients with nutcracker syndrome may present with proteinuria, hematuria, left-sided abdominal or flank pain, and pelvic pain.
Male patients may have left testicular pain and a left-sided varicocele.

Female patients may develop pelvic congestion syndrome with lower abdominal and back pain after prolonged standing, dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, abnormal uterine bleeding, chronic fatigue, and bowel issues.
Sonographically, nutcracker syndrome shows compression of the left renal vein with elevated pressure on Doppler evaluation; dilated pelvic veins may also be seen in females.
Renal artery stenosis is narrowing of the renal artery, most commonly from atherosclerosis.
Smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, and high blood pressure predispose patients to renal artery stenosis; fibromuscular disease may be the cause in younger women.
Patients with renal artery stenosis often have hypertension that does not respond to treatment.
Renal artery stenosis can lead to renal infarction and irreversible renal compromise.
Sonographic findings of renal artery stenosis include thickening and calcification of the renal artery.
A renal:aorta ratio greater than 3.5 supports the diagnosis of renal artery stenosis.
A tardus–parvus waveform distal to the stenosis may be present but is not always seen.
Renal vein thrombosis is clot within the renal vein and may be caused by renal tumors, trauma, infection, or occur after renal transplant.
Patients with renal vein thrombosis typically present with flank pain and hematuria.
Sonographically, the affected kidney may be enlarged and heterogeneous, the renal vein enlarged, and Doppler signals absent, although the thrombus itself may be difficult to visualize.
Renal Transplant: A transplanted kidney, or allograft, is usually placed in the right or left lower quadrant.
The donor renal artery and vein are typically anastomosed to the recipient external iliac artery and external iliac vein, and the donor ureter is attached to the bladder.
The donor kidney should appear sonographically similar to a normal kidney, and the native kidneys should also be examined.
Mild pelviectasis is considered a normal finding in the transplanted kidney.
Doppler and spectral analysis are required to assess transplant function and complications.
Interlobar artery spectral waveforms should be sampled in the upper, mid, and lower portions of the transplant kidney.
The main renal artery should be evaluated with color and spectral Doppler at the anastomosis and in the proximal and distal segments.
A normal transplant renal arterial waveform demonstrates low resistance with continuous diastolic flow.
Normal transplant resistive indices range from 0.6 to 0.8, whereas values greater than 0.9 are abnormal.
The renal vein should show continuous flow away from the kidney and may be evaluated at the iliac venous anastomosis.
Clinical signs of transplant rejection include anuria, oliguria, elevated creatinine and BUN, proteinuria, hypertension, and transplant enlargement.
Posttransplant fluid collections are common and may represent lymphocele, urinoma, hematoma, or abscess; sonographically they may appear echogenic, complex, or anechoic.
Complications include rejection, infection, obstruction, vascular stenosis, renal artery stenosis, renal artery thrombosis, renal vein thrombosis, pseudoaneurysm, and fistulas.

Renal artery stenosis is the most common vascular complication after transplant and is suggested by color aliasing, turbulence, PSV greater than 200 to 250 cm/s, and renal artery to external iliac ratio greater than 2.0 to 3.0.
Acute renal vein thrombosis in a transplant kidney is a surgical emergency requiring immediate correction to save the graft.
Pediatric Kidney: The most common cause of congenital hydronephrosis in infants and children is ureteropelvic junction obstruction.
Ureteropelvic junction obstruction may present with palpable abdominal mass, abdominal distention, and hematuria, and sonography shows a dilated collecting system without a visible distal ureter.
Vesicoureteral reflux is retrograde urine flow from the bladder into the ureter and possibly the kidney and is another cause of congenital hydronephrosis.
VUR is graded from I to V, progressing from reflux into the ureter only to severe hydronephrosis.
Posterior urethral valves are excessive urethral folds found only in males and cause dilation of the bladder, both ureters, and both renal collecting systems.
Prune belly syndrome is usually caused by megacystis from bladder outlet obstruction and is characterized by absent abdominal musculature, undescended testes, and urinary tract abnormalities.
Pediatric VUR is commonly due to an abnormal angle of insertion of the distal ureter at the ureterovesicle junction, creating a faulty valve.
Children with VUR may present with unexplained fever, irritability, flank pain, leukocytosis, bacteriuria, hematuria, dysuria, and urgency to void.
Sonography is not highly sensitive for VUR; minimal reflux may appear normal, whereas severe or chronic reflux may show hydroureter, hydronephrosis, renal scarring, and bladder debris.
Definitive evaluation of VUR may require voiding cystourethrogram or nuclear cystogram.
In duplicated systems, the Weigert–Meyer rule states the upper pole moiety is prone to obstruction from ectopic ureterocele, while the lower pole moiety is prone to reflux.
After subureteric Teflon injection treatment for VUR, the bulking agent appears as a hyperechoic focus at the vesicoureteral junction and may shadow.
Wilms tumor, or nephroblastoma, is the most common solid malignant pediatric abdominal mass and is usually discovered before age 5, with mean age 3.

Wilms tumor may invade the renal vein and inferior vena cava and metastasize to the liver and lungs; sonographically it is a large solid mostly echogenic mass that may contain anechoic or hypoechoic areas and may also be isoechoic.

Urachal anomalies result from failure of urachal closure and include patent urachus, urachal cyst, urachal sinus, and urachal diverticulum, seen as fluid-filled structures between the umbilicus and bladder apex.
Ureters: The ureters are paired muscular tubes that extend from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder.
The proximal connection of the ureter to the renal pelvis is the ureteropelvic junction.
The distal connection of the ureter to the urinary bladder is the ureterovesicle junction.
The ureters enter the bladder posteriorly at the superolateral margins of the trigone.
Their function is to propel urine from the kidneys to the bladder by peristalsis and gravity.
Normal ureters are usually not seen sonographically because of their small size.
When enlarged or distended with urine, ureters appear as anechoic tubular structures.
Whenever visualized, the ureters should be thoroughly assessed for obstruction.
Ureteral jets can be demonstrated with color Doppler over the inferoposterior bladder near the trigone and ureteral orifices.
Ureteral jets help prove ureteral patency in suspected obstruction.
Jets usually occur at least once every minute, although frequency varies with patient hydration.
A ureteral stone appears as an echogenic focus within the ureter with acoustic shadowing and usually causes proximal ureteral dilation.
Clinical findings of ureteral stones include renal colic, ipsilateral groin, labial, or testicular pain, and possible hematuria.

A ureterocele is a cystic dilation of the distal ureter entering the bladder, appears as an anechoic balloon-like structure near the ureterovesicle junction, and is often associated with duplicated systems.
Megaureter refers to congenital ureteral enlargement, whereas hydroureter is enlargement associated with reflux or obstruction; both appear as large anechoic tubular structures.
Urinary Bladder & Urethra: The urinary bladder is a retroperitoneal pelvic organ that serves as a reservoir for urine and lies posterior to the symphysis pubis.
In males, the bladder is superior to the prostate and anterior to the seminal vesicles; in females, it is anterior to the vagina, uterus, and rectum.
The bladder wall layers, from inner to outer, are mucosa, submucosa, muscularis, and serosa.
The detrusor muscle lies within the muscularis and controls proper emptying of the bladder.
The trigone lies at the bladder base and marks the openings of the urethra and both ureters.
A normal distended bladder appears smooth-walled and anechoic, square in transverse view and more elliptical in sagittal view.
The empty bladder normally has a thicker-appearing wall, while the fully distended bladder should have a thin wall.
A distended bladder wall measuring greater than 4 mm is considered thickened.
Bladder volume can be calculated sonographically using length × width × height × 0.56.

Neurogenic bladder results from neurologic dysfunction affecting the detrusor muscle and may show wall thickening, trabeculations, distention, excessive postvoid retention, and possible bladder stones.
A bladder diverticulum is an outpouching of the bladder wall; the neck should be demonstrated, and a Doppler jet may be seen at the neck.
Cystitis usually causes focal or diffuse hypoechoic bladder wall thickening greater than 4 mm and may show echogenic layering debris; chronic cystitis can cause scarring and trabeculation.

Bladder stones are echogenic mobile shadowing foci, whereas blood clots are echogenic nonshadowing masses that may be mobile or adherent; decubitus imaging helps distinguish mobile debris from wall masses.

Transitional cell carcinoma is the most common bladder malignancy and appears as a fixed smooth or papillary hypoechoic or hyperechoic vascular mass projecting into the lumen, unlike an avascular mobile clot.
The urethra begins at the trigone and ends at the urethral orifice; the male urethra is longer and part of it is surrounded by the prostate, so prostatic enlargement can cause obstruction.

Female urethral abnormalities that may be seen sonographically include urethral diverticulum and Skene duct cyst, and female urethra is better evaluated endovaginally, transperineally, or translabially than transabdominally.
